From readers with no coding experience to readers who want to implement deep learning themselves

AI Coding for Lawyers: A Self-Study Guide

A self-study guide that each reader takes by a different path. It starts from the development environment, Python, the debugger, AI coding assistants, and Git, and goes on to training pipelines, CNNs, Transformers, and language models. You run the book's code line by line, add comments to it, and rebuild it.

Edited by Bowon Kwon, Presiding Judge, Daegu District Court

Contents · Part 0 (introduction) + Part 1 (8 chapters) + Part 2 (17 chapters) + 5 appendices + colophon
Reading paths · A (from the start, [Basic]) · B (some Python experience, up to [Intermediate]) · C (some deep learning experience, mainly [Advanced]); see the self-check in Section 0.4
Practice · 59 Colab notebooks, chapter by chapter: github.com/BowonKwon/AI-Coding-for-Lawyers. The explanatory text in the notebooks is in Korean; their code is the same Korean-commented code as the listings in this book (the Add comments and Rebuild notebooks leave out comments or function bodies for you to fill in).
Listings · Code, commands, and program output are printed exactly as in the Korean edition, so comments and output labels in them are in Korean. A line beginning "In English:" under a listing gives their meaning.

Environment · Windows 11 · CPU · Python 3.13 · PyTorch 2.14 · measured September 6, 2026
Printing · Ctrl+P → Save as PDF prints the table of contents and the whole text (the contents rail on the left is left out).
Offline · Opens with this file and the fonts folder next to it.

Edition 1.0-en · November 18, 2026 · translated from Korean edition 1.0.1 · for the dates on which outside facts were checked, see "Sources and verification record" at the end of each chapter · text by the editor: CC BY-NC 4.0, practice code: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 · notes to the reader and the edition history are in the colophon at the end

These are personal study materials and do not represent the views or work of any institution the editor belongs to. Not legal advice.

Part 0

Part 0. How to read this book

0.1 Who this book is for

This book is a self-study guide to AI coding for lawyers. It is meant to serve, in one volume, readers who have never written a line of code and readers who have already written scripts in Python. Lawyers who set out to learn coding start from different places. So the part of the design that took the most work is the set of devices that let each reader take a different path through the book.

Reading alone and following along is the default. The book can be used as a course text, but it is written so that you can reach the end without a course. The code was actually run on the computer this book was written on, and its output is printed here as it came out (the few places that could not be run, such as cells that run only on Colab, are marked "not run"). If the same thing appears on your screen, you are on the right track.

0.2 What you will learn

The book has two parts.

Part 1, Coding with AI (Chapters 2 to 9). You set up a development environment, learn the minimum of Python syntax, read code with a debugger, and learn how to use AI coding tools while verifying them and how to manage changes with Git. The conclusion of Part 1 is that "coding in 2026 is more reading than writing," and it ends in Chapter 8 with reading one real piece of deep learning code. Chapter 9 is [Advanced]. It shows how to use VS Code on your own computer together with the GPU on Colab, so you can come back and read it when training starts to feel slow in Part 2.

Part 2, Implementing deep learning yourself (Chapters 10 to 26). After one lap around the training pipeline (Chapter 12), you go deeper by changing the ingredients one at a time. Images (CNN, ResNet, transfer learning), text (embeddings, RNN, Transformer), generation (language models), then how to turn an experiment into a claim (reproducibility), working with public language models, and showing the model you built.

What this book does not cover is also written down here. Building apps for legal work, processing data from real cases, the theoretical debate on AI and law. This book stops at building the technical footing on which that debate can be had.

0.3 Three devices

Reader markers

Each paragraph carries a marker. A paragraph with no marker is [Basic].

Marker Meaning Who reads it
[Basic] The main text that everyone reads Everyone
[Intermediate] Detail that a reader with Python experience can follow, or an explanation one level deeper If you have time
[Advanced] Principles, mathematics, alternative implementations When you are curious

The book is complete if you read only [Basic]. You can skip [Intermediate] and [Advanced] where they stand and come back later.

The three practice stages

Every chapter that has code repeats the same practice in three stages.

Stage What you do Intended reader
Follow along Read one line of the book's code with your eyes and type one line. No copying and pasting Basic
Add comments Write a comment in your own words on each line of the code you typed, then group the lines by idea and write a broader comment on each group Intermediate
Rebuild Restore the code from an empty file that keeps only the comments, and add one small variation Advanced

A Basic reader can aim for Follow along, an Intermediate reader for Add comments, and an Advanced reader for Rebuild. The comment skeleton you make here leads straight into "how to give instructions to AI" in Chapter 6.

Practice notebooks

The practice code and the notebooks for each chapter are collected in one repository. Its address is https://github.com/BowonKwon/AI-Coding-for-Lawyers. Each chapter has up to three notebooks, and they pair one to one with the three stages above.

Notebook What it contains
Follow along The book's code in order, together with the output from a run on the editor's computer. Cells that run only on Colab have no output, and every cell of the Chapter 2 notebook is of that kind
Add comments The code with the comments removed from the part you practice on. Write an explanation on each line, save, and run it to confirm that it still works
Rebuild The code with only the comments and function headers left and the bodies emptied. Fill in the empty places and run it. In chapters where the assignment is to add a feature, you copy the previous chapter's file and change it

Click the links under the "Three practice stages for this chapter" table in each chapter and the notebook opens in Google Colab. A Google account is all you need, and there is nothing to install. When you run the first cell, it fetches the repository and moves into that chapter's code folder.

The notebooks do not replace typing by hand. Use the Follow along notebook to compare when the output of the code you typed differs from the book, and to try things out before you finish the installation in Chapter 2. Chapter 5 (the debugger), Chapter 6 (AI coding assistants), and Chapter 7 (Git and GitHub) are practiced on your own computer, so they have no notebooks.

A note for this English edition. The explanatory text in the notebooks is in Korean. Their code is the same Korean-commented code as the listings in this book (the Add comments and Rebuild notebooks leave out comments or function bodies for you to fill in, as described above). The code listings, the commands, and the program output in this book are also printed exactly as in the Korean edition, so comments and output labels in them are in Korean. Where you need them to follow the text, a line beginning "In English:" under the listing gives their meaning.

How a chapter is organized

Every chapter runs in the same order. What you get from this chapter → who can skip this chapter → why it is needed → main text → where people get stuck → working with an AI assistant → check questions (by marker) → code-reading assignment (Part 2) → the three practice stages → further reading → sources and verification record. If every item on the "Who can skip this chapter" checklist is a "yes," you can do only the check questions for that chapter and move on.

0.4 Self-check: where to start

Answer the following ten questions. The number of "yes" answers decides your starting point.

  1. I have opened a terminal (Command Prompt) and moved between folders.
  2. I have created a Python file and run it.
  3. I can explain a for statement and a dictionary.
  4. I have defined a function and used import to bring it into another file.
  5. I know what class, self, and __init__ mean.
  6. I have set a breakpoint in a debugger and looked at variables.
  7. I have done a git commit.
  8. I can read torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]).
  9. I have written a training loop (zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → step).
  10. I have built a model by inheriting from nn.Module.
Number of "yes" answers Path Start
0 to 2 A. From the start From Chapter 2, in order. [Basic] only. Practice up to Follow along
3 to 7 B. Some Python experience In Chapter 2 (environment), only the check script → Chapter 5 (debugger) → Chapter 6 (AI) → Chapter 7 (Git) → Chapter 8 → Part 2. Up to [Intermediate]
8 to 10 C. Some deep learning experience Read Chapters 6 and 8, then go to Part 2. Pick what to read by each chapter's "Who can skip this chapter," and focus on [Advanced] and the code-reading assignments

A path is only a starting point. If you get stuck, go back to an earlier chapter, and if it is easy, skip ahead. The book is built to be read that way.

0.5 What you need

  • A personal computer (Windows 11 or macOS). You need administrator rights. The book does not assume a work PC (Chapter 2 explains why).
  • A Google account (for Colab and Drive) and a GitHub account (Chapter 7).
  • An internet connection. You download data and models (up to a few hundred MB).
  • Time. Allow 2 to 4 hours per chapter for Part 1 and 3 to 6 hours per chapter for Part 2. The whole book takes about three months at one weekend day a week, or about half a year at an hour a day. There is no reason to hurry.

0.6 Three principles of this book

The book says what was run and what was not. Every output is the result of an actual run, and anything that could not be run is marked "not run." The "Sources and verification record" at the end of each chapter says what was checked and how.

No material from real cases is used. The examples are invented cases, shapes drawn by a program, and statutory provisions, which are not protected by copyright. So that the invented cases do not overlap with real ones, the year in every case number is 2099 and the court is called the "Fictional District Court" (가상지방법원 in the code). Chapter 6 covers the reason and where the line is.

AI is a drafter, not a reviewer. The whole book teaches how to use AI tools while verifying them. From Chapter 3 on, the "Working with an AI assistant" section in every chapter is practice for that.

0.7 Why lawyers should read code

[Basic] Last, one point before you start this book. In 2026, AI writes the code. Should lawyers still read code?

[Basic] Yes, for two reasons. First, you can use AI only if you can judge the code AI writes. The measurement studies cited in Chapter 6 of this book report that a substantial share of AI-generated code has defects. If you cannot read it, you inherit those defects. Second, to understand the nature of AI output you need to know how it is made. When you build a language model yourself in Chapter 23, you will see that three things, "plausible is not the same as correct," "there is no source," and "the same input gives different outputs," are properties that come out of a few lines of code. For lawyers who will meet text written by AI as evidence, as reference material, and as drafts, those three are where judgment starts.

[Basic] A study that actually measured this question came out in March 2026. Researchers at ETH Zurich had 100 university students build and then revise small web applications in natural language alone, without being allowed to see or edit a single line of source code. This is what is now called "vibe coding." They then measured what predicted performance. Computer science achievement correlated with performance, and that correlation remained after controlling for general cognitive ability. Even under conditions where the code could not be seen at all, knowing code went together with performance.

[Intermediate] The figures are as follows. It is a preregistered cross-sectional study, and the sample is 100 students recruited from several universities in one metropolitan area (mean age 25.0, SD 3.5). The instruments are computer science achievement (SCS1), general cognition (ICAR16), writing (an essay), and three vibe coding tasks built by consensus among eight experts.

Predictor Simple correlation (r) After controlling for cognitive ability (partial r)
Computer science achievement 0.386 (p < .001) 0.281 (p = .005)
Writing proficiency 0.290 (p = .003) 0.186 (p = .066)
General cognitive ability 0.352 (p < .001) —

[Intermediate] Two points have to be read honestly. First, this is a cross-sectional correlational study, so it does not show causation. The authors say so themselves: "we do not wish to draw causal conclusions." Second, writing proficiency did not reach significance once cognitive ability was controlled for (p = .066). That is a tempting passage for lawyers, who write for a living, but this is as far as the data go.

[Intermediate] What this study does lend to this book lies in a limitation the authors wrote down themselves. Participants could not see the source, so computer science knowledge could act only indirectly (through how a problem is decomposed, through mental models of control flow), and the authors therefore wrote that "our estimates for the role of CS achievement in general LLM-augmented programming should be viewed as a lower bound." In an environment where the code can be read and edited, which is the environment this book is trying to take you to, the value would be larger. Of course the sample is Swiss university students, not lawyers, the setting is a controlled laboratory, and the writing instrument was used for the first time in this study. The limits on external validity remain as they are. (Thorgeirsson, Weidmann, and Su, CHI 2026, arXiv:2603.14133; see Appendix D)

[Basic] Lawyers do not write expert reports themselves but must be able to read and evaluate them. In the same way, this book aims at lawyers who can read and evaluate code. That aim is within reach if you follow the book to the end. Let's begin.

Part

Part 1. Coding with AI

Part 1

Chapter 2. Setting up the development environment

What you get from this chapter

  • You make a Python workspace (a virtual environment) on your computer and learn how to write and run code in it.
  • You understand what each of four tools, Anaconda, VS Code, Google Colab, and Google Drive, is for and how they connect to each other.
  • You create jucos, the environment in which every practice in this book runs, install PyTorch in it, and check it.

Who can skip this chapter If all four of the following are "yes," you can run only the check script in Section 2.6 and go on to Chapter 3.

  • [ ] I have made a virtual environment with conda create.
  • [ ] I have chosen an interpreter in VS Code.
  • [ ] I have turned on a GPU runtime in Colab and mounted Drive.
  • [ ] Google Drive for desktop is already installed.

2.0 Why start with setting up the environment

[Basic] The first place people learning to code get discouraged is not syntax but installation. Nine times out of ten, "I typed the example code exactly as it is and it doesn't run" is a problem with the environment, not the code. Which Python is running, whether the packages you need are installed in that Python, which folder the file is in. Get these three exactly right once at the start, and half the trial and error you would meet in later chapters goes away.

[Basic] To compare it with a lawyer's work: just as you check the case number, the parties, and jurisdiction before reviewing a case file, the goal of this chapter is the habit of checking "in which environment, in which folder" before you run code.

[Intermediate] If you have used Python, you may think, "Can't I just pip install?" The problem is that each project needs different package versions. When a version you upgraded for one project keeps breaking another project, you end up resetting the computer. A virtual environment is a device that isolates these conflicts project by project.

2.1 The big picture

[Basic] This book uses four tools. First look at what each one does in a figure.

Figure 2-1. The development environment of this book. Code and data are kept in a Google Drive folder; light work is done in VS Code on your computer, and training that needs a GPU is done by opening the same files in Colab and running them there.

Tool Role Comparison
Anaconda Manages Python itself and virtual environments A records room kept separately for each case
VS Code An editor for writing, running, and debugging code The desk
Google Colab Notebooks that run in the browser. Provides a free GPU A borrowed high-performance office
Google Drive File storage. Your computer and Colab see the same files The shared library stacks

[Basic] You may ask why you should work in two places (your computer and Colab) at all. Most of the practice in this book is fine on your computer's CPU, but models on the scale of Chapter 25, or larger, need a GPU for training to finish quickly. Most personal computers do not have such a GPU, and Colab lends one for free. On the other hand, debugging, where you read code while stopping it one line at a time (Chapter 5), is much easier in VS Code on your computer. So you use both. If the files are kept in Drive, they are the same files whichever side you open them from.

2.2 Before you start: two naming rules

[Basic] There are things to check before installing. They are hard to fix later, so they come first.

First, check that your Windows account name is in English letters. Open C:\Users\ in File Explorer. If the name of your account folder is in Korean or contains a space (for example, C:\Users\홍길동, C:\Users\Gil Dong), some tools cannot read the path and give errors that make no sense. In that case there are two ways to go.

  • Create a new local account with an English name and work in that account. (Recommended. Adding an account takes 10 minutes.)
  • Set the Anaconda installation path outside the account folder, such as C:\anaconda3. This does not avoid the account name problem completely, but it solves most of it.

On a Mac the account folder is usually in English, so this problem is rare.

Second, do not use spaces or Korean in the names of the folders and files you make from now on. Commands read a space as "the argument ends here," so a folder called 내 코드 ("my code") is mistaken for two, 내 and 코드. If you need a word break, use an underscore (_) or a hyphen (-). For example: ai_coding, week-01.

[Intermediate] Python itself handles Korean folder names well, but some C-based libraries and command-line tools trip over the encoding (the difference between CP949 and UTF-8). The time it takes to find the cause is much larger than the cost of naming things in English, so go with English from the start.

2.3 Installing Anaconda

2.3.1 What Anaconda is

[Basic] Python is a language, and Anaconda is "a bundle that packages that language for convenient use in data analysis and artificial intelligence." Python itself, several hundred commonly used packages, and conda, the tool that creates and manages virtual environments, come in with one installation. The July 2026 release (2026.07-1) contains Python 3.14.6 and conda 26.5.

[Note] Anaconda's terms, and why this book assumes a personal computer

Anaconda is free when an individual uses it for their own non-commercial purposes. Note that the requirement is not "your own computer": it is "non-commercial purpose" that is the requirement. The scope of free use narrowed after the 2024 revision of the terms, and the terms in effect from July 15, 2025 limit free use to four groups: ① individuals for non-commercial purposes, ② qualifying educational institutions, ③ qualifying non-profit and research institutions, ④ for-profit organizations with a total of 200 or fewer employees and contractors, including affiliates. For for-profit organizations with more than 200, the obligation to take a paid subscription is stated expressly. Government agencies are not named among those eligible for free use. This book assumes that you study on your own personal computer. If you want to install it on a work computer belonging to your organization, first check whether you fall under the requirements above.

The original text of the terms is at anaconda.com/legal, and the provisions can change, so if you are considering adoption at the level of an organization, you need to check the original text as it stands at that time.

[Alternative] Going without conda

[Intermediate] If Anaconda feels like a burden, there are two alternatives. Miniforge uses the same conda tool, but its default channel is a community repository (conda-forge), so you can avoid the paid subscription requirement of the Anaconda repository (the terms of use of individual packages and of channels you add later are separate). uv is a new tool unrelated to conda; a single executable handles installing Python, virtual environments, and installing packages, and it is very fast. This book goes with Anaconda for consistency of explanation, but the concepts of this chapter (virtual environments, installing packages, choosing the interpreter) apply as they are to both tools.

2.3.2 Installing on Windows

[Basic] Follow these steps in order.

  1. In your browser, go to anaconda.com/download. It may ask you to register an email address (if you see a skip link, you can click that). Download the Windows 64-Bit Graphical Installer.
  2. Run the downloaded file. Choose Just Me (Recommended). "All Users" needs administrator rights, and the setup afterward becomes complicated.
  3. Use the default installation path (C:\Users\<username>\anaconda3). If you found in Section 2.2 that your account name contains Korean, change it here to C:\anaconda3. The path must have no spaces or special characters.
  4. On the Advanced Installation Options screen:
    • "Create shortcuts": leave it on.
    • "Add Anaconda3 to my PATH environment variable": turn it off. If it is on, Python from other programs gets mixed in and causes problems whose cause is hard to find. Anaconda's own documentation does not recommend it either.
    • "Register Anaconda3 as my default Python": leave it on. It helps VS Code find Anaconda automatically.
    • "Clear the package cache upon completion": you may leave it on.
  5. When the installation is finished, find Anaconda Prompt in the Start menu and open it. If you see (base) in the black window, as in (base) C:\Users\<username>>, it worked.

[Basic] From now on, when this book says "open a terminal," on Windows it means this Anaconda Prompt. In the ordinary Command Prompt or PowerShell, the conda command may not work right away. At first, using only Anaconda Prompt is the way to get lost least.

2.3.3 Installing on a Mac

[Basic]

  1. At anaconda.com/download, download the 64-Bit (Apple silicon) Graphical Installer. Most Macs released since late 2020 are Apple silicon (M1 and later). For Intel Macs, new package builds stopped as of August 15, 2025 (only old installers remain), so if you have an Intel Mac, uv, in the [Alternative] box in Section 2.3.1, is recommended.

  2. Double-click the downloaded .pkg file and go on, agreeing to the Read Me and the license. The recommended choice on the installation scope screen is Install for all users of this computer (Recommended), and it installs to /opt/anaconda3. You enter the administrator password once.

    [Intermediate] The current graphical installer has no option to change the installation location to your home folder (the 2026.07-1 release notes record the removal of that option). To install in your home folder, you have to follow the official macOS command-line installation instructions.

  3. When the installation is finished, open Terminal (Launchpad → Other → Terminal). If you see (base) in front of the prompt, it worked.

[Intermediate] If you do not see (base), the installer was not able to touch your shell settings. In Terminal, run once whichever of the following matches your installation location, then close Terminal and open it again.

/opt/anaconda3/bin/conda init zsh     # 그래픽 설치기(권장값)로 설치한 경우
~/anaconda3/bin/conda init zsh        # 터미널 설치로 홈 폴더에 따로 설치한 경우

In English: 그래픽 설치기(권장값)로 설치한 경우 = if you installed with the graphical installer (recommended choice); 터미널 설치로 홈 폴더에 따로 설치한 경우 = if you installed separately in your home folder with the command-line installation.

2.3.4 Checking the installation

[Basic] In the terminal (Anaconda Prompt or Mac Terminal), type the following two lines one after the other, pressing Enter after each.

conda --version
python --version

If you get versions such as conda 26.x.x and Python 3.14.x, you are done. It is fine if the numbers differ a little.

2.4 Creating a virtual environment

2.4.1 What a virtual environment is

[Basic] What is now shown as (base) is Anaconda's base environment. You could install packages straight into it, but you will not. Instead, you create one environment just for this book.

A virtual environment is a folder that keeps one copy of Python and a set of packages separately for each project. Just as you keep a separate file for each case, you keep a separate environment for each project. Then

  • the package versions needed for this book's practice do not clash with other projects,
  • when something gets tangled, you need only delete one environment and create it again, and
  • you can reproduce the same environment exactly on another computer.

2.4.2 Six commands

[Basic] There are many conda commands, but this book uses only six. Type them in the terminal in order.

# 1) 환경 만들기: 이름은 jucos, 파이썬 3.13
conda create -n jucos python=3.13

# 2) 환경 켜기 (프롬프트 앞이 (base)에서 (jucos)로 바뀝니다)
conda activate jucos

# 3) 지금 어떤 환경들이 있는지 보기 (* 표시가 현재 환경)
conda env list

# 4) 이 환경에 설치된 패키지 보기
conda list

# 5) 환경 끄기 (다시 (base)로)
conda deactivate

# 6) 환경 지우기 (잘못 만들었을 때. 지금은 실행하지 마세요)
conda remove -n jucos --all

In English: 1) 환경 만들기: 이름은 jucos, 파이썬 3.13 = create the environment: the name is jucos, Python 3.13; 2) 환경 켜기 (프롬프트 앞이 (base)에서 (jucos)로 바뀝니다) = turn the environment on (the front of the prompt changes from (base) to (jucos)); 3) 지금 어떤 환경들이 있는지 보기 (* 표시가 현재 환경) = see which environments exist now (the * marks the current environment); 4) 이 환경에 설치된 패키지 보기 = see the packages installed in this environment; 5) 환경 끄기 (다시 (base)로) = turn the environment off (back to (base)); 6) 환경 지우기 (잘못 만들었을 때. 지금은 실행하지 마세요) = delete the environment (when you made it wrongly; do not run this now).

When you run conda create, it shows the list of packages to be installed and asks Proceed ([y]/n)?. Type y and press Enter. It takes 1 to 3 minutes.

[Basic] Why Python 3.13 and not 3.14? Anaconda's base environment uses 3.14, but packages related to deep learning take months to support a new Python. The code in this book was run and checked on 3.13 in September 2026. As of November 2026 the latest Python is 3.15 and 3.13 is at the stage of receiving only security fixes, but to see the same results as the book's output it is safer to stay on the same 3.13. Upgrading later is a one-line command.

[Intermediate] -n is short for --name. Do not use spaces or Korean in an environment name. The environment is created in the folder anaconda3/envs/jucos, and conda env list shows that path. This path is the location of the "interpreter" that you will tell VS Code about in Section 2.5.

2.4.3 What it means for an environment to be on

[Basic] When you run conda activate jucos, the prompt changes to (jucos). In this state, typing python runs the Python of the jucos environment, and pip install installs packages into the jucos environment. If you install while the prompt is still (base), they go to the wrong place, and later you get an error along the lines of "I definitely installed it, but it can't be found." The habit of looking at the parentheses in front of the prompt before typing a command is the most important habit in this chapter.

[Advanced] Activation is in fact the act of inserting that environment's folder at the very front of the environment variable PATH. That is why the same name, python, comes to point to a different file. You can see which file is being run right now with where python (Windows) or which python (Mac).

2.5 Installing VS Code and connecting the environment

2.5.1 What VS Code is

[Basic] Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is a free code editor made by Microsoft. You can write Python files in it, run them on the spot, look through them while stopping one line at a time (debug), and later even attach AI coding assistants. All the practice in Part 1 of this book is done in VS Code.

2.5.2 Installation

[Basic]

  1. At code.visualstudio.com, download the installer for your operating system and run it. On Windows, if there is an "Add to PATH" item during installation, leave it on (unlike with Anaconda, turning this on causes no problems, and you need it later to open VS Code from the terminal with code .).
  2. Open VS Code and click the icon of four squares (Extensions) in the vertical menu on the left. Type Python in the search box and install the Python extension made by Microsoft. Pylance (code assistance) and Python Debugger are installed with it. If you also see a separate Python Environments (Microsoft) extension in the list, install that too. You use it in Section 2.5.4 to choose the environment.
  3. In the same way, install the Jupyter extension (Microsoft) too. You need it to open notebook files (.ipynb) in VS Code.

[Intermediate] If you want the display in Korean, installing the Korean Language Pack extension changes the menus to Korean. This book, however, uses the English menu names, for ease of searching and troubleshooting.

2.5.3 Opening a working folder

[Basic] VS Code uses "one folder," not "one file," as its unit of work.

  1. Make an ai_coding folder inside the Google Drive you will install in Section 2.8, or for now, temporarily, inside your Documents folder. (Remember the naming rule? No spaces, no Korean.)
  2. Open that folder from the VS Code menu with File → Open Folder…. When it asks whether you trust the authors of this folder, click Yes, I trust the authors.
  3. In the Explorer on the left, click the new file icon, create hello.py, and write the following one line.
print("환경 구축 중입니다")

In English: "환경 구축 중입니다" = "Setting up the environment."

2.5.4 Choosing the interpreter: the key operation of this chapter

[Basic] VS Code needs to know which of the several Pythons on your computer to run with. This is called "choosing the interpreter."

  1. Press Ctrl+Shift+P (on a Mac, Cmd+Shift+P) to open the Command Palette.
  2. Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.
  3. From the list, choose the item that contains jucos (for example, Python 3.13.x ('jucos')).
  4. If you see 3.13.x ('jucos') in the status bar at the bottom right of the window, you are done. You can also change it by clicking this indicator.

[Basic] Now, with hello.py open, click the ▶ (Run Python File) button at the top right. If "환경 구축 중입니다" is printed in the terminal pane below, VS Code ran this file with the Python of the jucos environment. Also check whether (jucos) is attached in front of the terminal prompt. Once you choose an interpreter, the Python extension turns that environment on automatically in new terminals.

[Intermediate] If you open the Python view (the Python Environments extension), which has the Python logo in the vertical menu on the left, you see all the environments on your computer arranged by manager (Conda, venv, and so on). You can also create environments and install packages here. The extension finds environments by running conda info --envs, so if you installed Anaconda in the standard location they are picked up automatically. If they do not appear, click the refresh icon (Refresh All Environment Managers) at the top of the view.

2.6 Installing PyTorch and the final check

2.6.1 Why use pip inside a conda environment

[Basic] Part 2 of this book uses a deep learning library called PyTorch. You install it in the terminal. First check that the prompt is (jucos), then:

pip install torch torchvision

It downloads several hundred MB, so it takes a few minutes.

[Intermediate] "It's a conda environment, so why pip install and not conda install?" Good question. The PyTorch developers stopped distributing through their own conda channel in late 2024 (2.5 was the last), and since then the official installation route is pip. Using pip inside a conda environment is perfectly normal: conda takes care of the environment (isolation) and pip puts packages into it. Do avoid, however, installing the same package in one environment alternately with conda and pip.

[Intermediate] The command above is for computers without a GPU (the CPU version). If you have a Windows PC with an NVIDIA GPU, you could use the command for your CUDA version chosen on the "Get Started" page of pytorch.org, but this book does its GPU practice on Colab, so the CPU version is enough for now.

2.6.2 The check script

[Basic] Create a file check_env.py in the ai_coding folder and type the following exactly as it is (this is the chapter's Follow along file).

# 2장 확인 스크립트: 지금 실행 중인 파이썬이 어느 환경의 것인지, PyTorch가 잘 설치됐는지 확인합니다.
# 실행: (jucos) 환경에서  python check_env.py

import sys          # 파이썬 실행 파일의 위치와 버전을 알려 주는 표준 모듈
import platform     # 운영체제 정보를 알려 주는 표준 모듈

print("파이썬 버전 :", sys.version.split()[0])
print("실행 파일   :", sys.executable)      # 경로에 'jucos'가 보여야 우리 환경입니다
print("운영체제    :", platform.system(), platform.release())

try:
    import torch                             # PyTorch 불러오기
    print("PyTorch 버전:", torch.__version__)
    print("GPU 사용 가능:", torch.cuda.is_available())  # 개인 PC는 대개 False. 정상입니다.
    x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
    print("텐서 연산 확인:", (x @ x).tolist())          # 행렬 곱 한 번
except ImportError:
    print("PyTorch가 아직 설치되지 않았습니다. 2.6절의 pip 명령을 먼저 실행하세요.")

In English: the first comment = "Chapter 2 check script: checks which environment the Python now running belongs to and whether PyTorch was installed properly"; 실행: (jucos) 환경에서 = run it: in the (jucos) environment; 파이썬 버전 = Python version; 실행 파일 = executable, with the comment "if the path shows 'jucos', it is our environment"; 운영체제 = operating system; PyTorch 버전 = PyTorch version; GPU 사용 가능 = GPU available, with the comment "usually False on a personal PC; this is normal"; 텐서 연산 확인 = tensor operation check (one matrix multiplication); the last message = "PyTorch is not installed yet. Run the pip command in Section 2.6 first."

Click ▶ in VS Code, or type python check_env.py in the terminal. If you get something like the following, you have reached the goal of this chapter.

파이썬 버전 : 3.13.15
실행 파일   : C:\Users\<계정명>\anaconda3\envs\jucos\python.exe
운영체제    : Windows 11
PyTorch 버전: 2.14.0+cpu
GPU 사용 가능: False
텐서 연산 확인: [[7.0, 10.0], [15.0, 22.0]]

In English: the labels are those glossed under the script above; <계정명> = your username.

(This is the actual output, on 2026-09-06, of a jucos environment made by this book's procedure on Windows 11. On a Mac the executable path ends in …/anaconda3/envs/jucos/bin/python (the front part depends on where Anaconda is installed) and the operating system line shows Darwin.)

[Basic] There are three lines to check. Does the executable path contain jucos? Is a PyTorch version printed? Is the tensor operation check [[7.0, 10.0], [15.0, 22.0]]? GPU available being False is normal on a personal computer.

2.7 Google Colab

2.7.1 What Colab is

[Basic] Colab (Colaboratory) is a Python notebook from Google that runs in the browser. There is nothing to install, a Google account is all you need, and it lends you a GPU for free. In Google's own description, it is a hosted Jupyter notebook service that needs no setup and provides computing resources, including GPUs and TPUs, free of charge.

[Basic] To explain briefly what a notebook is: it is a document format in which you write code in small boxes called "cells," run them one at a time, and see the result right below. Explanatory text, code, and results are mixed in one document, which makes it good for learning. The practice notebooks for each chapter of this book are in this format too.

2.7.2 Your first notebook and turning on the GPU

[Basic]

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with your Google account. Click New notebook.
  2. Write print("Colab입니다") ("This is Colab") in the first cell and press Shift+Enter. The first time, the result appears after about 10 seconds spent connecting to a runtime.
  3. To turn on the GPU, in the menu Runtime → Change runtime type, change Hardware accelerator to a GPU (T4 or similar) and save. The runtime restarts.
  4. Put the following in a cell and run it to see whether the GPU has been picked up.
import torch
print(torch.cuda.is_available())        # True면 GPU가 켜진 것
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))    # 예: Tesla T4

In English: True면 GPU가 켜진 것 = True means the GPU is on; 예: Tesla T4 = for example, Tesla T4.

Colab already has PyTorch installed, so you do not need pip install.

[Basic] Free use comes with conditions. Google does not publish the exact limits (it says that usage limits fluctuate from time to time), but a free notebook lasts at most 12 hours, a GPU is not guaranteed, and it disconnects if there is no activity for a while. The practice in Part 2 is built to run well within these bounds.

[Intermediate] If you need longer runs or a better GPU, there are paid plans. As of the pricing page (colab.research.google.com/signup) on September 6, 2026, they are as follows. A "compute unit" is the unit that measures GPU usage; how many are used per hour differs by GPU type, and units you buy expire after 90 days.

Plan Price What you get
Free 0 No GPU guarantee, sessions up to 12 hours
Pay As You Go USD 9.99 for 100 units / USD 49.99 for 500 units Buy as much as you need, without a subscription
Colab Pro USD 9.99 a month 100 units every month
Colab Pro+ USD 49.99 a month Pro benefits plus 500 units every month; continuous runs up to 24 hours if you have enough compute units (FAQ)

If you subscribe to an eligible plan among Google's paid AI plans, Colab compute units are included in it every month as well (Colab FAQ, checked 2026-11-17). Plans that only add storage are not eligible, and the benefits differ from plan to plan. Prices change, so check the page again before you pay. You do not need a paid plan to finish this book.

2.7.3 Connecting (mounting) Drive

[Basic] A Colab runtime is a temporary space whose files disappear when the session ends. So you keep files in Google Drive and "attach" Drive from the notebook. Put the following in a cell and run it.

from google.colab import drive
drive.mount('/content/drive')

When a window asks for permission, allow it. If you click the folder icon on the left, the files in your Drive appear under drive/MyDrive. Now you can read and write files using paths like /content/drive/MyDrive/ai_coding/.

[Intermediate] If there are thousands of files in the Drive root, mounting and listing become slow. Google advises not keeping about 10,000 or more items in the root folder. Gather your practice files in a subfolder such as ai_coding.

2.8 Google Drive for desktop

2.8.1 Why you need it

[Basic] In Section 2.7, Colab read files from Drive. To open those same files in VS Code on your computer, Drive has to appear as a folder on your computer. That is what Google Drive for desktop (Drive for desktop) does. Once installed, Google Drive appears as a new drive letter on Windows (for example, G:) and in the list of locations in Finder on a Mac, and 내 드라이브(My Drive) inside it is synced with the cloud automatically.

2.8.2 Installation

[Basic]

  1. At google.com/drive/download, download GoogleDriveSetup.exe for Windows or GoogleDrive.dmg for a Mac, and run it.
  2. On first launch, sign in to your Google account with Get started → Sign in.
  3. Check that a Google Drive item has appeared in File Explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac).
  4. Move the ai_coding folder you made in Section 2.5.3 into 내 드라이브. Now open the folder again from this location in VS Code with File → Open Folder….

2.8.3 Streaming and mirroring

[Intermediate] Drive for desktop works in two ways. With Stream files (streaming), files stay in the cloud and are downloaded only when opened, so it uses almost no disk space. With Mirror files (mirroring), a copy of every file is kept on your computer, so files open even offline. To save disk space, choose streaming; if you always work offline or often write to large files, consider mirroring. You can also use streaming while marking only the files you need as available offline. You change the setting from the Drive for desktop icon → Settings → Preferences → Folders from Drive → "My Drive syncing options".

[Intermediate] Code files are small, so either way is fine, but for folders that handle data or video of several hundred MB, mirroring is safer. If you read large files one after another while streaming, the downloads cannot keep up and you get errors where the file "is there but will not open." The same thing happened while this book was being made.

2.9 Reproducing and sharing the environment

[Intermediate] Once the environment is set up well, leave its "specification" in a file. You use it to make the same environment again when you change computers or when the environment gets tangled.

# 내가 직접 설치한 패키지만 기록 (권장)
conda env export --from-history > environment.yml

# 그 파일로 같은 환경을 다시 만들기
conda env create -f environment.yml

In English: 내가 직접 설치한 패키지만 기록 (권장) = record only the packages I installed myself (recommended); 그 파일로 같은 환경을 다시 만들기 = make the same environment again from that file.

[Intermediate] The reason to add --from-history is that without it, hundreds of lines of lower-level dependencies that vary by operating system are recorded, and that makes it more likely to fail on another computer. Packages installed with pip (PyTorch and so on) are not picked up in this file automatically, so add a pip entry by hand or keep a separate requirements.txt alongside it.

pip freeze > requirements.txt          # pip 패키지 목록 저장
pip install -r requirements.txt        # 그 목록대로 설치

In English: pip 패키지 목록 저장 = save the list of pip packages; 그 목록대로 설치 = install according to that list.

[Advanced] If full reproduction is the goal, container technology such as Docker is the next step. It is outside the scope of this book, but Chapter 24 (experiment records and reproducibility) comes back to "what has to be recorded for someone else to reproduce it."

Where people get stuck

[Basic] These are the places where people actually get stuck most in this chapter. They are written in the order symptom → cause → fix.

Symptom Cause Fix
You type conda and get "command not found" You opened the ordinary Command Prompt or PowerShell On Windows, open Anaconda Prompt. On a Mac, restart Terminal after conda init zsh
pip install worked, but import torch fails in VS Code The environment you installed into differs from the interpreter VS Code chose Check that (jucos) in the prompt matches ('jucos') in the status bar. Do Section 2.5.4 again
conda activate says the shell has not been initialized conda is not connected to this shell Use Anaconda Prompt, or run conda init and restart the terminal
Strange errors because the installation path or account name has Korean or spaces Section 2.2 Create a new account with an English name, or install to C:\anaconda3
torch.cuda.is_available() is False on Colab The runtime type is CPU Runtime → Change runtime type → choose GPU, then run again
Colab disconnects suddenly Idle timeout or the 12-hour limit Put in code that saves training results to Drive (Chapter 13)
Files do not appear after mounting Drive Signed in with a different Google account Check that the Colab account and the Drive account are the same
conda create is very slow or stops Network or package resolution Wait a while and try again. If it keeps happening, try again after conda clean --all

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] You cannot ask AI to "do it for you" for the work in this chapter. Installation has to be done on your own computer, with your own hands. Instead, AI is a great help in interpreting error messages. When you get an error, copy the whole message and ask like this.

On Windows 11, I ran conda activate jucos in Anaconda Prompt and got the message below. Tell me the cause and the steps to fix it, in order. (paste the message)

[Basic] And do not forget verification. Ask what a command that AI gave you does, even in one line (for example, "What does conda init change?"), and run commands that change the system (init, remove, --all, rm) only after you understand what they mean. The installation methods AI suggests are sometimes out of date because they mix in material from before 2024. For example, an answer telling you to "run conda install pytorch -c pytorch" is wrong advice as of 2026 (Section 2.6.1).

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. If you run pip install torch while (base) is shown in front of the prompt, where does it get installed? What happens in VS Code's jucos environment as a result?
  2. Explain in one sentence why the executable line in the output of check_env.py matters.
  3. Write down the menu path for turning on the GPU in Colab.

[Intermediate]

  1. Why do you install PyTorch with pip inside a conda environment?
  2. Why do you add --from-history to conda env export, and what is left out of that file?

[Advanced]

  1. What does conda activate actually change? Check for yourself how the output of where python (or which python) differs before and after activation, and explain it.
  2. Make a table of what the three tools Anaconda, Miniforge, and uv have in common and how they differ in the way they create a "virtual environment."

Stage What to do
Follow along Type the six commands of Section 2.4.2 and check_env.py from Section 2.6.2 exactly as they are, and run them
Add comments Next to each command, write one line in your own words on "what this command changes"
Rebuild Close the book, create an environment called jucos2 from an empty terminal, install PyTorch, pass the check script, and then delete it

Part 1

Chapter 3. Python basics I: values, collections, flow

What you get from this chapter

  • You get a feel for the fact that Python code runs "from top to bottom, one line at a time," and you learn how to read error messages.
  • You read and write small programs with three kinds of building blocks: values (numbers, text, true or false), collections (lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets), and flow (conditions, loops).
  • You follow along to the end as you build a 30-line program that tallies a list of invented cases. It is a miniature of all the code you will meet in Part 2.

Who can skip this chapter If all of the following are "yes," you can read the comprehensive example in Section 3.11, do only the [Intermediate] check questions, and go on to Chapter 4.

  • [ ] I can read at once what for r in records: total += r["claim"] does.
  • [ ] I can explain the difference between a list and a dictionary.
  • [ ] I know when IndexError and KeyError occur.

3.0 Why learn syntax when AI writes the code

[Basic] Let's start with an honest question. In 2026, if you tell AI, "Write code that picks out only the damages cases from a case list and totals the amount claimed," the code comes out right away. Should you still learn syntax?

[Basic] You should. But the purpose has changed. Before, you learned it in order to write; now you learn it in order to read. To judge whether the code AI gave you really does what you asked, whether it has left out a condition, whether it is adding up amounts as text, you have to be able to read code. It is the same as with an expert report: a lawyer does not write one, but must be able to read and evaluate it.

[Basic] This chapter covers the minimum you need for that "reading." It is not the whole of Python syntax. Only what actually appears in the deep learning code of Part 2 was chosen. Three kinds of values, four kinds of collections, two kinds of flow. With these nine, you can read 80 percent of the code in Part 2.

3.1 Three ways to run Python

[Basic] With the environment you built in Chapter 2, there are three ways to run Python.

Way When to use it In this book
Running a file: make a .py file, then press ▶ or type python filename.py When building a program The default in Part 1
Interactive (REPL): type just python in the terminal, >>> appears, and each line runs right away When trying out a single line For checking
Notebook cells: .ipynb in Colab or VS Code Step by step, watching the results The default in Part 2

[Basic] The examples in this chapter are run as files. Inside the ai_coding folder you made in Chapter 2, make a ch03 folder, create and save one file for each example, and press ▶. To leave interactive mode, press Ctrl+Z and then Enter (Windows), or Ctrl+D (Mac).

3.2 Your first program and reading errors

[Basic] Type the following into the file p01_print_and_errors.py and run it.

# 3.2 첫 프로그램: print, 주석, 실행 순서
# 위에서 아래로 한 줄씩 실행됩니다.

print("안녕하세요")            # 화면에 글자를 보여 주는 함수
print("두 번째 줄입니다")      # 이 줄은 위 줄이 끝난 뒤에 실행됩니다
# 이 줄은 주석입니다. 파이썬은 # 뒤를 읽지 않습니다.
print(3 + 4)                   # 따옴표가 없으면 계산합니다
print("3 + 4")                 # 따옴표가 있으면 글자 그대로 보여 줍니다
print("사건번호:", "2099가합1234")   # 쉼표로 여러 개를 이어서 보여 줄 수 있습니다

안녕하세요
두 번째 줄입니다
7
3 + 4
사건번호: 2099가합1234

In English: 안녕하세요 = hello; 두 번째 줄입니다 = this is the second line; 사건번호 = case number; 2099가합1234 = an invented case number: year 2099, case-type code 가합 (gahap, a first-instance civil case before a panel of judges), serial 1234.

[Basic] Check three things. First, execution runs from top to bottom, one line at a time. Second, what comes after # is a comment and is not run. A comment is a note for people, and stage 2 of this book's practice ("Add comments") is exactly practice in writing them. Third, whether there are quotation marks or not decides between "calculation" and "text."

Error messages are there to be read

[Basic] Now make a mistake on purpose. Add the line print(claim) at the very bottom of the file and run it. Red text appears.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...\p01_print_and_errors.py", line 10, in <module>
    print(claim)
          ^^^^^
NameError: name 'claim' is not defined

[Basic] It is frightening at first, but an error message is a helpful diagnosis written by Python. You read it from the bottom up.

  1. The last line is the conclusion. NameError: name 'claim' is not defined: "the name claim has never been defined." In other words, you used a variable you never made.
  2. The line 10 above it is the location. Line 10 of the file.
  3. The ^^^^^ marks point to exactly where in that line the problem is.

[Basic] Reading just these three is enough to fix most errors yourself. If you cannot fix it, copy the whole message and ask AI; that is this chapter's "Working with an AI assistant" box. Six errors you will see often are collected, with their actual messages, in "Where people get stuck" at the end of the chapter.

3.3 Variables and data types: giving values names

[Basic] A variable is a name tag attached to a value. claim = 350000000 means "I will call the value 350000000 claim." It is not the equals sign of mathematics. It means put the value on the right into the name on the left. That is why a statement like claim = claim + 10000000 works: it computes the right side first and puts the result back into the name on the left.

[Basic] Values come in kinds (data types). This chapter needs four.

Data type Meaning Example
str (string) Text. Wrapped in quotation marks "2099가합1234"
int (integer) A number with no decimal point 350000000
float (floating-point number) A number with a decimal point 0.05
bool (Boolean) One of two values, true or false True, False

p02_variables.py:

# 3.3 변수와 자료형

case_no = "2099가합1234"      # 문자열(str): 따옴표로 감싼 글자
claim = 350000000             # 정수(int): 청구금액 3억 5천만 원
rate = 0.05                   # 실수(float): 연 이율 5%
is_final = False              # 불리언(bool): 확정 여부. True 또는 False만 가능

print(case_no, claim, rate, is_final)
print(type(case_no), type(claim), type(rate), type(is_final))

# 계산과 갱신
interest = claim * rate       # 1년치 이자
print("1년 이자:", interest)
claim = claim + 10000000      # 변수는 다시 채울 수 있습니다 (청구취지 확장)
print("확장 후 청구금액:", claim)

# 형 변환
amount_text = "1200000"       # 서류에서 읽어 온 금액은 글자입니다
print(amount_text + "원")     # 글자끼리는 이어 붙습니다
print(int(amount_text) + 1)   # 숫자로 바꿔야 계산됩니다
print(str(claim) + "원")      # 숫자를 글자로

# f-string: 글자 안에 변수 값을 끼워 넣기
print(f"{case_no} 사건의 청구금액은 {claim:,}원, 이자는 {interest:,.0f}원입니다.")

2099가합1234 350000000 0.05 False
<class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'>
1년 이자: 17500000.0
확장 후 청구금액: 360000000
1200000원
1200001
360000000원
2099가합1234 사건의 청구금액은 360,000,000원, 이자는 17,500,000원입니다.

In English: 1년 이자 = interest for one year; 확장 후 청구금액 = amount claimed after the claim is expanded; 원 = won (the Korean currency unit); "2099가합1234 사건의 청구금액은 …원, 이자는 …원입니다." = "The amount claimed in case 2099가합1234 is … won, and the interest is … won."

[Basic] The place to look closely is type conversion. "1200000", read from a document or a file, looks like a number but is text. Adding + "원" (the currency unit, won) to text joins the two, and to turn it into a number you have to wrap it in int(). When you read data in Part 2, missing this distinction is the cause of "why is the total strange?" You can check the kind at any time with type().

[Basic] The f-string on the last line is a way to put {variable} inside text. You put f in front of the quotation mark. {claim:,} is a thousands separator, and {interest:,.0f} is a format that says to insert commas and drop the digits after the decimal point. It is the tool you use most often when printing results so that people can read them easily.

[Intermediate] Variable names are made of lowercase English letters, with the _ character between words (case_no, total_claim). Python also allows Korean variable names, but we do not use them, for the same reason as the folder-naming rule in Chapter 2. A name should show what the value is. claim and rate instead of a, x, tmp. Later, when you have AI explain code, good names also make the explanation accurate.

[Intermediate] interest comes out with a decimal point, as 17500000.0, because the result of an integer × a floating-point number is a floating-point number. If you want only an integer, use int(interest) or round(interest).

3.4 Working with strings

[Basic] Legal data is mostly text. Case numbers, parties, the gist of judgments. So you often cut, search, and replace strings. p03_strings.py:

# 3.4 문자열 다루기

case_no = "2099가합1234"

# 인덱싱: 0부터 셉니다
print(case_no[0])        # 첫 글자
print(case_no[-1])       # 마지막 글자

# 슬라이싱: [시작:끝]  끝은 포함하지 않습니다
year = case_no[:4]       # 0,1,2,3번 글자
code = case_no[4:6]      # 4,5번 글자
number = case_no[6:]     # 6번부터 끝까지
print(year, code, number)

# 자주 쓰는 메서드
title = "  손해배상(기)  "
print(title.strip())                  # 양쪽 공백 제거
print("2099가합1234".startswith("2099"))  # 앞부분 확인
print("원고, 피고, 참가인".split(", "))  # 쉼표로 나누어 리스트로
print("가합".replace("합", "단"))       # 바꾸기
print(len(case_no))                   # 글자 수

# 검색과 포함
print("합" in case_no)   # 포함 여부는 True/False
print(case_no.find("합"))  # 위치(없으면 -1)

2
4
2099 가합 1234
손해배상(기)
True
['원고', '피고', '참가인']
가단
10
True
5

In English: 손해배상(기) = a case name, damages (other); 원고 = plaintiff; 피고 = defendant; 참가인 = intervenor; 가단 = the case-type code gadan (a first-instance civil case before a single judge), made here by replacing 합 with 단.

[Basic] Python counts from 0. case_no[0] is the first character, 2, and case_no[-1] is the first character from the end, 4. The slice [4:6] is positions 4 and 5; that is, the end position is not included. Everyone is confused by this rule at first, but if you memorize "the start is included, the end is excluded," a convenience comes with it: joining [:4] and [4:] gives you the original.

[Basic] Things attached after a dot, such as .strip() and .split(), are called methods. They are "actions that value can perform." "원고, 피고, 참가인".split(", ") (plaintiff, defendant, intervenor) cuts the text at the commas and makes it into a list (Section 3.5). You use it just like this when you pull a list of parties out of a document.

[Intermediate] For text with a fixed format such as a case number, pulling out the year, the code, and the number by cutting at fixed positions, as above, breaks when the length of the code changes (가합 and 카합 are two characters, but 재가합, the code for a retrial of a gahap case, is three). When the formats vary, use regular expressions (Chapter 4 [Advanced]). For now, just learn the principle.

3.5 Lists: collections with an order

[Basic] When there are several values, you need a collection. The most basic one is the list. You line values up inside square brackets [ ], separated by commas. It has an order, and it can be changed. The first part of p04_collections.py:

# ---- 리스트: 순서가 있고 바꿀 수 있는 묶음
parties = ["원고", "피고"]
parties.append("보조참가인")          # 끝에 추가
print(parties, len(parties))
print(parties[0], parties[-1])        # 첫째, 마지막
print(parties[1:])                    # 둘째부터 끝까지
parties[1] = "피고 주식회사 가나"      # 바꾸기
print(parties)
print("원고" in parties)              # 포함 여부

amounts = [3000, 1200, 5400, 800]
print(sorted(amounts))                # 정렬한 새 리스트 (원본은 그대로)
print(sum(amounts), max(amounts), min(amounts))

['원고', '피고', '보조참가인'] 3
원고 보조참가인
['피고', '보조참가인']
['원고', '피고 주식회사 가나', '보조참가인']
True
[800, 1200, 3000, 5400]
10400 5400 800

In English: 원고 = plaintiff; 피고 = defendant; 보조참가인 = supporting intervenor; 피고 주식회사 가나 = defendant Gana Co., Ltd. (an invented company).

[Basic] The indexing, slicing, in, and len() you learned with strings work the same way on lists. That is because Python uses one syntax for handling "things that have an order." What is new is .append() (add at the end), sorted() (sort), and sum(), max(), min().

[Intermediate] sorted(amounts) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original as it is. By contrast, amounts.sort() sorts the original in place and returns nothing (None). If you write x = amounts.sort(), x becomes None. This is a trap beginners often fall into, so remember it.

3.6 Tuples: collections that cannot be changed

[Basic] A tuple is a list made with parentheses ( ) that cannot be changed once it is made. You use it to hold values that must not change, such as the date a judgment was pronounced.

# ---- 튜플: 순서가 있지만 바꿀 수 없는 묶음
judgment_date = (2026, 9, 6)
year, month, day = judgment_date      # 언패킹: 한 번에 꺼내기
print(f"{year}. {month}. {day}. 선고")

2026. 9. 6. 선고

In English: 선고 = pronounced (the line means "judgment pronounced on this date").

[Basic] The unpacking on the second line is syntax that splits the values of a tuple into three variables at once. In Part 2 it appears every time you unpack a batch of data, as in images, labels = batch. Get used to this shape now.

[Intermediate] Because it cannot be changed, a tuple can be used as a dictionary key (a list cannot), and it is also the default form when a function returns several values (Chapter 4).

3.7 Dictionaries: collections you look up by name tag

[Basic] You look things up in a list by "which position," but in a dictionary by "what." You line up key: value pairs inside curly braces { }. It is a container that fits the information of one case exactly.

# ---- 딕셔너리: 이름표(키)로 값을 찾는 묶음
case = {
    "case_no": "2099가합1234",
    "court": "가상지방법원",
    "claim": 350000000,
    "parties": ["원고", "피고"],      # 값으로 리스트도 들어갑니다
}
print(case["court"])                  # 키로 값 찾기
case["result"] = "일부 인용"          # 새 키 추가
print(case.get("judge", "미입력"))    # 없는 키는 get으로 안전하게
print(list(case.keys()))              # 키 목록
for key, value in case.items():       # 키와 값을 함께 순회
    print(f"  {key}: {value}")

가상지방법원
미입력
['case_no', 'court', 'claim', 'parties', 'result']
  case_no: 2099가합1234
  court: 가상지방법원
  claim: 350000000
  parties: ['원고', '피고']
  result: 일부 인용

In English: 가상지방법원 = Fictional District Court (an invented court); 미입력 = not entered; 일부 인용 = granted in part.

[Basic] You look up a value by putting the key in square brackets, as in case["court"], and if you put a value into a key that does not exist, it is added as a new one. Reading a missing key with square brackets raises KeyError, so for a key that may or may not be there, it is safer to read it with .get(key, default). .items() returns keys and values in pairs, and the for key, value in ... above is the unpacking of Section 3.6 placed inside a loop.

[Intermediate] In Part 2, dictionaries are central in two places. As a container that holds the hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, and so on) together, and as the state_dict that stores the weights of a trained model. The latter is, as its name says, a dictionary whose keys are layer names and whose values are weight tensors. If you can read a dictionary, you can look inside a saved model (Chapter 13).

3.8 Sets: collections without duplicates

[Basic] A set is a collection that allows no duplicates and has no order. It is handy for finding "what overlaps," such as the provisions that two judgments both cite.

# ---- 집합: 중복이 없고 순서도 없는 묶음
cited_a = {"민법 제750조", "민법 제751조", "민사소송법 제202조"}
cited_b = {"민법 제750조", "상법 제401조"}
print(cited_a & cited_b)              # 교집합: 둘 다 인용한 조문
print(cited_a | cited_b)              # 합집합
print(cited_a - cited_b)              # 차집합: A에만 있는 조문
print(len(set(["민법 제750조", "민법 제750조", "민법 제751조"])))  # 중복 제거

{'민법 제750조'}
{'상법 제401조', '민법 제750조', '민사소송법 제202조', '민법 제751조'}
{'민사소송법 제202조', '민법 제751조'}
2

In English: 민법 제750조 = Civil Act (민법) Article 750; 민법 제751조 = Civil Act Article 751; 민사소송법 제202조 = Civil Procedure Act (민사소송법) Article 202; 상법 제401조 = Commercial Act (상법) Article 401.

[Caution] The display order of a set changes from run to run. The order in which the elements appear in the output above may differ from your screen, and that is not wrong. As said at the start of Section 3.8, a set has no order, and the order in which Python prints it on the screen can change with each run. Check only that the elements and their number are the same. If you want to fix the order as well, print it sorted, as in print(sorted(cited_a | cited_b)). The other output in this chapter reproduces as it is, but set output alone has this exception. The results of training in Part 2 may differ slightly in their numbers depending on the environment you run them in (Chapter 24).

[Basic] Did you notice that the output order of the union differs from the input order? That is because a set has no order. Use a list when you need order, and a set when you need to judge overlap or inclusion. As on the last line, wrapping a list in set() removes the duplicates, so it is often used to count "how many different values there are."

3.9 Conditionals: flow that branches

[Basic] Until now, the flow has run only from top to bottom. A conditional splits the flow. The first part of p05_control.py:

# 아래 기준 금액과 이율은 설명을 위한 가정값입니다. 실제 규정과 다릅니다.

# ---- 조건문
claim = 350000000
if claim > 500000000:
    print("A 유형")
elif claim > 100000000:
    print("B 유형")
else:
    print("C 유형")

is_final = False
has_appeal = True
if not is_final and has_appeal:       # and, or, not 으로 조건을 잇습니다
    print("상소심 계속 중")

In English: the first comment says that the threshold amounts and the interest rate below are assumed values for explanation and differ from the actual rules; A 유형 / B 유형 / C 유형 = type A / type B / type C; 상소심 계속 중 = appeal pending.

B 유형
상소심 계속 중

[Basic] Here comes Python's most distinctive rule. Indentation is syntax. The lines indented four spaces after the colon (:) at the end of the if line are "the group to run when the condition is true." Indentation does the job that curly braces do in other languages. VS Code indents for you when you press Enter after a colon, so trust it, but check code you paste in, since its indentation can get scrambled.

[Basic] if → elif → else checks in order from the top and runs only the first place that turns out true. 350 million is not greater than 500 million, so the first condition is false; it is greater than 100 million, so it stops at the second condition. To compare, use >, >=, <, <=, == (equal), and != (not equal), and to join conditions, use and, or, and not.

[Basic] = and == are different. One sign means "put into," two signs mean "is it equal." If you write if claim = 5:, you get a SyntaxError.

3.10 Loops: flow that repeats

[Basic] With five cases you have to do the same thing five times; with fifty thousand cases, fifty thousand times. That is what a loop is for, and it is where coding beats doing things by hand.

# ---- for: 묶음을 하나씩 꺼내며 반복
amounts = [3000, 1200, 5400, 800]
total = 0
for a in amounts:
    total = total + a
print("합계:", total)

for i, a in enumerate(amounts):       # 번호와 값을 함께
    print(f"{i + 1}번째: {a}")

for n in range(3):                    # 0, 1, 2
    print("range:", n)

# ---- 조건과 반복을 함께
big = []
for a in amounts:
    if a >= 3000:
        big.append(a)
print("3000 이상:", big)

# 같은 일을 한 줄로 (리스트 컴프리헨션)
print("3000 이상:", [a for a in amounts if a >= 3000])

# ---- while: 조건이 참인 동안 반복
balance = 1000
years = 0
while balance < 2000:
    balance = balance * 1.05          # 가정 이율 5%
    years += 1                        # years = years + 1 과 같습니다
print(f"{years}년 뒤 {balance:.0f}")

# ---- break, continue
for a in amounts:
    if a < 1000:
        continue                      # 이번 차례는 건너뜀
    if a > 5000:
        break                         # 반복을 아예 끝냄
    print("처리:", a)

In English: 조건과 반복을 함께 = conditions and loops together; 같은 일을 한 줄로 (리스트 컴프리헨션) = the same thing in one line (list comprehension); 가정 이율 = assumed interest rate.

합계: 10400
1번째: 3000
2번째: 1200
3번째: 5400
4번째: 800
range: 0
range: 1
range: 2
3000 이상: [3000, 5400]
3000 이상: [3000, 5400]
15년 뒤 2079
처리: 3000
처리: 1200

In English: 합계 = total; …번째 = position … (1st, 2nd, …); 3000 이상 = 3000 or more; …년 뒤 = after … years; 처리 = processed.

[Basic] for a in amounts: means "take the items out of amounts one at a time, call each one a, and run the group below." As with total in the first example, preparing an empty container before the loop, filling it inside the loop, and using the result after the loop is the basic three-beat frame of tallying. The training loop in Part 2 has exactly this frame. For each epoch you set the loss to 0, add to it for each batch, and take the average at the end.

[Basic] enumerate gives you the number along with the value, and range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 (the end is excluded, the same rule as slicing). while keeps going around as long as the condition is true, so if there is no line inside it that makes the condition false (such as years += 1), it goes around forever. When that happens, stop it in the terminal with Ctrl+C.

[Intermediate] The example under "conditions and loops together" and the one-line list comprehension below it give the same result. The comprehension is "take a out of amounts, but collect only those where a is 3000 or more into a list," written in one line. It appears often in Part 2 code, so you need to be able to read it, but at first you may write the four-line version.

[Intermediate] break ends the loop, and continue skips only the current turn. In the example above, the loop ended with break at 5400, so the 800 after it was never reached (had it been reached, it is less than 1000 and would have been skipped with continue). That is why there is no "processed: 800" line in the output.

3.11 Comprehensive example: tallying a case list

[Basic] Using all the building blocks so far, you tally five cases. The data are invented cases made up for explanation. case_records.py:

# 3.11 종합 예제: 사건 목록 집계
# 아래 데이터는 설명을 위해 지어낸 가상의 사건입니다.

records = [
    {"case_no": "2099가합1001", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 420000000, "result": "인용",    "days": 310},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1002", "type": "대여금",   "claim": 150000000, "result": "기각",    "days": 198},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1003", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 880000000, "result": "일부인용", "days": 455},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1004", "type": "부당이득", "claim": 67000000,  "result": "인용",    "days": 120},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1005", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 230000000, "result": "기각",    "days": 260},
]

# 1) 전체 건수와 청구금액 합계
total_claim = 0
for r in records:
    total_claim += r["claim"]
print(f"사건 {len(records)}건, 청구금액 합계 {total_claim:,}원")

# 2) 사건 유형별 건수
count_by_type = {}
for r in records:
    t = r["type"]
    count_by_type[t] = count_by_type.get(t, 0) + 1
print("유형별 건수:", count_by_type)

# 3) 결과별 평균 처리일수
days_by_result = {}
for r in records:
    days_by_result.setdefault(r["result"], []).append(r["days"])
for result, days in days_by_result.items():
    print(f"{result}: 평균 {sum(days) / len(days):.0f}일 ({len(days)}건)")

# 4) 조건에 맞는 사건 고르기: 손해배상이면서 청구금액 3억 원 이상
selected = [r["case_no"] for r in records if r["type"] == "손해배상" and r["claim"] >= 300000000]
print("손해배상·3억 이상:", selected)

# 5) 청구금액 순 정렬 (큰 순)
for r in sorted(records, key=lambda r: r["claim"], reverse=True):
    print(f"  {r['case_no']}  {r['claim']:>13,}원  {r['result']}")

사건 5건, 청구금액 합계 1,747,000,000원
유형별 건수: {'손해배상': 3, '대여금': 1, '부당이득': 1}
인용: 평균 215일 (2건)
기각: 평균 229일 (2건)
일부인용: 평균 455일 (1건)
손해배상·3억 이상: ['2099가합1001', '2099가합1003']
  2099가합1003    880,000,000원  일부인용
  2099가합1001    420,000,000원  인용
  2099가합1005    230,000,000원  기각
  2099가합1002    150,000,000원  기각
  2099가합1004     67,000,000원  인용

In English: 사건 …건, 청구금액 합계 …원 = … cases, total amount claimed … won; 유형별 건수 = count by type; 손해배상 = damages; 대여금 = loan repayment; 부당이득 = unjust enrichment; 인용 = claim granted; 기각 = claim dismissed; 일부인용 = granted in part; 평균 …일 (…건) = average … days (… cases); 손해배상·3억 이상 = damages, 300 million won or more.

[Basic] Look at the structure. records is a list of dictionaries. One case is a dictionary; several cases are a list. The datasets in Part 2 have exactly this shape too (one image is a tensor; several images are a batch). On top of it, (1) a total, (2) counts by type, (3) averages by group, (4) selection by condition, and (5) sorting, the five basic operations of statistical work, were all done with nothing but loops and dictionaries.

[Basic] count_by_type.get(t, 0) + 1 in (2) means "get the current count for that type, treat it as 0 if there is none, and add 1." It is an idiom that keeps KeyError from being raised when a type shows up for the first time. setdefault in (3) has the same purpose. If the key is missing, it puts in an empty list; if the key is there, it returns that list.

[Intermediate] key=lambda r: r["claim"] in (5) means "sort by each case's claim value." lambda is a nameless one-line function. Functions are covered in Chapter 4, so for now read it only as "the way to say what to sort by." {r['claim']:>13,} is right-aligned in 13 places with a thousands separator. That is why the output lines up like a table.

[Intermediate] If you write this program with a library such as pandas, it becomes five lines. The reason to write it with loops first anyway is that only after you have gone through by hand, once, what a library does inside can you doubt the library's results. The sense for judging "is this really an average by group?" when AI writes pandas code for you comes from here.

Where people get stuck

[Basic] Most errors in this chapter are one of the following six. The messages are the actual output as it came out (with the paths shortened).

Last line Meaning Cause and fix
NameError: name 'claim' is not defined No such name You used the variable before making it, or the spelling differs. Upper and lower case are also distinguished
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed Syntax error A parenthesis or quotation mark was not closed. Look at the line the ^ points to and the line before it
IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1 Indentation error The line after a colon was not indented. It also happens when spaces and tabs are mixed
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str Type mismatch Text + number. Use str(1200) or an f-string
IndexError: list index out of range Position out of range [2] on a two-item list. Counting starts at 0, so the last one is [1] or [-1]
KeyError: 'judge' Missing key The dictionary does not have that key. Use .get('judge', default)

[Intermediate] Cases where no error occurs but the result is strange are scarier. Remember just three.

  • The list-copy trap. b = a is not a copy; it puts one more name on the same list. If you do b.append(4), a also becomes [1, 2, 3, 4]. To copy, use b = a.copy() or b = list(a).
  • Two kinds of division. 7 / 2 is 3.5, 7 // 2 is 3 (the quotient), and 7 % 2 is 1 (the remainder). If you use / when dividing counts, you get a floating-point number.
  • Floating-point error. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. This error comes from the computer storing floating-point numbers in binary, so it is not Python's fault. Do money calculations in integers (in units of won), and compare by whether the difference is small instead of with ==. A loss value in Part 2 that comes out as 1e-7 instead of 0.0 has the same cause.

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] The best way to learn this chapter's content with AI is to have it explain, then check. Paste in the whole code of Section 3.11 and ask like this.

Explain the Python code below line by line, as you would to someone learning to code for the first time. In particular, tell me why count_by_type.get(t, 0) + 1 is needed and what happens if get is not used.

[Basic] Then check. If AI answers "without get, a KeyError occurs," actually change .get(t, 0) to [t], run it, and see whether that error really occurs. Not believing the answer but checking the answer by experiment is what this book means by using AI. Once you have reproduced an error, you will never be confused by it again.

[Basic] When you ask for code, give the shape of the data along with the request. If you say only "a case list," AI makes up the shape. If you write "Each case is a dictionary with the keys case_no, type, claim, result, and days, and the data is a list of such dictionaries," you get code with the same structure as Section 3.11. Being able to describe the shape of the data in words is itself what this chapter achieves.

[Intermediate] Two old habits you often see in Python code from AI. print "...", print without parentheses, is Python 2 syntax and is now a SyntaxError. "%s" % x and .format() still work, but these days we use f-strings. When you see them, you can just ask it to "fix this for Python 3.13."

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. In case_no = "2099가합1234", what is case_no[4:6], and why is it not [4:5]?
  2. Using a loop, write code that pulls out into a list only the case numbers of the cases in records whose processing time (days) is over 300 days.
  3. Predict the output of the following code without running it, then run it to check. a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4); print(len(a))

[Intermediate]

  1. Rewrite (2) of Section 3.11 without .get(), using the conditional if t in count_by_type:. What are the advantages and disadvantages of the two approaches?
  2. Write code that determines whether records contains "a case with an amount claimed under 100 million won that was granted," and end the loop as soon as you find one.
  3. Use a set to count how many kinds of result there are in records. Why is it wrong to do this with only a list and len()?
