Part 1

Chapter 4. Python basics II: functions, modules, files, exceptions, classes

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn to bundle repeated work into functions, split functions into modules (files), and bring them into other files to use.
  • You read and write text, CSV, and JSON files, and you handle exceptions so that a program does not die when it meets bad data.
  • You learn what a class is, and you become able to read what class MyDataset(Dataset): and def __init__(self, ...), which you will see every day in Part 2, mean.
  • You rebuild the tallying program of Chapter 3 with a module and class structure that reads from a CSV file.

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I have used def, return, import, with open(...), and try/except.
  • [ ] I can explain what class, self, and __init__ mean.
  • [ ] I know what changes when you define __len__ and __getitem__.

If the third is "no," you can read just Section 4.5. The Dataset in Part 2 is made of exactly those two methods.

4.0 Why you need this

[Basic] The comprehensive example in Chapter 3 was 30 lines. Real deep learning code runs to hundreds of lines and is split across several files. To read that code, "what does this line do" is not enough; you have to be able to follow "what does this chunk do, and where is that chunk defined." This chapter covers three ways of bundling code into chunks (functions, modules, classes) and two ways in which chunks meet the outside world (file input and output, exceptions).

[Basic] To compare it with a written judgment: if Chapter 3 was at the level of sentences, this chapter is at the level of numbered sections and attached schedules. Just as a judgment does not write out the same determination every time but refers to it, as in "same as the determination in paragraph 2," code defines the same task once as a function and calls it by name.

4.1 Functions: named bundles of work

[Basic] A function is a bundle of work that takes input, does the work, and returns a result. You define it with def name(parameters):, and inside the indented group you return the result with return. p01_functions.py:

# 4.1 함수: 이름 붙인 작업 묶음

def yearly_interest(principal, rate):        # 매개변수 두 개
    """원금과 연이율로 1년 이자를 계산한다."""   # 설명문(docstring). 없어도 되지만 붙이는 습관
    return principal * rate                   # 결과를 돌려준다

print(yearly_interest(100000000, 0.05))       # 인자 두 개를 넣어 호출
print(yearly_interest(rate=0.03, principal=5000000))   # 이름을 붙여 순서 무관

def interest(principal, rate=0.05, years=1):  # 기본값이 있는 매개변수
    return principal * rate * years

print(interest(100000000))                    # rate, years는 기본값
print(interest(100000000, years=3))           # 일부만 지정

def split_case_no(case_no):                   # 값을 여러 개 돌려주기 (튜플)
    return case_no[:4], case_no[4:6], case_no[6:]

year, code, number = split_case_no("2099가합1234")
print(year, code, number)

def describe(case_no, *tags):                 # 개수가 정해지지 않은 인자
    print(case_no, "태그:", tags)

describe("2099가합1234")
describe("2099가합1234", "손해배상", "항소")

# 돌려주는 값이 없는 함수는 None을 돌려준다
def greet(name):
    print(f"{name}님, 안녕하세요")

result = greet("홍길동")
print(result)

# 함수 안에서 만든 변수는 밖에서 보이지 않는다 (지역 변수)
def make_total(amounts):
    total = 0
    for a in amounts:
        total += a
    return total

print(make_total([1, 2, 3]))
try:
    print(total)
except NameError as e:
    print("밖에서는 못 씀:", e)

5000000.0
150000.0
5000000.0
15000000.0
2099 가합 1234
2099가합1234 태그: ()
2099가합1234 태그: ('손해배상', '항소')
홍길동님, 안녕하세요
None
6
밖에서는 못 씀: name 'total' is not defined

In English: 2099가합1234 = an invented case number: year 2099, case-type code 가합 (gahap, a first-instance civil case before a panel of judges), serial 1234; 태그 = tags; 손해배상 = damages; 항소 = appeal; 홍길동님, 안녕하세요 = "Hello, 홍길동" (홍길동 is a stock placeholder name); 밖에서는 못 씀 = cannot be used outside.

[Basic] When you read, distinguish definition from call. def yearly_interest(...) is a definition, and by itself it runs nothing. yearly_interest(100000000, 0.05) is a call, and only then does the code inside run. In Part 2 code, if def train(...) is near the top of the file and train(...) is at the very bottom, execution starts at the bottom and jumps into the definition above.

[Basic] You can give parameters default values (rate=0.05), and when you call, you can pass them with names attached (years=3). DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True) in Part 2 has exactly this shape. If you look at a function's definition, it tells you everything: which arguments you can give, and what happens if you do not.

[Basic] A function without return returns None. That is why result, which holds the result of greet, is None. It is the same principle as amounts.sort() returning None in Chapter 3.

[Intermediate] A variable made inside a function (total) cannot be seen outside the function (a local variable). The other way around, a variable outside the function can be read inside it. Thanks to this rule, using the name total inside one function does not clash with total in another function. *tags means "take the remaining arguments as a tuple," and its partner **kwargs takes named arguments as a dictionary. When you see def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) in Part 2 code, read it as "take any arguments at all and pass them on."

[Intermediate] The triple-quoted string on the first line of a function is a docstring. In VS Code, when you hover the mouse over a function name, this description appears. When you read someone else's code, too, checking the docstring first lets you grasp quickly what the function does (you read other people's code in Chapter 8).

4.2 Modules: splitting into files

[Basic] When functions multiply, you split the file. One Python file (.py) is a module, and other files bring it in with import filename to use it. First, make caselib.py.

# 4.2 모듈: 이 파일 자체가 모듈입니다. 다른 파일에서 import caselib 로 불러 씁니다.

def parse_case_no(case_no):
    """'2099가합1234' -> (2099, '가합', 1234)"""
    year = int(case_no[:4])
    number = int(case_no[6:])
    code = case_no[4:6]
    return year, code, number


def total_claim(records):
    """사건 목록의 청구금액 합계"""
    return sum(r["claim"] for r in records)


def count_by(records, key):
    """records를 key 값별로 센다. 예: count_by(records, 'type')"""
    counts = {}
    for r in records:
        counts[r[key]] = counts.get(r[key], 0) + 1
    return counts


if __name__ == "__main__":            # 이 파일을 직접 실행했을 때만 아래가 돈다
    print("caselib 자체 실행:", parse_case_no("2099가합1234"))

In English: the docstrings say: '2099가합1234' -> (2099, '가합', 1234); 사건 목록의 청구금액 합계 = total amount claimed in a case list; "records를 key 값별로 센다" = "counts records by the value of key"; caselib 자체 실행 = caselib run directly.

In the same folder, p02_modules.py:

# 4.2 모듈 불러오기

import caselib                                # 같은 폴더의 caselib.py
from caselib import count_by                  # 필요한 것만 이름으로

print(caselib.parse_case_no("2099가합1234"))
records = [
    {"case_no": "2099가합1001", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 420000000},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1002", "type": "대여금", "claim": 150000000},
]
print(caselib.total_claim(records))
print(count_by(records, "type"))

# 표준 라이브러리: 파이썬에 처음부터 들어 있는 모듈들
import math
import random
import os
import datetime as dt                         # 별명(alias)

print(math.sqrt(2), math.floor(3.7))
random.seed(0)                                # 같은 난수를 다시 얻으려면 seed를 고정
print(random.choice(["원고", "피고"]), random.randint(1, 6))
print(os.getcwd())                            # 지금 작업 폴더
print(os.path.join("data", "cases.csv"))      # 운영체제에 맞는 경로 구분자로 이어 붙임
today = dt.date(2026, 9, 6)
print(today, today + dt.timedelta(days=14))   # 14일 뒤

(2099, '가합', 1234)
570000000
{'손해배상': 1, '대여금': 1}
1.4142135623730951 3
피고 4
…\code\04
data\cases.csv
2026-09-06 2026-09-20

In English: 손해배상 = damages; 대여금 = loan repayment; 피고 = defendant (the value that random.choice in the code above picked from 원고 = plaintiff and 피고).

[Basic] import caselib reads caselib.py and lets you use the functions in it as caselib.function_name. from caselib import count_by brings in just one and lets you use it without the prefix. The import torch, import torch.nn as nn, and from torch.utils.data import DataLoader at the top of Part 2 code each have one of these three shapes. as nn attaches a short alias to a long name.

[Basic] if __name__ == "__main__": looks like a magic spell the first time you see it, but it means one thing. "Run what is below only when this file is run directly." If you run caselib.py directly, the lines under it run, but when p02_modules.py does import caselib, they do not. So you can put a self-test in a module. train.py in Part 2 has this statement at the very bottom and calls main() inside it.

[Basic] math, random, os, datetime, and the csv and json of Section 4.3 are the standard library, which comes with Python from the start. You need no installation, only import. By contrast, torch is an external library that you installed separately with pip install in Chapter 2. If import fails, check in turn: "Is it standard? Did I install it? Is the environment I installed it in the environment I am in now?"

[Intermediate] random.seed(0) fixes the seed of the random numbers so that you get the same result again. To reproduce an experiment in Part 2, you use torch.manual_seed(0) for the same reason (Chapter 24). os.path.join takes care of the difference between \ on Windows and / on Mac for you, so do not join paths by hand. When Python looks for a file, it starts from the current working folder (os.getcwd()), so if it "cannot find a file that is definitely there," first check which folder VS Code is running in.

[Advanced] If you put __init__.py in a folder, the folder becomes a package, and you can bring things in through levels, as in from networks.mylenet import LeNet. This is covered in Chapter 14, when the code is split into networks/ and utils/.

4.3 Reading and writing files

[Basic] Data comes from files. You need to know only three formats. Text (running prose), CSV (tables), and JSON (stores dictionaries and lists as they are). p03_files.py:

# 4.3 파일 읽고 쓰기 (텍스트, CSV, JSON)
import csv
import json

# ---- 텍스트 파일 쓰기와 읽기
with open("memo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:     # w: 새로 쓰기 (있으면 덮어씀)
    f.write("첫 줄\n")
    f.write("둘째 줄\n")

with open("memo.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:     # r: 읽기
    text = f.read()
print(repr(text))                                       # repr: 줄바꿈 문자까지 보이게

with open("memo.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:           # 한 줄씩
    for line in f:
        print("줄:", line.strip())

# ---- CSV: 표 형식. 엑셀에서 열리는 가장 단순한 형식
records = [
    {"case_no": "2099가합1001", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 420000000},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1002", "type": "대여금", "claim": 150000000},
]
with open("cases.csv", "w", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:   # utf-8-sig: 엑셀 한글 깨짐 방지
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["case_no", "type", "claim"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(records)

with open("cases.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
    loaded = list(csv.DictReader(f))
print(loaded)
print(type(loaded[0]["claim"]))                          # CSV에서 읽은 값은 전부 글자!
print(sum(int(r["claim"]) for r in loaded))              # 숫자로 바꿔 합계

# ---- JSON: 딕셔너리·리스트를 그대로 저장하는 형식 (설정 파일, 결과 저장에 씀)
with open("cases.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(records, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)  # ensure_ascii=False: 한글 그대로

with open("cases.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded2 = json.load(f)
print(loaded2[0]["claim"], type(loaded2[0]["claim"]))    # JSON은 숫자를 숫자로 보존

'첫 줄\n둘째 줄\n'
줄: 첫 줄
줄: 둘째 줄
[{'case_no': '2099가합1001', 'type': '손해배상', 'claim': '420000000'}, {'case_no': '2099가합1002', 'type': '대여금', 'claim': '150000000'}]
<class 'str'>
570000000
420000000 <class 'int'>

In English: 첫 줄 = first line; 둘째 줄 = second line; 줄: = line:; 손해배상 = damages; 대여금 = loan repayment.

[Basic] with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f: is the standard form for opening a file. With with, the file is closed automatically when the group ends. For the mode, remember just three: "r" (read, the default), "w" (write new, erases the existing content), and "a" (append at the end). encoding="utf-8" is the setting that keeps Korean text from being garbled, and on Windows you always add it. If you leave it out, the file is read in the Windows default encoding (CP949), and files made on other computers come out garbled.

[Basic] Look at two things in the output. The claim read from CSV is '420000000', text, and the claim read from JSON is 420000000, a number. CSV reads every cell as text, so you have to convert with int() before calculating (Section 3.3), while JSON keeps the kind. This is why Part 2 saves hyperparameters as JSON (Chapter 13).

[Intermediate] The reason for using encoding="utf-8-sig" when writing the CSV is Excel. Excel sometimes garbles the Korean text in a UTF-8 file that has no marker (BOM) at the front, so -sig adds the marker. If you give the same encoding when reading, the marker is removed automatically. newline="" is an idiom the CSV module requires, and it keeps blank lines from creeping in on Windows.

[Intermediate] For large tabular data, you use pandas instead of this chapter's csv module. One line, pd.read_csv("cases.csv"), reads it, and you can calculate by column. The principle is the same, so this chapter uses only the standard library.

4.4 Handling exceptions: not dying when an error occurs

[Basic] In Chapter 3 you learned to read error messages. This section is about expecting an error and catching it in advance. Data always has strange values mixed in. An amount cell that says "undecided," for example. When that happens, the whole program must not stop; it should skip just that row and record it. p04_exceptions.py:

# 4.4 예외 처리: 오류가 나도 프로그램이 죽지 않게

amount_texts = ["1200000", "350,000", "미정", "800000"]

# 처리하지 않으면 두 번째 값에서 프로그램이 멈춥니다
total = 0
for t in amount_texts:
    try:
        total += int(t)
    except ValueError:                        # 숫자로 못 바꾸는 경우만 잡는다
        print(f"건너뜀: {t!r}")               # !r: repr 형태로 출력
print("합계:", total)

# 쉼표 제거를 먼저 시도하고, 그래도 안 되면 건너뛰기
def to_int(text):
    try:
        return int(text.replace(",", ""))
    except ValueError:
        return None

print([to_int(t) for t in amount_texts])

# 여러 종류의 예외, else, finally
def read_first_line(path):
    try:
        f = open(path, encoding="utf-8")
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("파일이 없습니다:", path)
        return None
    else:                                     # 예외가 없었을 때만
        line = f.readline()
        f.close()
        return line.strip()
    finally:                                  # 예외가 있든 없든 항상
        print("read_first_line 끝")

print(read_first_line("memo.txt"))
print(read_first_line("없는파일.txt"))

# 직접 예외 일으키기: 잘못된 입력을 초기에 걸러낸다
def parse_case_no(case_no):
    if len(case_no) < 7 or not case_no[:4].isdigit():
        raise ValueError(f"사건번호 형식이 아닙니다: {case_no!r}")
    return int(case_no[:4]), case_no[4:6], int(case_no[6:])

print(parse_case_no("2099가합1234"))
try:
    parse_case_no("가합1234")
except ValueError as e:
    print("오류:", e)

건너뜀: '350,000'
건너뜀: '미정'
합계: 2000000
[1200000, 350000, None, 800000]
read_first_line 끝
첫 줄
파일이 없습니다: 없는파일.txt
read_first_line 끝
None
(2099, '가합', 1234)
오류: 사건번호 형식이 아닙니다: '가합1234'

In English: 미정 = undecided; 건너뜀 = skipped; 합계 = total; 파일이 없습니다 = the file does not exist; read_first_line 끝 = end of read_first_line; 없는파일.txt = a file name meaning "a file that does not exist"; 오류 = error; 사건번호 형식이 아닙니다 = this is not in case-number format.

[Basic] If an error occurs inside the try: group, Python stops on the spot and jumps to the except ErrorName: group. If no error occurs, except is skipped. In the first example, int() failed on "350,000" and "미정", so they were skipped, and only the other two went into the total. The second example removed the comma and tried again, which rescued "350,000". How much to rescue and where to start throwing away is decided by the person who knows the data; the code only holds that decision.

[Basic] It matters that you name the kind of error, as in except ValueError:. If you write just except:, it swallows every error, and even real bugs (for example, a NameError from a typo in a variable name) pass by silently. The names in the error table of Chapter 3 are used here.

[Intermediate] else runs only when there was no exception, and finally always runs, whether there was an exception or not. That is why the line marking the end of read_first_line appears both times in the output. raise raises an error yourself. If you filter out bad input at the start of a function, you keep the error from going off somewhere unexpected. When you see raise IndexError in the Dataset code of Part 2, read it as "refusing a request that is out of range."

4.5 Classes and objects: the key to reading Part 2

[Basic] This section is the core of the chapter. In Chapter 3 you represented one case as a dictionary. But a case has more than data (case number, amount); it also has behavior (getting the filing year from the case number, judging whether a result has come out). The template that defines data and behavior as one bundle is a class, and each actual value stamped out from that template is an object. A type of lawsuit is the template, and each individual case is an object. The first part of p05_classes.py:

class Case:
    """사건 하나를 나타내는 틀(클래스)"""

    def __init__(self, case_no, claim, result=None):   # 객체를 만들 때 자동 실행
        self.case_no = case_no                          # self.이름 = 이 객체가 가진 값(속성)
        self.claim = claim
        self.result = result

    def year(self):                                     # 메서드: 이 객체가 할 수 있는 동작
        return int(self.case_no[:4])

    def is_decided(self):
        return self.result is not None

    def __repr__(self):                                 # print 할 때 보이는 모양
        return f"Case({self.case_no}, {self.claim:,}, {self.result})"


c1 = Case("2099가합1001", 420000000, "인용")   # 객체 만들기 = 클래스 이름을 함수처럼 호출
c2 = Case("2099가합1002", 150000000)          # result는 기본값 None
print(c1)
print(c1.case_no, c1.year(), c1.is_decided())
print(c2.is_decided())
c2.result = "기각"                            # 속성은 나중에 바꿀 수 있다
print(c2)

Case(2099가합1001, 420,000,000, 인용)
2099가합1001 2099 True
False
Case(2099가합1002, 150,000,000, 기각)

In English: 인용 = claim granted; 기각 = claim dismissed.

[Basic] You need to read only three things.

  1. __init__ is the function that runs automatically when an object is made. If you write Case("2099가합1001", 420000000, "인용") (the last value means claim granted), Python makes an empty object and calls __init__ to fill in the values. The two _ characters before and after mark it as "a special name that Python has defined."
  2. self is "that very object that is being made now (or that is acting now)." It comes as the first parameter of every method, but you do not write it when you call. If you call c1.year(), Python puts c1 in the place of self for you. self.case_no is "this object's case_no."
  3. Attributes and methods. If there are no parentheses after the dot, as in c1.case_no, it is a value (an attribute); if there are parentheses, as in c1.year(), it is an action (a method). "abc".upper() in Chapter 3 was in fact a method of a string object.

[Basic] Now let's read, ahead of time, code you will see in Part 2.

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden, out_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_dim, hidden)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden, out_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(torch.relu(self.fc1(x)))

"Define a template called MLP. When it is made, it takes three numbers and keeps two layers (fc1, fc2) as its own attributes. The action called forward passes the input x through the two layers in order." If you can read it this far, that is enough. nn.Module and super().__init__() are explained just below, under inheritance.

Inheritance: inheriting and changing only a little

[Basic] An appeal case is mostly the same as a first-instance case, with one more item, "the lower-court case number." In such a case, you do not write Case again from scratch; you inherit from it.

# ---- 상속: 기존 틀을 물려받아 조금만 바꾸기
class AppealCase(Case):                       # Case의 모든 것을 물려받는다
    def __init__(self, case_no, claim, result=None, lower_case_no=None):
        super().__init__(case_no, claim, result)       # 부모의 __init__ 먼저
        self.lower_case_no = lower_case_no

    def is_decided(self):                     # 부모 메서드를 덮어쓰기(override)
        return self.result in ("항소기각", "취소", "변경")


a1 = AppealCase("2099나5001", 420000000, "항소기각", lower_case_no="2099가합1001")
print(a1, a1.year(), a1.is_decided(), a1.lower_case_no)

Case(2099나5001, 420,000,000, 항소기각) 2099 True 2099가합1001

In English: 2099나5001 = an invented appeal case number with case-type code 나 (na, civil appeal); 항소기각 = appeal dismissed; the tuple in is_decided in the code above also lists 취소 = (lower judgment) revoked and 변경 = (lower judgment) modified.

[Basic] What is inside the parentheses of class AppealCase(Case): is the parent. AppealCase inherited year() and __repr__ as they are (the Case(...) shape in the output is the evidence), and it overrode __init__ and is_decided with its own. super().__init__(...) means "please run the parent's __init__ first." It almost always comes on the first line of a child's __init__, so that the attributes the parent fills in (case_no and so on) are not missed.

[Basic] Now class MLP(nn.Module): and super().__init__() can be read. "MLP inherits from a parent called nn.Module, which PyTorch has already made. Do the parent's preparation first." nn.Module has every kind of function needed for training (managing weights, saving, moving to the GPU), so we need to write only __init__, which defines the layers, and forward, the order of computation. This is the frame of all of Part 2.

Special methods: using len() and [ ] on your own object

[Basic] Names wrapped in two _ characters on each side, like __init__ and __repr__, are special methods connected to Python's syntax. If you know two more of them, you can read the Dataset in Part 2.

# ---- 특수 메서드: 2부의 Dataset이 쓰는 두 가지
class CaseList:
    def __init__(self, cases):
        self.cases = cases

    def __len__(self):                        # len(obj) 가 호출한다
        return len(self.cases)

    def __getitem__(self, i):                 # obj[i] 가 호출한다
        return self.cases[i]


cl = CaseList([c1, c2, a1])
print(len(cl), cl[0], cl[-1])
for c in cl:                                  # __getitem__ 이 있으면 for 문도 된다
    print(" ", c.case_no)

3 Case(2099가합1001, 420,000,000, 인용) Case(2099나5001, 420,000,000, 항소기각)
  2099가합1001
  2099가합1002
  2099나5001

[Basic] Define __len__ and len(cl) works; define __getitem__ and cl[0] works. And even for c in cl works. That is because Python tries 0, 1, 2, … in turn and stops when an IndexError occurs. The Dataset classes in Part 2 consist of exactly these two methods. __len__ is "how many data items are there," and __getitem__ is "give me the i-th data item (and its correct label)." The DataLoader relies on those two alone to take the data out (Chapter 15).

[Intermediate] __repr__ sets the string used when an object is shown by print(obj) or in interactive mode. If you do not make one, only an address appears, as in <__main__.Case object at 0x000001...>, and debugging becomes painful. The habit of adding __repr__ first whenever you make a class makes the debugger screens of Chapter 5 easier to read.

[Advanced] When a child overrides is_decided, a call with the same name behaves differently depending on the kind of object (polymorphism). for c in cl works because of the old iteration protocol based on __getitem__; the modern way is to define __iter__. torch.utils.data.Dataset uses the __getitem__ and __len__ protocol, and IterableDataset uses the __iter__ protocol.

4.6 Comprehensive example: from CSV to objects, and then a report

[Basic] You rebuild the comprehensive example of Chapter 3 with this chapter's building blocks. Four things are different. The data is read not from inside the code but from a CSV file, each case is made not as a dictionary but as a Case object, the tallying functions come from the caselib module, and bad rows are skipped with exception handling. case_report.py:

# 4.6 종합 예제: CSV에서 사건을 읽어 객체로 만들고 보고서를 출력한다
# 3장의 case_records.py 를 함수·모듈·파일·예외·클래스로 다시 쓴 것.
# 실행: python case_report.py cases_all.csv   (파일이 없으면 만들어 줍니다)
import csv
import sys

from caselib import count_by                  # 4.2에서 만든 모듈 재사용


class Case:
    def __init__(self, case_no, case_type, claim, result, days):
        self.case_no = case_no
        self.type = case_type
        self.claim = claim
        self.result = result
        self.days = days

    @classmethod
    def from_row(cls, row):
        """CSV 한 행(딕셔너리, 값은 전부 글자)에서 Case를 만든다. 형식이 틀리면 ValueError."""
        return cls(
            row["case_no"],
            row["type"],
            int(row["claim"].replace(",", "")),
            row["result"],
            int(row["days"]),
        )

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Case({self.case_no}, {self.type}, {self.claim:,}, {self.result}, {self.days}일)"


SAMPLE = [
    ["case_no", "type", "claim", "result", "days"],
    ["2099가합1001", "손해배상", "420000000", "인용", "310"],
    ["2099가합1002", "대여금", "150,000,000", "기각", "198"],      # 쉼표 있는 금액
    ["2099가합1003", "손해배상", "880000000", "일부인용", "455"],
    ["2099가합1004", "부당이득", "67000000", "인용", "120"],
    ["2099가합1005", "손해배상", "230000000", "기각", "260"],
    ["2099가합1006", "손해배상", "미정", "인용", "90"],            # 잘못된 행: 건너뛰어야 함
]


def ensure_sample(path):
    """예제 파일이 없으면 만든다."""
    try:
        open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig").close()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
            csv.writer(f).writerows(SAMPLE)
        print(f"예제 파일을 만들었습니다: {path}")


def load_cases(path):
    cases, skipped = [], []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            try:
                cases.append(Case.from_row(row))
            except (ValueError, KeyError) as e:
                skipped.append((row.get("case_no", "?"), str(e)))
    return cases, skipped


def report(cases):
    records = [c.__dict__ for c in cases]     # 객체 → 딕셔너리 (caselib 함수에 넘기기 위해)
    print(f"사건 {len(cases)}건, 청구금액 합계 {sum(c.claim for c in cases):,}원")
    print("유형별 건수:", count_by(records, "type"))
    print("결과별 건수:", count_by(records, "result"))
    longest = max(cases, key=lambda c: c.days)
    print(f"최장 처리: {longest.case_no} ({longest.days}일)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    path = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "cases_all.csv"   # 명령줄 인자
    ensure_sample(path)
    cases, skipped = load_cases(path)
    report(cases)
    for case_no, why in skipped:
        print(f"건너뜀 {case_no}: {why}")

예제 파일을 만들었습니다: cases_all.csv
사건 5건, 청구금액 합계 1,747,000,000원
유형별 건수: {'손해배상': 3, '대여금': 1, '부당이득': 1}
결과별 건수: {'인용': 2, '기각': 2, '일부인용': 1}
최장 처리: 2099가합1003 (455일)
건너뜀 2099가합1006: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '미정'

In English: 예제 파일을 만들었습니다 = created the sample file; 사건 …건, 청구금액 합계 …원 = … cases, total amount claimed … won; 유형별 건수 = count by type; 결과별 건수 = count by result; 부당이득 = unjust enrichment; 일부인용 = granted in part; 최장 처리 = longest processing time; …일 = … days; 건너뜀 = skipped.

[Basic] You read it starting from the bottom. The flow is under if __name__ == "__main__":. Set the path → make sure the sample file exists → read → report → announce what was skipped. Each step is one function, and the function names are the table of contents. train.py in Part 2 has the same structure, so if you start at the bottom and follow the function names upward, you see the whole thing.

[Basic] Confirm that the sixth row ("미정", undecided) was skipped, and that "150,000,000" in the second row survived because the commas were removed. The try/except in load_cases confined one row's problem to that row. Without exception handling, the program would have stopped at the sixth row, and the tally of the five cases before it would not have come out either.

[Intermediate] sys.argv is the list of arguments passed on the command line. If you run python case_report.py other.csv, sys.argv[1] is "other.csv". It is the first way to change the input without changing the code, and argparse in Chapter 13 puts it on a systematic footing. from_row, marked with @classmethod, is "a method you call directly on the class, without an object," and it is the idiomatic way to make an object from a file row. c.__dict__ returns an object's attributes as a dictionary, and it is the same idea as state_dict() in Part 2.

[Advanced] Chapter 3 said that parsing a case number by position breaks when the code has a different length, as with the retrial code. Regular expressions (the re module) are the solution.

import re
pat = re.compile(r'(\d{4})([가-힣]+)(\d+)')   # 숫자 4개, 한글 1개 이상, 숫자 1개 이상
for s in ['2099가합1234', '2099재가합12', '2099나50001', '가합1234']:
    m = pat.fullmatch(s)
    print(s, '->', m.groups() if m else None)

In English: the comment says: 4 digits, 1 or more Hangul characters, 1 or more digits.

2099가합1234 -> ('2099', '가합', '1234')
2099재가합12 -> ('2099', '재가합', '12')
2099나50001 -> ('2099', '나', '50001')
가합1234 -> None

[Advanced] \d{4} is four digits, [가-힣]+ is one or more Hangul syllables, \d+ is one or more digits, and the parts wrapped in parentheses come out through groups(). Regular expressions are the strongest tool for pulling dates, amounts, and provisions out of legal documents, but they are not in the required scope of this book.

Where people get stuck

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'caselib' caselib.py is in a different folder from the file being run. Check the current folder of the VS Code terminal and move with cd
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch' Not installed, or a different environment. Chapter 2, "Where people get stuck," second row
TypeError: Case.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'claim' An argument needed to make the object was left out. Compare with the parameter list of __init__
TypeError: Case.year() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given self was left out of the method definition. The first parameter of every method is self. As for "1 was given," that 1 is the object itself
AttributeError: 'Case' object has no attribute 'case_number' A typo in the attribute name, or the attribute was made as a local variable in __init__ without self.
A file cannot be read, with UnicodeDecodeError encoding="utf-8" is missing (Windows). If that does not fix it, the file may be CP949, so try encoding="cp949"
What you wrote to a file disappeared "w" mode overwrites. To append, use "a"
You used only open() without with, did not close it, and the file is locked Always use the with form

[Intermediate] Be wary when you see code that uses only except:. It swallows every error and hides the cause. At the very least, catch it with except Exception as e: and print or record e. Also, the convention is to gather import statements at the very top of the file. With code that does import inside a function, the reader misses the dependencies.

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] From this chapter on, questions that have AI explain the structure become useful. Paste in case_report.py and ask:

Explain the execution flow of this file in the order of function calls, starting from if __name__ == "__main__":. Put what each function takes and what it returns in a table.

[Basic] Verify it in two ways. First, check whether AI's table says that load_cases "returns a tuple (cases, skipped)." That is how the code is written. Second, if AI answers only that "bad rows are ignored," that is not enough. An accurate explanation also points out that they are recorded in skipped and printed at the end. If AI's explanation is simpler than the code, something is missing.

[Basic] When you first learn classes, this is the best question.

Explain what self is, what Python actually does when c1.year() is called, and whether it is the same as Case.year(c1).

The answer to the last question is "it is the same," and you can confirm it by running it yourself. The moment you confirm it, you understand self.

[Intermediate] If a class that AI wrote for you has only __init__ and no __repr__, ask it to add one. And if AI uses except:, demand that it "specify which exceptions to catch." These two are the most common omissions in AI code.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. In def f(a, b=2): return a * b, what are the results of f(3), f(3, 4), and f(b=5, a=1)?
  2. Write in one sentence why "caselib run directly: …" appears when you run caselib.py directly and does not appear when you import it.
  3. To double "420000000" read from CSV and 420000000 read from JSON, how do you have to write each one differently?
  4. In class Case:, delete the self of def year(self):, actually try it to see what error occurs, and write down the message.

[Intermediate]

  1. Add a days attribute to Case, and make a method mean_days() in CaseList that returns "the average processing time in days."
  2. Why does load_cases also catch KeyError? Give an example of a CSV that raises that error.
  3. If you delete the super().__init__(...) line in AppealCase, what breaks? Run it to confirm.

[Advanced]

  1. Define __iter__ in CaseList so that the for statement works even without __getitem__. Explain the difference between the two approaches.
  2. Write a regular expression pattern that pulls the year, month, and day out of a date in the format "2026. 9. 6." Make it also catch cases with no spaces, such as "2026.9.6".

Part 1

Chapter 5. Reading code with a debugger

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn how to stop a program at the line you want, walk through it one line at a time, and look into the values of the variables at that moment.
  • You use the five operations of the VS Code debugger (breakpoint, continue, step over, step into, step out) and its five panels.
  • You practice the procedure for finding, with the debugger, "bugs that raise an error" and "bugs that give a wrong value without an error."
  • In Part 2 you will use this skill every day, when you look at why the shapes of tensors do not match.

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I have set a breakpoint in VS Code, run the program with F5, and looked at the Variables panel.
  • [ ] I know the difference between F10 and F11.
  • [ ] I have put args into launch.json.

If all three are "yes," you can do only the bug-hunting exercise in Section 5.7 and move on.

5.0 Why a debugger

[Basic] When code is wrong, the first thing people do is stick print() in here and there. It works. But if there are several values the output gets jumbled, inside a loop hundreds of lines pour out, and once you have seen it all you have to delete the print calls you inserted. And, decisively, you have to know in advance where to look before you can insert a print. Yet not knowing where the problem is, is the problem.

[Basic] A debugger is a different approach. You stop the program at any line, see all the variables that exist at that moment on one screen, and move ahead one line at a time, watching how the values change. To use the analogy of examining a witness, print is reading from a list of questions prepared in advance, and the debugger is keeping the witness on the stand and deciding the next question as you hear the answers.

[Basic] There is a reason the title of this chapter is not "catching bugs with a debugger" but "reading code with a debugger." The debugger is also the fastest tool for understanding someone else's code. When you receive training code that AI wrote for you in Part 2, walk through it once with the debugger before you read it. Which function calls which, and what shape the data has as it flows along, show up faster than any explanation.

5.1 Three things a debugger does

[Basic] A debugger seems to have many features, but in essence it does three things.

Task Operation Meaning
Stop Breakpoint "Stop when you reach this line"
Walk Continue / Step Over / Step Into / Step Out How to proceed after stopping
Look inside Variables / Watch / Call Stack / Debug Console See the state at the moment it stopped

Figure 5-1. The basic cycle of debugging. Stop, look, take one step, and look again.

5.2 Running the VS Code debugger for the first time

[Basic] Start with case_records.py from Chapter 3. Open the file and do the following in order.

  1. Set a breakpoint. Move the cursor to the count_by_type[t] = ... line of the loop that counts cases by type, and press F9. A red dot appears to the left of the line number. You can also click that spot with the mouse.
  2. Start debugging. Click the small ▼ next to the ▶ button at the top right and choose Python Debugger: Debug Python File. Or open the icon with a bug and a triangle in the vertical menu on the left (Run and Debug, Ctrl+Shift+D), click the Run and Debug button, and choose Python File.
  3. The program prints its first output (5 cases, the total) and then stops at the line with the red dot. That line is highlighted in yellow, and a small control bar appears at the top of the screen.

[Basic] Now look at the panel on the left. Variables shows records, total_claim, count_by_type, r, and t with their current values. Expand the ▶ next to r and the keys and values inside the dictionary appear. count_by_type is still {}. That is because that line has not run yet. A breakpoint stops "just before that line runs."

[Basic] Press the five buttons on the control bar one after another.

Button Key What it does If you press it now
Continue F5 Runs to the next breakpoint The loop goes around once and stops again at the same line, and one entry appears in count_by_type
Step Over F10 Runs one line. Even if there is a function call, it runs it whole without going inside The yellow line moves to the next line
Step Into F11 Runs one line, but if it is a function call, it goes inside that function .get(...) is built in, so it does not go in (justMyCode, Section 5.4)
Step Out Shift+F11 Runs until the current function ends and returns to where it was called This is the top level, so it runs to the end of the program
Stop Shift+F5 Stops debugging

[Basic] Press F5 five times and the loop goes around five times, and each time you can see in Variables how count_by_type grows. This is an experience that is hard to get with print. Seeing the moment a value changes with your own eyes.

[Intermediate] In the Watch panel you can type an expression directly. Click + and type count_by_type.get(t, 0), and the value of that expression is updated every time the program stops. But "updated" means that the expression is run again every time the program stops. So in Watch you should type only expressions that just read values. If you put in a function call that takes a long time or an expression that saves a file, it runs again every time you stop at a breakpoint, and debugging slows down or the file keeps being overwritten. That is why, when you handle tensors in Part 2, you do not put an expression like model(x) in Watch (if you only want to see the shape, read just the value, as in x.shape). Call Stack shows "which function you are in now, and who called that function." Debug case_report.py from Chapter 4 and you see the stack built up as from_row ← load_cases ← <module>. Debug Console is a window that runs Python expressions while the program is stopped. You can ask right away about whatever you are curious about, such as len(records) or r["claim"] * 2.

5.3 Walking through someone else's code: the comprehensive example from Chapter 4

[Basic] Open case_report.py from Chapter 4. This time, walk through it with the debugger before reading the code.

  1. Set a breakpoint on the cases, skipped = load_cases(path) line at the very bottom and start debugging.
  2. When it stops, press F11 (Step Into). The yellow line jumps into the first line of the load_cases function. In Call Stack, load_cases is stacked on top of <module>.
  3. Move ahead one line at a time with F10, and at cases.append(Case.from_row(row)) press F11 again. This time you go inside from_row. Expand row in Variables and one row of the CSV appears as a dictionary. Confirm that all the values are text (the point made in Section 4.3).
  4. Leave from_row with Shift+F11, and repeat going into the next row with F11. At the sixth row you see the moment int("미정") ("undecided") fails and execution jumps to except.

[Basic] Once you have walked through it like this, the flow "one row of the CSV is read as a dictionary, it is turned into a Case object, and if that fails it piles up in skipped" sinks in without any explanation. This is exactly the second of the three code-reading steps in Chapter 8 ("run it").

[Intermediate] You can also have it stop automatically at the moment an exception occurs. In the Breakpoints list at the bottom of the Run and Debug panel there are three entries that stop when an exception occurs. Raised Exceptions (stops whenever an exception is raised; off by default), Uncaught Exceptions (stops when the program ends with an unhandled exception; on by default), and User Uncaught Exceptions (stops when an exception passes out into library code; off by default). The names may differ between versions. If you turn on Raised Exceptions, it stops the moment an exception occurs even when the exception is quietly handled inside a try, so it is the fastest way when you do not know where an exception occurs. But it also stops at normal exceptions inside libraries, so turn it off when you are done. Uncaught Exceptions is on by default, so you can leave it as it is.

5.4 launch.json: writing down in a file how to run the program

[Basic] So far you have debugged "the file that is open now." But a program that takes command-line arguments, like case_report.py in Chapter 4, or a program that has to run from a particular folder, needs a place to write down how it is run. That place is .vscode/launch.json.

[Basic] How to make it: in the Run and Debug panel, click the create a launch.json file link and choose Python Debugger → Python File. A .vscode/launch.json is created inside the working folder, with one default configuration in it. Here is an example with one more configuration added to that file.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "Python Debugger: Current File",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${file}",
            "console": "integratedTerminal",
            "cwd": "${fileDirname}",
            "justMyCode": true
        },
        {
            "name": "Python Debugger: case_report with args",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/ch04/case_report.py",
            "args": ["cases_all.csv"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal",
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}/ch04"
        }
    ]
}

[Basic] What each line means:

Entry Meaning
name The name shown in the drop-down of the Run and Debug panel
type: "debugpy" Marks that the Python debugger is used
program The file to run. ${file} is "the file open now," and ${workspaceFolder} is "the folder opened in VS Code"
args The list of command-line arguments. The latter part of python case_report.py cases_all.csv
console Where to show the output. integratedTerminal is the terminal at the bottom of VS Code
cwd The current folder when it runs. The thing that caused "the file cannot be found" in Chapter 4
justMyCode If true, it walks only through your code and does not go into libraries

[Basic] Once you have made a configuration, choose its name in the drop-down at the top of the Run and Debug panel and just press F5. Later, in Part 2, when you experiment by changing arguments, as in train.py --epochs 3 --lr 0.001, this book keeps several configurations with the arguments written in args and picks one to use (Chapter 13).

[Intermediate] If you set cwd to ${fileDirname}, the program runs in "the folder of the file open now," so code that opens a CSV next to the file with a relative path works as it is. It is the most practical setting for not having to cd every time. If you want to give different args each time, set "args": "${command:pickArgs}" and it asks you every time you run.

[Advanced] If you set justMyCode: false, F11 goes all the way inside PyTorch. When you wonder what the forward of nn.Linear actually does, it is worth going in once. But the internal code is huge, so if you go in without a purpose you get lost.

5.5 Conditional breakpoints and the Debug Console

[Basic] If there are 50,000 cases instead of 5, you cannot press F5 50,000 times. A conditional breakpoint is "stop only under this condition." Right-click the red dot → Edit Breakpoint, and type an expression.

r["case_no"] == "2099가합1004"

In English: 2099가합1004 = an invented case number (year 2099; case-type code 가합, gahap, a first-instance civil case before a panel of judges; serial 1004).

Now it stops only when that case's turn comes. If you choose Hit Count in the same box, you can also do "stop the nth time it passes." In Part 2 you use this feature to look at "why does the loss jump at the 100th training batch?"

[Basic] While the program is stopped, type a Python expression in the Debug Console (a tab in the bottom panel) and it is computed on the spot. r, r["claim"] / 10000, type(r["claim"]). You can change variables too. Type r["claim"] = 0 and press F5, and the program goes on with the changed value. This is a way to experiment with "what would have happened if this value had been this," without changing the code.

5.6 Without VS Code: breakpoint() and pdb

[Intermediate] In an environment with only a terminal (a remote server, or when you are in a hurry), use pdb, the debugger built into Python. Put the one line breakpoint() in your code, and the program stops there and shows the (Pdb) prompt.

# breakpoint() 는 VS Code 없이 터미널에서 쓰는 디버거(pdb)를 켭니다.
records = [{"claim": 100}, {"claim": 250}, {"claim": 50}]
total = 0
for r in records:
    breakpoint()          # 여기서 멈춥니다
    total += r["claim"]
print("합계:", total)

In English: the first comment says that breakpoint() turns on the debugger used in the terminal without VS Code (pdb); 여기서 멈춥니다 = it stops here; 합계: = Total:.

When you run it, it stops as follows. Below is the actual record of typing p r, p total, n, p total, c, c, and c in turn (the paths are shortened).

> ...\pdb_demo.py(5)<module>()
-> breakpoint()          # 여기서 멈춥니다
(Pdb) p r
{'claim': 100}
(Pdb) p total
0
(Pdb) n
> ...\pdb_demo.py(6)<module>()
-> total += r["claim"]
(Pdb) p total
0
(Pdb) c
> ...\pdb_demo.py(5)<module>()
-> breakpoint()          # 여기서 멈춥니다
(Pdb) c
> ...\pdb_demo.py(5)<module>()
-> breakpoint()          # 여기서 멈춥니다
(Pdb) c
합계: 400

[Intermediate] The commands correspond one to one with the VS Code buttons. n (next) = F10, s (step) = F11, r (return) = Shift+F11, c (continue) = F5, p expression (print) = Debug Console, and q quits. Five are enough. If you deploy code with breakpoint() left in it, it stops there, so be sure to delete it when you are done.

[Intermediate] In a notebook environment such as Colab, if you type %debug in the next cell right after a cell raises an error, pdb opens at the point where the error occurred (an IPython feature). This book did not run it to check.

5.7 Practice: finding three bugs

[Basic] bugs.py has three bugs. One raises an error, and two give a wrong value without an error. The expected output is written at the top of the file, so find them by comparing against it.

# 5장 실습: 이 파일에는 버그가 세 개 있습니다. 오류 메시지가 나는 것은 하나뿐이고,
# 나머지 둘은 조용히 틀린 값을 냅니다. 디버거로 찾으세요.
# 기대하는 출력:
#   사건 5건, 청구금액 합계 1,747,000,000원
#   유형별 건수: {'손해배상': 3, '대여금': 1, '부당이득': 1}
#   평균 처리일수: 269일

records = [
    {"case_no": "2099가합1001", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 420000000, "days": 310},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1002", "type": "대여금",   "claim": 150000000, "days": 198},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1003", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 880000000, "days": 455},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1004", "type": "부당이득", "claim": "67000000", "days": 120},
    {"case_no": "2099가합1005", "type": "손해배상", "claim": 230000000, "days": 260},
]


def total_claim(records):
    total = 0
    for r in records:
        total += r["claim"]
    return total


def count_by_type(records):
    counts = {}
    for r in records:
        t = r["type"]
        counts[t] = counts.get(t, 0) + 1
        return counts


def mean_days(records):
    total = 0
    for r in records:
        total += r["days"]
    return total / len(records) // 1


print(f"사건 {len(records)}건, 청구금액 합계 {total_claim(records):,}원")
print("유형별 건수:", count_by_type(records))
print(f"평균 처리일수: {mean_days(records):.0f}일")

In English: the header comment says: this file has three bugs; only one produces an error message, and the other two quietly give wrong values; find them with the debugger. 기대하는 출력 = expected output; 사건 …건, 청구금액 합계 …원 = … cases, total amount claimed … won; 유형별 건수 = count by type; 평균 처리일수: …일 = average days to disposition: … days; 손해배상 = damages; 대여금 = loan repayment; 부당이득 = unjust enrichment.

Run it as it is and you get this:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "...\bugs.py", line 39, in <module>
    print(f"사건 {len(records)}건, 청구금액 합계 {total_claim(records):,}원")
                                                  ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^
  File "...\bugs.py", line 20, in total_claim
    total += r["claim"]
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +=: 'int' and 'str'

[Basic] Look for them yourself first, then compare with the procedure below. The procedure, more than the answer, is what this chapter is about.

Bug 1 (raises an error). The message already tells you a lot. Line 20: it tried to add a str to an int. To see which case it is, set a breakpoint on line 20 and give it the condition type(r["claim"]) == str, and it stops only at the problem case. Expand r in Variables and claim: '67000000' is wrapped in quotation marks. The data is at fault, and you either make the code withstand it with int(r["claim"]) or fix the data.

Bug 2 (silent). Fix bug 1 and run it, and the count by type comes out as {'손해배상': 1}. Only one. Set a breakpoint on counts[t] = ... inside count_by_type and press F5. It stops only once and the program ends. The loop went around only once. Follow the yellow line with F10 and you see return counts run inside the first pass. The return is indented inside the for. One level of indentation is the bug, and though it is hard to see with your eyes, the debugger reveals it as "stops only once."

Bug 3 (silent). The average comes out as 268일 (days). The expected value is 269일. It is off by 1, so it is easy to mistake it for a problem in the data. Set a breakpoint on the return line of mean_days and type total / len(records) in the Debug Console, and you get 268.6. The return expression is total / len(records) // 1, and // 1 keeps only the quotient and throws away the decimal part (the two kinds of division in Chapter 3). So it becomes 268.0, and the :.0f format prints that as 268. If rounding was wanted, round() should have been used, and for an average the right thing is simply to return it with /.

[Basic] The fixed version is bugs_fixed.py. Output:

사건 5건, 청구금액 합계 1,747,000,000원
유형별 건수: {'손해배상': 3, '대여금': 1, '부당이득': 1}
평균 처리일수: 269일

[Basic] Look at what the three bugs have in common. Bugs without an error message are more dangerous. The program says it ran fine, and the result is wrong. In Part 2, the cause of "training seems to be going well, but the accuracy is odd" is usually of this kind, and the tools that catch it are the debugger and the verification habits of the next chapter.

Where people get stuck

[Basic] Confusing the Debug Console with the terminal is the classic mistake at the start. To print a variable while the program is stopped at a breakpoint, you have to type it in the Debug Console. If you type it in the terminal below, that is not the stopped program but a separate, new Python, so the variable you want to see cannot be there (you get a NameError). It is even more confusing if you have typed python in the terminal and started interactive Python. Commands typed in that state have nothing to do with the program being debugged.

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
The breakpoint is a gray circle, not a red dot The debugger does not treat that file as something it runs. Either you are not debugging, or justMyCode makes it treat the file as a library file. If it is your file, check program in launch.json
It does not stop at the breakpoint The program does not pass that line (the other branch of a conditional, a loop that runs 0 times). Set a breakpoint on the first line and follow along with F10
The debug run uses "a different Python" (import torch fails) Check that the interpreter from Section 2.5.4 is jucos. The debugger uses the interpreter shown in the status bar
The output does not appear If console is set to internalConsole, it appears in the Debug Console tab. integratedTerminal is recommended
A variable is missing from Variables Either that line has not run yet (a breakpoint stops just before it runs), or it is a local variable of another function. Click a frame in Call Stack to switch
F11 does not go into a function Built-in functions and libraries are skipped with justMyCode: true. If it is your own function and it does not go in, there is no call on that line
The program stops because breakpoint() was not removed Delete breakpoint() once you are done with it. If (Pdb) is showing, leave with q

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] The debugger and AI have different roles. AI quickly produces hypotheses, and the debugger confirms them. Give AI the error message from bugs.py and it will name several candidate causes, but which of them is the real one you can know only by looking with the debugger.

The error below occurred. Tell me three possible causes and, for each, how to confirm it with the debugger (which line to set the breakpoint on and what to look at). (paste the error message)

[Basic] Conversely, giving AI what you saw in the debugger makes its answers more accurate. If you write "I set a breakpoint in count_by_type, and it stops only once and then ends. The code is as follows," AI will almost certainly point to the indentation. Giving observed facts is the heart of a good question, and the debugger is the tool that produces those observations.

[Intermediate] It is also useful to ask AI "where in this function, and with what condition, should I put a conditional breakpoint?" It helps you decide where to look in a large body of code. But run the condition AI suggests in the Debug Console first to check that its syntax is right.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. Design an experiment that confirms that a breakpoint stops "just before that line runs," not "after that line has run."
  2. Press F10 and F11 in turn on the cases.append(Case.from_row(row)) line of case_report.py, and explain the difference.
  3. To find bug 2 of bugs.py by eye without the debugger, what would you have had to look at? How did the debugger reveal it?

[Intermediate]

  1. Add a configuration for case_records.py from Chapter 3 to launch.json, with cwd set to ch03. Explain why cwd is needed, connecting it to reading files in Chapter 4.
  2. Set the conditional breakpoint r["claim"] > 300000000 and count how many times it stops. How does it differ from Hit Count 3?
  3. Run pdb_demo.py in the terminal and see for yourself the difference between s and n. Why do the two look the same in this example?

[Advanced]

  1. Set justMyCode: false and use F11 to go into sorted(records, key=lambda r: r["claim"]). How far in can you go, and what do you see? Based on that experience, explain why the default is true.

Part 1

Chapter 6. AI coding assistants: how to instruct them, how not to trust them

What you get from this chapter

  • You can sort AI coding tools into three layers (chat window, editor integration, agent) and know what can be used for free in each layer as of November 2026.
  • You know, with evidence, what AI does well and what it does not, and you learn a four-step procedure for using it on the premise of verification.
  • You practice the three forms of a good request (comment skeleton, shape of the data, observed facts) on the code of Chapters 3 to 5.
  • You draw the line around what must not be given to AI in connection with your work.

Who can skip this chapter You are advised not to skip this chapter. You may already know how to use the tools, but the verification procedure in Section 6.4 and the principle in Section 6.5 are premises of this whole book.

6.0 Tools change, principles remain

[Basic] This is the chapter of this book that will go out of date fastest. Tool names, prices, and free limits change every few months. So it is split into two parts. The principles (Sections 6.2 to 6.5) stay the same when the tools change, and the state of the tools (Sections 6.1 and 6.6) carries the date "checked on November 17, 2026." If that date is old, check the current state again at the links in Section 6.6.

[Basic] One thing you have already experienced in the earlier chapters. In the box in Chapter 3 you had AI explain code, and in the box in Chapter 5 you received candidate causes for an error and confirmed them with the debugger. This chapter puts that experience into a system.

6.1 Three layers

[Basic] AI coding tools fall into three layers by "where they meet you."

Layer Where What it does Representative tools as of 2026-11 (free or not)
Chat window A chat in the browser or an app Questions, explanations, code generation. You copy and paste the result yourself Claude (free tier available), ChatGPT (free tier available), Gemini (free tier available)
Editor integration Inside VS Code or Colab Completion suggestions as you type, explaining or editing selected code, chat inside the editor GitHub Copilot (free plan: 2,000 completions a month, limited usage for chat and agent), Gemini in Colab (Learn Mode, Custom Instructions), the Claude Code extension for VS Code (requires a paid subscription or a usage-billed account)
Agent The terminal or a dedicated app Reads the whole folder, edits files, runs commands, and carries out several steps on its own Claude Code (Pro subscription or higher, or usage billing), Codex CLI (log in with a ChatGPT account; the CLI is on the Plus plan or higher), Antigravity CLI (Google; free use available with a personal account. The earlier Gemini CLI has been for enterprise licenses or paid API keys since June 18, 2026)

[Basic] For Part 1 of this book, the chat window and the free tier of editor integration are enough. Try installing an agent in Section 6.6 after you have learned Chapter 7 (Git), but you can do without one until the later chapters of Part 2. An agent edits files directly, so using one without a way to undo (Chapter 7) is dangerous.

[Intermediate] The higher the layer, the more the AI does and the less you see. In a chat window you carry the code over yourself, so you see it line by line, but an agent edits ten files and says "done." The degree of automation and the burden of review are not inversely proportional. They are directly proportional. The more convenient it gets, the more deliberately you have to review.

6.2 What AI does well and what it does not, with evidence

[Basic] First, what it does well. These are tasks within the scope of this book where AI is faster than a person and mostly accurate.

  • Syntax and boilerplate code. Code at the level of Chapter 4, such as reading files, loops, and tallying with a dictionary, is almost never wrong.
  • Interpreting error messages. Paste in any of the six errors from Chapter 3 and it identifies the cause well.
  • Explanation. Working through someone else's code line by line. You use this in the code reading of Chapter 8.
  • Translation. Another expression with the same meaning, such as "this loop as a list comprehension" or "this csv code in pandas."

[Basic] Next, what it does not do well, or what calls for care.

  • It states things that do not exist as if they did (hallucination). Function names that do not exist, options a library does not have. Advice that used to be right but is now wrong, like the "conda install pytorch -c pytorch" in the Chapter 2 box, is especially common. This is because an AI's knowledge stops at some point in time.
  • Silent logic errors. AI also produces code that gives wrong values with no error message, like bugs 2 and 3 in Chapter 5. And AI does not run its own code (agent tools sometimes do run it, but judging whether the result is right is still the person's job).
  • Security weaknesses. Here there are measurements. A study that analyzed 733 code snippets generated by three tools, Copilot, CodeWhisperer, and Codeium, in public projects on GitHub (Fu et al., ACM TOSEM 2025) found security weaknesses in 29.5% of the Python snippets and 24.2% of the JavaScript snippets, and identified 43 types of weakness. An earlier study (Pearce et al., IEEE S&P 2022) reported that about 40% of 1,689 programs generated in 89 scenarios were vulnerable. Both studies are measurements of particular tools at particular times and cannot be applied as they are to today's tools, but the conclusion that "a substantial share of AI code is not good enough to use without review" is consistent.
  • It does not know the shape of your data. As the Chapter 3 box said, if you do not tell it the structure of the data, it makes one up.

[Basic] In short, AI is a drafter, not a reviewer. The reviewer is you. You take the AI's code and review it the way you take a draft brief that someone else wrote and review it. Just as no lawyer files a draft without reading it, you must not become a user who runs code without reading it.

[Intermediate] The studies above counted security weaknesses (CWE). They did not measure "the code was wrong." Within the range this book checked, no large-scale measurement of general functional error rates was found (no quantitative evidence found; search scope: arXiv and academic search, 2026-09-06). There are many benchmark scores (for example, the share of coding problems answered correctly), but those are not the same thing as "the share of code received by real users that meets the requirement."

6.3 Three forms of a good request

[Basic] What you say to AI, and how, is half the result. This book uses three forms, and all of them have already appeared in earlier chapters.

Form 1: give a comment skeleton and have it filled in. This is the habit of "writing the logic as comments first" before typing code. Those comments become the request as they are.

Fill in Python code according to the comment skeleton below. Python 3.13, standard library only.

# cases_all.csv 를 읽는다 (utf-8-sig)
# 각 행을 Case 객체로 만든다. claim 은 쉼표를 제거하고 int 로. 실패한 행은 건너뛰고 기록한다
# 유형별 건수와 청구금액 합계를 출력한다

In English: the three comment lines say: read cases_all.csv (utf-8-sig); turn each row into a Case object, converting claim to int after removing commas, and skip and record the rows that fail; print the number of cases for each type and the total amount claimed.

The advantage of this form is that you decided the structure. The AI only turns sentences into code, and review becomes as simple as "does it follow the comments?" The "Add comments" stage of the three practice stages was practice in making this skeleton.

Form 2: state the shape of the data. This appeared in the Chapter 3 box.

Each case is a dictionary with the keys case_no, type, claim, result, and days, and there is a list records of such dictionaries. claim is an integer (in won). …

If you do not state the shape, the AI assumes a common shape (a pandas DataFrame, for example), and that assumption does not fit your code.

Form 3: give observed facts. This appeared in the Chapter 5 box. The whole error message, the values of variables you saw in the debugger, observations such as "it stops once and then ends." "This is what happens" is a hundred times better than "it doesn't work."

[Intermediate] There is something to attach to all three forms. Environment information (Python 3.13, PyTorch 2.14, Windows 11, CPU only) and constraints (standard library only, no pandas, and so on). If you do not state the environment, the AI may answer for an old version or a different operating system.

6.4 The four verification steps

[Basic] Code from AI becomes yours after it has gone through the following four steps. The earlier chapters are the tools for each step.

Figure 6-1. The verification cycle for AI code. On failure, go back with observed facts (form 3).

  1. Read it. Compare it with the comment skeleton (form 1). If the AI added something that is not in the skeleton, ask why. If there is a function you do not know, ask about that first.
  2. Run it. In your environment, with your data. "It worked in the example" is not a run.
  3. Walk through it. If the result looks odd or the code is long, take one lap with the debugger (Section 5.3).
  4. Test it. Check it with a small input whose answer you know. Python's assert is the simplest tool.
def count_by(records, key):
    counts = {}
    for r in records:
        counts[r[key]] = counts.get(r[key], 0) + 1
    return counts

records = [{"type": "손해배상"}, {"type": "대여금"}, {"type": "손해배상"}]
assert count_by(records, "type") == {"손해배상": 2, "대여금": 1}
assert count_by([], "type") == {}
print("count_by: 테스트 2개 통과")

def mean_days(records):
    return sum(r["days"] for r in records) / len(records) // 1   # 5장의 버그를 일부러 남김

try:
    assert mean_days([{"days": 1}, {"days": 2}]) == 1.5, "평균이 틀립니다"
except AssertionError as e:
    print("mean_days: 실패 ->", e)

In English: 손해배상 = damages; 대여금 = loan repayment; "테스트 2개 통과" = "2 tests passed"; "평균이 틀립니다" = "the mean is wrong"; the comment on mean_days says the Chapter 5 bug is left in on purpose.

count_by: 테스트 2개 통과
mean_days: 실패 -> 평균이 틀립니다

In English: 실패 = failed.

[Basic] assert condition, message raises an AssertionError on the spot if the condition is false. Just by putting in inputs whose answers you know (with 3 cases, 2 damages and 1 loan repayment; the mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5), the silent bug from Chapter 5 was caught. When you receive code from AI, if you also ask it to "write three assert tests for this function too," the tests have the added effect of documenting the intent of the code. But the fact that tests written by AI pass on code written by AI does not make the code right. You have to calculate the expected values by hand and put them in yourself.

[Intermediate] When there are several tests, pytest is convenient. Collect functions whose names start with test_ and the single command pytest runs them all. In Part 2, the tests that check whether a Dataset returns tensors of the right shape are written this way.

6.5 What must not be given

[Basic] This section is short, but it is the firmest part of this book.

Do not enter case files, information about clients and parties, unpublished judgments and briefs, or the internal documents of your institution into an AI service. The moment you paste them into a chat window, the content is sent to an outside server, and under the terms of service it may be retained or used to improve the model. The terms differ by service, by plan, and over time, so the general statement "this service is safe" does not hold.

[Basic] This is why every example in this book uses invented cases. When you write code or ask about an error, you almost never need real data. Make fictional data with only the same shape, like records in Chapter 3, and ask your question with that. Use a fake case number that only has the right format, like 2099가합1001 (year 2099, case-type code 가합 for a first-instance civil case before a panel of judges, serial 1001), call the parties "plaintiff" and "defendant," and use any number for the amount.

[Basic] With agent-type tools there is one more thing to be careful about. They read the whole folder. If you start an agent in a folder that contains case materials, those materials can be read and sent. Start an agent only in a folder that has nothing but code (the repository of Chapter 7). This is one more reason why Section 7.6 told you to keep the repository and the data apart.

6.6 Getting started with each tool (checked 2026-11-17)

[Basic] These are in the order you need them to follow this book. All are for personal accounts.

Chat window. Create a free account on at least one of Claude (claude.ai), ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), and Gemini (gemini.google.com). All three have a free plan, and the free plan is enough for code generation and explanation. The requests in the boxes of this book can be used as they are on any of them.

Gemini in Colab. Open it with the Gemini icon at the top right of the Colab notebook you made in Chapter 2. Learn Mode, added in April 2026, is a "tutor" mode that guides you step by step instead of writing the code for you, and it fits the purpose of the practice in this book. If you write something like "Python 3.13, standard library first, explanations in Korean" in Custom Instructions, you do not have to say it every time. The scope of what is provided to free accounts was not stated in the official documentation at the time of checking.

GitHub Copilot Free. You need the GitHub account from Chapter 7. Install GitHub Copilot from Extensions in VS Code and log in with GitHub. The free plan gives 2,000 completions a month, and chat and agent mode can be used to a limited extent within a usage unit called "GitHub AI credits." The number of credits in the free plan is not published (github.com/features/copilot/plans, 2026-11-17). Completion suggestions appear in gray text as you type, and you accept them with Tab. You are advised to keep completions turned off for the first month. "Follow along" in Chapters 3 and 4 means something only if you type with your own hands, and autocompletion does that for you.

Agents. Try these after you finish Chapter 7.

  • Claude Code: Install it with irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex in Windows PowerShell or curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash in the Mac terminal, and run claude in your project folder. There are also a VS Code extension and a desktop app. To use it you need a Claude Pro subscription (USD 20 a month, or USD 17 a month billed annually) or higher, or a usage-billed account. It is not included in the free chat plan. On Windows, having Git for Windows (Chapter 7) installed is recommended.
  • Codex CLI (OpenAI): On Mac and Linux, curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh. On Windows, a native or WSL installation is described. Run codex in your project folder and log in with a ChatGPT account. The official pricing documentation (checked 2026-11-17) lists the CLI used in the terminal as an item of the Plus plan (USD 20 a month) or higher. The Free (USD 0) and Go plans list only Codex used in the desktop app, and even that comes with the proviso that it is being rolled out gradually.
  • Antigravity CLI (Google): Google's terminal agent. Download it from antigravity.google/download, install it, and run it with agy. It can be used for free with a personal Google account. The figures for the free limit could not be confirmed. The open-source Gemini CLI (npm install -g @google/gemini-cli) used to stand in this place, but from June 18, 2026, free personal use and use under Google AI plans were moved to Antigravity CLI. Gemini CLI can now be used only with an enterprise Gemini Code Assist license or a paid API key (Gemini CLI GitHub README, 2026-11-17). If an old article describes a free limit for Gemini CLI, it no longer applies.

[Basic] Prices and free limits may have changed since the date this book was checked. Before you pay, check each service's pricing page yourself.

6.7 Rules of use in this book

[Basic] From here on, this is how AI is used in every chapter.

Practice stage Use of AI
Follow along Not used. Type by hand, one line at a time. Turn off autocompletion too
Add comments Write your own comments first, and ask AI "what does this line do" only for the lines where you are stuck
Rebuild If you are stuck, ask only for a hint ("just the next line"). Do not accept finished code
The AI box of the chapter Practice requests of forms 1 to 3 on that chapter's code, and verify with the four steps of Section 6.4

[Basic] There will come a moment when this rule feels stifling. That is the moment the rule is working. After the middle of Part 2, once you can read and change training code, you can relax the rule. By then you will already have the eye to review code that AI gives you.

Where people get stuck

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
Code from AI fails at import The module does not exist or is not installed. Search for the module name to confirm that it exists, then pip install
Code from AI uses a different Python syntax (print "x", xrange) Material from the Python 2 era. State "for Python 3.13"
The answer to the same question is different every time Normal. AI answers probabilistically. If the results diverge, verify with Section 6.4 and choose one
The AI says "I have checked" but it is wrong AI does not run the code (or misreads what the result of a run means). Run it yourself
Copilot completions get in the way of practice Turn completions off from the Copilot icon in the status bar. Turning them off during the Follow along stage is the rule
An agent has changed a pile of files Chapter 7. Commit before the work, diff after the work, or else git restore .

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] The box in this chapter is a meta question. Ask AI about AI.

Tell me the five kinds of mistake you commonly make when you generate Python code, and how the user should verify each of them.

Compare the answer with Section 6.2. They usually overlap, and the AI itself will tell you to "run it." AI, too, tells you to verify it. Do as it says.

[Intermediate] Making the same request to two tools and comparing the answers is also good verification. If the two differ, where they differ is exactly what to review. If the two agree, there is no guarantee that they are right, but where they differ is a place you must look.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. Summarize each of the three forms of Section 6.3 in one sentence, and match the boxes in Chapters 3 to 5 to the forms they used.
  2. Add one more test of count_by to the assert example in Section 6.4. Calculate the expected value by hand.
  3. Point out what is wrong with the following request. "This is my case file. Write code that predicts the outcome of the judgment. (case file pasted in)"

[Intermediate]

  1. Write a form 1 comment skeleton for case_report.py from Chapter 4, have AI fill it in, and compare it with the original using diff (Chapter 7). What was different?
  2. Why is it wrong to restate the 29.5% figure of the Fu et al. (2025) study as "30% of AI code is wrong"? Explain it with the data type analogy of Chapter 3 (what was counted).

[Advanced]

  1. Install pytest, write a test file test_case_report.py for Case.from_row in case_report.py, and run it. Include three cases: an amount with commas, "미정" (undecided), and an empty string.
