Part 1

Chapter 7. Git and GitHub: seeing what changed, undoing it, and keeping a record

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn how to keep changes to code as snapshots, see what changed between two points in time, and undo a change if it went wrong.
  • You use six Git commands (init, status, add, commit, diff, log) and undoing (restore), and learn how to do the same things in the Source Control view of VS Code.
  • You learn how to create a repository on GitHub, upload to it, and download it on another computer.
  • You get the tools for the habit of reviewing only the changes after AI has edited your code.

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I have used git add, git commit, and git diff.
  • [ ] I know what .gitignore is.
  • [ ] I have created a repository on GitHub and pushed to it.

If all three are "yes," you can read only Section 7.7 (AI and Git).

7.0 Why Git now

[Basic] In traditional coding courses, Git comes several weeks in. That is because it is seen as a collaboration tool. This book puts it in the first part. The reason connects to Chapter 6. Where AI edits your code, the ability to see "what changed" is the ability to review. When an AI tool has changed ten files at once, review is impossible without a tool that picks out and shows only the lines that changed. Git's diff is that tool.

[Basic] To compare it to a lawyer's work, Git is version control for records. You have probably saved drafts of a brief as 서면_v1.hwp, 서면_v2_수정.hwp, and 서면_최종_진짜최종.hwp (brief_v1, brief_v2_revised, brief_final_really-final). Git does that job systematically. It does not rename files; it leaves a snapshot at each point in time, shows the difference between two snapshots line by line, and lets you go back to any point.

7.1 Three concepts

[Basic] You need three concepts to understand Git.

Concept Meaning Analogy
Repository A history archive attached to a project folder. Its substance is .git, a hidden folder inside that folder The case file binder
Commit A snapshot of all the files at one point in time, plus a message A record stamped with the date
Stage (staging area) A waiting area where you set aside the changes to go into the next commit The tray of documents waiting to be filed

Figure 7-1. Changes flow from the working folder → the stage → the repository, and undoing goes the other way. GitHub keeps a copy of the repository on the internet.

[Basic] Why is there an intermediate step called the stage? So that when you have edited several files at once, you can group related changes together into a commit. If you mix "add error handling" and "fix a typo" in one commit, the history is hard to read later. At first it is enough to make "everything you changed into one commit," and you will come to feel what the stage is for, without trying, as your code grows.

7.2 Installation and first-time setup

[Basic] Check in the terminal (the Anaconda Prompt from Chapter 2, or Terminal on a Mac).

git --version

If it shows something like git version 2.50.1.windows.1, you already have it. If not:

  • Windows: Download and install Git for Windows from git-scm.com. You can leave the installation options at their defaults. VS Code may also show installation guidance when it detects that Git is missing.
  • Mac: Type git --version in Terminal, and if Git is missing it asks whether to install the command line tools. Click Install.

[Basic] There is a setting you make only once after installation: the name and email that record "who" for each commit. They do not have to be your real name, but using the same email as your GitHub account makes things easier later.

git config --global user.name "Hong Gildong"
git config --global user.email "hong@example.com"

7.3 Six commands

[Basic] Make a new folder gitdemo to hold caselib.py from Chapter 4, and work inside it. Below is the record of an actual run (only the paths are shortened).

1) git init: makes this folder a repository.

git init

Initialized empty Git repository in .../gitdemo/.git/

2) git status: shows the current state. This is the command you use most often. When in doubt, status first.

On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

Now create caselib.py and write two lines in it. Then git status --short again:

?? caselib.py

?? means "a file Git does not know yet (untracked)."

3) git add: puts it on the stage.

git add caselib.py

git status --short changes to A caselib.py. A means it is to be added. To put all changes on the stage at once, use git add . (the dot means "everything in the current folder").

4) git commit: takes a snapshot.

git commit -m "caselib: total 함수 추가"

In English: "caselib: total 함수 추가" = "caselib: add total function".

What follows -m is the message. Write what you changed and why in one line. Messages like "fix" or "update" give you no information later.

5) git diff: shows what changed. After editing the second line of caselib.py:

diff --git a/caselib.py b/caselib.py
index 2d08a0f..ceb3a29 100644
--- a/caselib.py
+++ b/caselib.py
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 def total(amounts):
-    return sum(amounts)
+    return sum(int(a) for a in amounts)   # 글자가 섞여도 견디게

In English: 글자가 섞여도 견디게 = so that it copes even when text is mixed in.

[Basic] A - line is what was deleted, a + line is what was newly added, and a line with no mark in front is unchanged context. This screen is the heart of this chapter. When AI edits a file, you review it on this screen. You need to look only at the changed lines, so even if the file is 500 lines long, the review is a few lines.

6) git log: shows the history. After you add and commit the change:

git log --oneline

fe3f53a total: 글자 금액도 처리
38d463f caselib: total 함수 추가

In English: "total: 글자 금액도 처리" = "total: also handle amounts written as text".

The first seven characters are the beginning of the unique number (hash) attached to each commit. git log -1 -p also shows the diff of the last commit.

[Basic] Memorize the six commands as one flow. Edit → look with status → check with diff → add → commit → see with log that it was recorded. For the first few times, just follow this order as it is.

[Intermediate] On Windows, when you git add, a warning like warning: in the working copy of 'caselib.py', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it appears. It is a notice that comes from the line-ending character being different on Windows (CRLF) and on Mac and Linux (LF), and it is not an error. Python reads both, so you can ignore it, and if it bothers you, set git config --global core.autocrlf true (Windows).

7.4 .gitignore: what to keep out of the history

[Basic] There are files you should not put in the repository. The __pycache__ folder that Python makes automatically, the training results folder and the weight files of hundreds of MB that will appear in Part 2, and the VS Code settings. Make a file called .gitignore at the top of the folder and write them in it, one per line, and Git treats them as if they did not exist.

__pycache__/
*.pyc
results/
data/
*.pt
*.ckpt
.vscode/

[Basic] .gitignore itself is committed. That way the same rules apply on other computers too.

[Intermediate] There is one more reason, besides size, for excluding data and weights. GitHub warns about files larger than 50MiB and blocks files larger than 100MiB, and it recommends that a repository be ideally under 1GB. If in Part 2 you commit the CIFAR10 data (about 170MB) or a trained model by mistake, the push is blocked. Putting data/ and results/ on the exclusion list from the start is the convention in this book.

7.5 Doing the same things in VS Code

[Basic] Now that you know the commands, you can use buttons instead. Open the icon of three dots joined by lines in the vertical menu on the left of VS Code (Source Control, Ctrl+Shift+G).

What you want to do VS Code operation Same command
Create a repository The Initialize Repository button git init
See the changed files The Changes list. Click a file for the side-by-side comparison (diff) git status, git diff
Put on the stage + next to the file git add
Commit Type in the message box at the top, then Commit git commit -m
See the history Timeline at the bottom of the Explorer (per file), or the graph view git log
Undo ↶ next to the file (Discard Changes) git restore

[Basic] In particular, get used to the side-by-side comparison that opens when you click a file. The left is the last commit, the right is the file as it is now, and the changed lines are marked in color. You use this screen in Chapter 6 when you review code that AI has edited.

[Intermediate] The ✨ icon in the commit message box is a feature in which AI (Copilot and others) reads the changes and writes the message for you. It is convenient, but check that the message matches the actual changes by comparing it with the diff.

7.6 GitHub: keeping a copy on the internet

[Basic] Git is the history inside your computer, and GitHub is a service that keeps a copy of that repository on the internet. It serves as a backup, lets you continue working on another computer, and lets you show your work to others. A free account is enough.

  1. Create an account at github.com.
  2. At the top right, + → New repository. Enter a name such as ai_coding and choose Private (even for practice code, private is safer at first). Do not check "Add a README file" (because you already have a repository locally). Create repository.
  3. The easiest way to connect is from VS Code. Click Publish to GitHub in the … menu of the Source Control view or on its prompt button, and it takes you through a sign-in window, creates the repository, and uploads to it. If you use this method, you can skip step 2.
  4. To do it with commands, copy and run the two lines that GitHub shows right after the repository is created.
git remote add origin https://github.com/<계정>/ai_coding.git
git push -u origin main

In English: <계정> = (your GitHub account name).

[Basic] From then on, you push (upload) each time you commit, and on another computer you pull (download). The sync icon in the VS Code status bar does both at once. The first time you download to another computer, it is a clone (copy).

git clone https://github.com/<계정>/ai_coding.git

In VS Code, Clone Git Repository… on the Welcome page or Git: Clone in the Command Palette does the same thing.

[Intermediate] Do not put a Git repository inside a Google Drive folder. Chapter 2 told you to keep your code in Drive, but .git, the hidden folder of a Git repository, is made up of thousands of small files, so it often conflicts with Drive sync, and in the worst case the history breaks. The recommended setup is this. Keep the code repository outside Drive (for example, C:\Users\<account>\code\ai_coding) and sync it through GitHub, fetch it in Colab with git clone, and keep only data and training results in Drive. The ai_coding folder you made in Drive in Chapter 2 can stay, for data and notebooks.

[Intermediate] The moment you upload to GitHub, the content is stored on an internet service. Do not upload case-related material or personal information, even to a Private repository. It is the same principle as in Chapter 6.

7.7 AI and Git: what this chapter is really for

[Basic] Among the AI tools covered in Chapter 6, the agent type (Claude Code, Codex CLI, and others) edits files directly. Fix the order of work for those times with Git.

  1. Commit before you give AI a task. This leaves a clean starting point.
  2. After AI has edited, use git status to see which files changed, and git diff (or the VS Code comparison view) to see only the changed lines.
  3. If you like the result, commit. If not, undo.
git restore caselib.py          # 이 파일을 마지막 커밋 상태로
git restore .                   # 모든 파일을

In English: 이 파일을 마지막 커밋 상태로 = this file, back to its state at the last commit; 모든 파일을 = all files.

[Basic] Let's actually try it. Suppose AI edited the total function wrongly: change it to return 0, and then:

$ git status --short
 M caselib.py
$ git diff --stat
 caselib.py | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git restore caselib.py
$ git status --short
(아무것도 없음 = 깨끗함)

In English: (아무것도 없음 = 깨끗함) = (nothing shown = clean).

Open the file and it is back to the original code. Whatever AI does, you can always go back to the state you committed. You need this safety net before you can hand AI a big job.

[Intermediate] There are other levels of undoing too. git restore --staged file only takes the file off the stage and leaves the changes in the working folder. To cancel something you have already committed, git revert <hash> makes a new "cancellation commit" (it does not erase history, so it is safe). git reset --hard erases the history itself, so this book does not use it.

[Advanced] For big experiments, use branches. Make a branch with git switch -c experiment-lr, change things freely inside it, and if it works, merge it into main; if it does not, throw the branch away. In Part 2, an experiment such as "let's try a different optimizer" is one branch. It is not within this book's required scope, but if you have an AI agent make a branch when you give it an experiment, main is always safe.

Where people get stuck

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
git commit refuses with "Please tell me who you are" You have not set user.name and user.email from Section 7.2
fatal: not a git repository You ran it outside the repository folder. Move there with cd, or git init
The LF will be replaced by CRLF warning Not an error (Section 7.3, [Intermediate])
A push is refused for exceeding 100MB You committed data or weights. Add them to .gitignore and remove them from the commit (git rm --cached file)
Source Control is empty in VS Code The folder you opened is not a repository. Initialize Repository
The repository in a Drive folder behaves strangely (files vanish or are duplicated) Drive sync conflict (Section 7.6, [Intermediate]). Move the repository outside Drive
GitHub sign-in refuses your password in the terminal Use a token or the VS Code sign-in instead of a password. Publish/Sync in VS Code is the easiest

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] Git is a good subject to ask AI about. There are many commands and the messages are unfamiliar. But if AI suggests a command that erases history (reset --hard, push --force, clean -f), be sure to ask what it means before you run it. These are among the few commands that cannot be undone.

git status showed the following. Explain the current state, and tell me what to do to commit these changes. (paste the output)

[Basic] Conversely, it is also good to have AI explain the diff of code that AI edited. "Summarize in three lines what the diff below changes. Point out any changes that were not intended." Here the diff is not code but a record of changes, so it is hard for AI to make up an explanation.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. If you only do git commit without git add, what is committed? Try it.
  2. Explain the difference between git diff and git diff --staged. (Hint: which arrow in Figure 7-1 is it?)
  3. If you put data/ in .gitignore, what happens to a data/ folder that was already committed?

[Intermediate]

  1. Plant a bug in case_report.py from Chapter 4 and commit it, then cancel it with git revert, and see what remains in git log.
  2. Explain why it is risky to keep a repository inside a Google Drive folder, connecting it to the structure of the .git folder.

[Advanced]

  1. Make a branch and edit caselib.py, go back to main and confirm that the file is as it was, and then merge.

Stage What to do
Follow along Run the six commands of Section 7.3 in the gitdemo folder exactly as written, through the undo in Section 7.7
Add comments After each command, write "how which box in Figure 7-1 changed before and after this command"
Rebuild Make a new ai_coding repository outside Drive that collects the code from Chapters 3 and 4, add a .gitignore, commit chapter by chapter, and upload it to GitHub (Private). Clone it into another folder and confirm that it runs

Part 1

Chapter 8. Code-reading practice: other people's code, AI's code

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn a procedure for reading unfamiliar code in three steps (trace the flow → run → implement a small piece), and apply it to one real piece of public code.
  • That code is the MNIST training script from the official PyTorch examples (143 lines in this book's file). You read it first, as the finished form of what you will build in Part 2.
  • You practice having AI explain code and finding what is wrong in its explanation. This is what this book means by code reading in the age of AI.
  • You repeat this procedure in the "code reading" assignment at the end of every chapter of Part 2.

Who can skip this chapter Skipping this chapter is not recommended. It is the first place where the tools of Part 1 (Python, the debugger, AI, Git) are used together on one real piece of code, and the whole of Part 2 is a process of building, piece by piece, the code this chapter reads.

8.0 Reading comes before writing

[Basic] Put in one sentence, the conclusion of Part 1 is that "coding in 2026 is more reading than writing." Chapter 3 gave the reason, and in Chapter 6 you saw measurements showing that much of AI's code is not good enough to use without review. Then reading has to be trained, and reading is not something you do by "just looking." Just as lawyers read a case file in an order (the outline of the case → the issues → the evidence), code too has an order in which it is read.

[Basic] This chapter fixes that order as three steps and applies it to one real piece of code. The code is the MNIST (handwritten digits) classification example that PyTorch provides officially. The file in code/08/ is 143 lines, and everything you will build in Part 2 (loading data, the model, the training loop, evaluation, saving, command-line arguments) is in it. It is normal not to understand even half of this code now. The goal is not understanding but knowing "what is where," and when you finish Part 2 you will be able to read all of this code. You read it once now so that you can compare before and after.

8.1 Three steps

Figure 8-1. The three steps of code reading. At each step AI assists, and you do the verifying.

Step What you do Tools How far to go
1. Trace the flow List the definitions (def, class), and starting from the entry point (if __name__ == "__main__":), draw the order of calls The editor's search, Chapter 4 In most cases this is enough
2. Run Run it in your environment, walk through it once with the debugger, and look at the shapes of the data The Chapter 2 environment, the Chapter 5 debugger When the flow alone does not make it clear, or when you need to check values
3. Implement a small piece Take out one piece (one function, one class), rewrite it by hand, and compare it with the original Chapters 3 and 4, diff from Chapter 7 When you need to make that piece your own

[Basic] The three steps are an order of depth, not a required course. For most other people's code, all you need from step 1 is "what the code does." Step 2 is for when you need to use that code, and step 3 for when you need to change it or learn from it.

8.2 Step 1: trace the flow

[Basic] Open mnist_main.py in VS Code (it is in code/08/; the original source and the license are written at the top of the file). Do not read the 143 lines from the top. Instead, look for three things.

First, the list of definitions. Put def and class into the editor search (Ctrl+F), or extract them in the terminal.

14:class Net(nn.Module):
40:def train(args, model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch):
57:def test(model, device, test_loader):
76:def main():

Only four. In 30 seconds you have learned that this code is made of "one model, a training function, an evaluation function, and a main that ties them together." It is the same structure as when you built caselib, Case, load_cases, report, and main in Chapter 4.

Second, the entry point. At the very bottom, if __name__ == '__main__': main(). So you read from main(). Picking out only the lines inside main() that call other definitions:

134:        train(args, model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch)
135:        test(model, device, test_loader)
136:        scheduler.step()
139:        torch.save(model.state_dict(), "mnist_cnn.pt")

These four are inside and around for epoch in range(...). That is, "for each epoch, train → test → scheduler.step, and save at the end." That is the whole flow of this code.

Third, the preparation part of main(). Skim from the top, just the names, what is prepared before train is called. parser (arguments), device (CPU/accelerator), transform, dataset1, dataset2 (data), train_loader, test_loader (data supply), model, optimizer, scheduler. The ingredients of training appear in turn. Data, model, loss (F.nll_loss inside train), optimizer, and the loop that runs them.

[Basic] That is step 1, and it takes 10 minutes. Write down now what you did not understand. nn.Conv2d, F.log_softmax, Adadelta, StepLR, Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,))… That is normal. That list is the table of contents of Part 2, and Section 8.6 has a table of which chapter resolves each item.

[Intermediate] If you draw a flow diagram, it stays with you. main → [preparation] → for: train → test → step → save. Five boxes in Mermaid or on paper are enough. When code runs to thousands of lines, this diagram becomes a map. When you view code on GitHub, clicking a function name takes you to its definition, and from the definition you can see "where it is used" (references), so you do the same thing with clicks. In VS Code it is F12 (Go to Definition) and Shift+F12 (Go to References).

8.3 Step 2: run it and walk through it

[Basic] This code can be run. The data (MNIST, about 64MB) is downloaded automatically the first time you run it. Full training (14 epochs) takes a long time on a CPU, so run it with the --dry-run option (one batch only) that the example provides. Move to the code/08 folder in the terminal and:

python mnist_main.py --dry-run --no-accel --epochs 1

(내려받기 진행률 …)
Train Epoch: 1 [0/60000 (0%)]   Loss: 2.329474

Test set: Average loss: 2.2906, Accuracy: 1010/10000 (10%)

In English: (내려받기 진행률 …) = (download progress …).

[Basic] Let's read the two lines. The first batch of the 60,000 training images was trained on once, and the loss was 2.33. Accuracy on the 10,000 test images is 10%. There are ten digits, so the level that a model that has learned nothing reaches by guessing is exactly 10%. It was trained on only one batch, so this is to be expected. The purpose of this run is not accuracy but confirming that "the code runs to the end in your environment." On this computer it took 29 seconds, including the download.

[Basic] Now walk through it with the debugger (Chapter 5). Set a breakpoint on the train(args, model, ...) line inside main() and start debugging, and when it stops, look at the following in Variables.

  • Expand args and all the command-line arguments are there as attributes (batch_size: 64, dry_run: True …). You will build this in Chapter 13.
  • device is cpu.
  • train_loader does not tell you much even when expanded. Instead, type len(train_loader.dataset) in the Debug Console and you get 60000, and len(train_loader) gives 938 (60000 ÷ 64, rounded up). It means that the 60,000 images are supplied in 938 bundles of 64, which is the subject of Chapter 15.

Go into train with F11, stop at the output = model(data) line, and type data.shape in the Debug Console, and you get torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]). 64 images, 1 channel (grayscale), 28×28 pixels. How to read these four numbers is Chapter 11, and the value you will look at most often with the debugger in Part 2 is this very shape.

[Intermediate] The VS Code screen was not actually operated while this book was written, so the Variables and Debug Console values above are expected values calculated from the code. len(train_loader) is math.ceil(60000/64) = 938, and data.shape is the standard shape of an MNIST batch. Running it yourself to confirm them is the assignment for this section.

8.4 Step 3: implement a small piece

[Basic] There is one piece of this code that you can rewrite by hand right now: the last print of the test function. It is an exercise that takes only the accuracy calculation out of the original output and simplifies it (the original file also prints the average loss), and the material of Chapter 3 is enough for it.

correct = 1010
total = 10000
print('\nTest set: Accuracy: {}/{} ({:.0f}%)\n'.format(correct, total, 100. * correct / total))

[Basic] Rewrite it as an f-string (Chapter 3) and check that the result is the same as the original's. It may not seem like much, but the experience "I can write one line of this code in a different way" is the difference between reading code and knowing it. In Part 2 you use this method to rewrite the whole train function (Chapter 12) and the Net class (Chapter 16).

[Intermediate] The formal version of step 3 is this. Keep the original file, rewrite the piece by hand in a new file, compare the output of the two files, and look at the difference in the code with the diff of Chapter 7. If the results are the same but the code differs, it is "a different way of saying it"; if the results differ, there is "something you missed," and what you missed is what there is to learn.

8.5 Having AI explain it and finding what is wrong

[Basic] After you finish step 1, have AI explain the same code.

Explain the flow of execution of the Python code below, in the order of function calls starting from if __name__ == '__main__':. Then put in a table the things that main() prepares before it calls train(). (paste mnist_main.py)

[Basic] Then compare AI's explanation with your step 1 results. There are three things to check.

  1. Is the call order AI gave the same as the four in Section 8.2 (train → test → step → save)? If it changed the order or left out scheduler.step(), that is where it is wrong.
  2. If AI states flatly that "this code runs on a GPU," it is wrong. There is the --no-accel option and the torch.accelerator.is_available() check, so it also runs on a CPU. It is common for AI to leave out conditions that are in the code.
  3. If AI explains --dry-run only as "a quick test mode," that is not enough. Look at the code and you see that it calls break inside train after the first log, while test runs in full. If the explanation is simpler than the code, something is missing (the AI box in Chapter 4).

[Basic] The point of this exercise is not to hope that AI gets it wrong. AI's explanations are mostly right and very useful. The point is that you could judge AI's explanation because you had done step 1 first. If you read AI's explanation first, without step 1, you have no standard to judge it by, and that explanation simply becomes your understanding. It is like skimming the case file before you read a review report someone else wrote.

[Intermediate] Move up to harder questions. "Why are F.nll_loss and F.log_softmax used together?" "What do model.train() and model.eval() change?" AI's answers are usually accurate, but in Part 2 you will confirm those answers in code (Chapters 12 and 16). For now, write the answers down and put them on the list of things to check later.

8.6 A map of what you did not understand

[Basic] Connect the list of "what I don't know" that you wrote in step 1 to the chapters of Part 2. This table is the reading map for Part 2.

Element of mnist_main.py What it is (one line) Chapter that covers it
torch.manual_seed(args.seed) Fixes the random seed. The same reason as random.seed in Chapter 4 11, 24
Shapes such as torch.Size([64, 1, 28, 28]) The shape of a tensor. Batch, channel, height, width 11
nn.Module, __init__/forward, super().__init__() The frame of a model. The classes and inheritance of Chapter 4, as they are 11, 12
transforms.Compose, ToTensor, Normalize Turn images into tensors and standardize the values 15
datasets.MNIST, DataLoader The dataset and the supply mechanism. The __len__ and __getitem__ of Chapter 4 15
optimizer.zero_grad() → loss.backward() → optimizer.step() One step of training. Clear the gradients → compute them → update 10, 12
F.nll_loss, F.log_softmax The loss function for classification problems 12
model.train(), model.eval(), torch.no_grad() Training mode and evaluation mode, turning off gradient computation 12, 13
output.argmax(dim=1), computing correct Comparing predictions with correct labels → accuracy 12, 13
torch.save(model.state_dict(), ...) Saving weights. The dictionary of Chapter 3 13
argparse Command-line arguments. A systematic version of sys.argv from Chapter 4 13
nn.Conv2d, max_pool2d, Dropout, flatten The parts of a convolutional neural network 16
Adadelta, StepLR, gamma Kinds of optimizer and adjusting the learning rate 12 (up to optimizers and learning rates; schedulers are outside the scope of this book)
torch.accelerator, .to(device) Choosing between CPU and GPU, and moving to it 11, 12

[Basic] The table also shows why Part 2 is in the order it is. You have to learn tensors and nn.Module in Chapter 11 before you can write the training loop in Chapter 12, you need Chapters 12 and 13 before you can swap in other data in Chapter 15, and only after that do you change the inside of Net in Chapter 16. When you finish Part 2, you will be able to read every line of this table. Then come back to this chapter and do step 1 again. How much the time it takes and the depth of your understanding have changed is your report card for Part 2.

8.7 The format of the "code reading" assignments in Part 2

[Basic] At the end of every chapter of Part 2 there is a "code reading" assignment. The format is always the same.

  1. Apply step 1 to the assigned code (what you built in that chapter, or a part of some public code) and write down the list of definitions and the order of calls.
  2. Have AI explain it, and find and write down at least one place where it is wrong or leaves something out. If you could not find one, write "none found." That too is a record.
  3. If needed, use step 2 to check one shape in the debugger and write it down.

[Basic] Keep your answers to the assignments in files and commit them to the repository from Chapter 7. By around Chapter 12, those files become a history of "how I have been reading code."

Where people get stuck

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
You read the 143 lines from the top and give up at line 20 The order is wrong. List of definitions → entry point → order of calls (Section 8.2)
So many unknown functions that it feels hopeless That is normal. Write them in a list and match them to the table in Section 8.6. No need to understand them now
The download stalls during the --dry-run run The network. Run it again a little later and it resumes. Check whether the code/data/MNIST folder was created
ModuleNotFoundError: torchvision Whether you ran pip install torch torchvision in Chapter 2, and whether the interpreter is jucos
AI's explanation differs from the code, and you cannot tell which is right The code is right. The code is a fact that runs, and the explanation is an interpretation. Check with the debugger (step 2)
On GitHub you cannot jump to a function's definition Open the file and click the function name, and a pop-up appears (you may need to sign in). If that fails, clone the repository and use F12 in VS Code

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] The AI box for this chapter is Section 8.5 itself. Just one addition. When you have AI explain code, saying "for someone who doesn't know" makes it easier but less accurate, and saying "for a code reviewer" makes it more accurate but harder. After step 1, use the latter. You already know the flow, so you can judge even a hard explanation.

[Intermediate] When reading a large repository, agent-type tools (Chapter 6) are strong. They read the whole folder and answer "explain this project's entry point and main modules." But the rule is to compare that answer too with the list of definitions from step 1, and you do not turn them on in a folder that contains case material (Section 6.5).

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. In mnist_main.py, who calls test(), and how many times? With --epochs 3?
  2. With --dry-run on, at which line of train() does the loop end? Does test() get shorter too?
  3. In the table in Section 8.6, mark the lines whose meaning you can guess right now. After finishing Part 2, mark them again and compare.

[Intermediate]

  1. For each of the six arguments that main() passes to train, write the line number of the line in main() where it is created.
  2. Rewrite the print of Section 8.4 as an f-string, and check that the output is the same as the original's down to the last character (watch out for \n and \t).

[Advanced]

  1. Read Net.forward the step 1 way and predict what shape the input [64, 1, 28, 28] becomes as it passes each line, then confirm with the debugger. Explain by calculation why the input of fc1 is 9216.

Part 1

Chapter 9. (Advanced) Using the Colab GPU from VS Code on your own computer: the answer in 2026

This whole chapter is [Advanced]. Unlike the other chapters of Part 1, it is a short chapter that explains "why this book does not do it that way" rather than "do it this way," and it is the basis for the way of working in Part 2 (code on your own computer, runs in a Colab notebook).

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] Running the training in Part 2 on my own computer does not feel slow to me.
  • [ ] I think that when I need a GPU, I can just use a Colab notebook then.
  • [ ] I have no particular wish to look for a way to "connect VS Code on my own computer directly to the Colab GPU."

If all three are "yes," you can read only Section 9.3 and go on to Chapter 10. Come back when training feels slow in Part 2.

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn the answer, as of September 2026, to the natural question "can't I use the Colab GPU directly from my VS Code screen?" and the basis for it (the Colab terms).
  • You see why the alternative this book chose (carry the code with Git and run it in a notebook) is enough.
  • You learn the route open to paying users and its conditions.
  • You see from actual measurements how many times faster (or not faster) the free Colab GPU is on this book's models.

9.1 The question

[Advanced] Chapter 2 said that you write code in VS Code (on your own computer) and do GPU training in Colab (a notebook in the browser). That naturally raises a question. Can't you connect directly to a Colab GPU runtime from inside VS Code? If you could use the debugger from Chapter 5 as it is on top of a GPU, that would be the most convenient.

[Advanced] Technically it is possible. There is a workaround: start an SSH server inside a Colab notebook, open a tunnel (a tool such as colab-ssh does this), and connect with the Remote-SSH extension of VS Code. Whether to include this method was also considered at the design stage of this book.

9.2 The answer in 2026: on the free tier, we do not do it

[Advanced] The Colab FAQ (checked again on 2026-09-09) states which activities are restricted on runtimes that run free of charge without a compute unit balance. The two items below are not direct quotations of the original but summaries of its gist.

Gist of the FAQ ①: on managed runtimes that run free of charge without a positive compute unit balance, a number of activities are restricted, and the list includes remote control such as SSH shells and remote desktops.

[Advanced] In other words, SSH access is restricted on runtimes that run free of charge without a compute unit balance, and such runtimes can be terminated without warning. The same document also states the condition for lifting this.

Gist of the FAQ ②: if you buy a paid plan and keep a positive compute unit balance, you can have restrictions of this kind lifted.

The next sentence is the original, word for word (checked on 2026-09-09).

"Paid users whose compute unit balance is exhausted will revert to the free-of-charge tier policies and restrictions until the balance is increased."

[Advanced] To sum up, there are three cases.

How the runtime is billed Connecting VS Code over SSH Basis
Running free of charge + no balance Restricted. The runtime may be terminated The FAQ's list of additional restrictions
Paid plan bought (subscription or pay as you go) + compute unit balance > 0 That additional restriction is lifted (other policies and resource limits still apply) The FAQ's condition for lifting
Paid plan, but balance 0 Same as free FAQ "revert to the free-of-charge tier"

[Advanced] The test is not the type of account but how that runtime is being billed. And what is lifted is this additional restriction. It does not mean that SSH becomes an officially supported feature or that resources are guaranteed.

[Advanced] This book assumes free use (Section 2.7), so it does not use this method. If you follow an old blog post because "it used to work," you end up breaking the terms. What Chapter 6 said, "AI gives outdated information," applies here too. If you ask AI "how to connect to Colab from VS Code," it usually answers with the SSH method from 2020 to 2022.

9.3 This book's alternative: code by Git, runs in the notebook

[Advanced] Part 2 of this book is set up so that you work in the following flow.

Figure 9-1. Code is written on your own computer and carried with Git, and only the runs that need a GPU are done in a Colab notebook cell. The results come back through Drive.

[Advanced] This flow is enough because of how this book's code is structured. From Chapters 13 and 14 on, every training run starts with the single line python train.py --arguments, and the results are left in the results/{run}/ folder (Chapter 13). All you do in the Colab notebook is fetch the repository and run that one line.

# Colab 노트북의 셀
!git clone https://github.com/<계정>/ai_coding.git
%cd ai_coding/ch14
!pip install -q -r requirements.txt        # 필요한 경우
!python train.py --model mlp --epochs 10 --run mlp-gpu --results /content/drive/MyDrive/ai_coding/results

In English: Colab 노트북의 셀 = a cell in a Colab notebook; <계정> = ; 필요한 경우 = if needed.

[Advanced] Debugging (Chapter 5) is done on your own computer's CPU with small data and short epochs, and the verified code is run for a long time on the GPU. This separation is not an inconvenience but a good habit. If you debug on the GPU, you spend GPU time every time, and you upload the data again each time you fix an error. So this book uses "get it right small, on your own computer; run it big, remotely" as its working procedure.

[Advanced] The reason for saving results to Drive is the same as in Section 2.7.3. A Colab runtime disappears when the session ends, so the results survive only if you give --results a path on the mounted Drive, and they then appear in VS Code on your own computer through the desktop Drive of Section 2.8. That is how the cycle in Figure 9-1 closes.

9.4 If you are a paying user

[Advanced] If you have bought a paid plan (a subscription or pay-as-you-go; the prices are in Section 2.7.2) and have a compute unit balance, the additional restriction of Section 9.2 is lifted (this does not make SSH an officially supported feature). The procedure then is roughly as follows. The details of the tool (colab-ssh) change from version to version, so follow the current README of its repository.

  1. In a Colab notebook, run a cell that starts an SSH server and a tunnel (cloudflared or similar).
  2. Install the Remote-SSH extension in VS Code on your own computer and connect to the address the cell gave you.
  3. If you open a folder in the connected remote window, the debugger from Chapter 5 runs on the GPU runtime.

[Advanced] However, the moment the balance reaches 0 you go back to the free policy (Section 9.2), so you can be cut off in the middle of a long job. And the FAQ recommends two proper alternatives. "local runtime": connecting the Jupyter on your own computer (or on a server you rent) to the Colab screen, which goes in the direction of using your own computer with a GPU through the Colab UI (the opposite direction from this book's purpose). GCP Marketplace and Colab Enterprise: buying paid cloud resources. This goes beyond the scope of individual self-study.

9.5 How much faster with a GPU: measurements

[Advanced] This book said "go to Colab when you need a GPU," but how much faster is a GPU actually on this book's models? The same code was measured in three places (2026-09-13).

Measurement This book's PC, CPU Colab CPU Colab T4 GPU
Chapter 12 MLP, all of 2 epochs 10 s 17 to 18 s 17 to 18 s
Chapter 17 ResNet (about 20 layers), one training step 125ms 164 to 172ms 11ms
Chapter 22 Transformer, one training step 35ms 34 to 46ms 7 to 8ms
Chapter 25 KoELECTRA-small + LoRA, one training step 500ms 1,496ms 43ms

This book's PC has a laptop CPU (Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, 8 threads). Colab CPU has 2 logical cores and PyTorch used only 1 thread, so the measurement is unfavorable to the CPU. "One step" is measured after taking a batch of 32 out in advance, so it does not include the time to read the data. The ranges are from two measurements, and Chapter 25 is from one. The GPU that free Colab assigns can differ from day to day.

[Advanced] There are two things to read.

  • A small model does not get faster when moved to a GPU. The Chapter 12 MLP took the same 17 to 18 seconds on the T4 as on the CPU. The computation is too small for the GPU to make a difference, and the time appears to be spent on the CPU side preparing images (the two were not timed separately).
  • The heavier the computation, the wider the gap. Compared with this book's PC, the T4 was about 5 times faster on the Transformer, about 11 times faster on ResNet, and about 12 times faster on the 14-million-parameter model of Chapter 25. This is a tendency seen in four models, not a general law.

[Advanced] So for this book's exercises, your own computer's CPU is enough for most of them. A GPU earns its keep from the scale of Chapter 25, and for models larger than that or for long training you use Colab with the flow of Section 9.3.

9.6 What this chapter leaves you with

[Advanced] The point of this chapter is not a technique but a judgment. "A method that works" and "a method you are allowed to use" are different, the latter is written in a document called the terms of service, and that document changes. This is where the reason this book writes a date of checking for each tool (Section 6.0) is clearest. If the FAQ has changed by the time you read this chapter, the changed document takes precedence over this chapter.

Where people get stuck

[Advanced]

Symptom Cause and fix
I followed the SSH method in a blog post and the runtime was cut off Section 9.2. Restricted on runtimes that run free of charge without a compute unit balance
git clone on Colab cannot fetch a private repository Authentication is needed. Put a personal access token in the URL (it is a secret, so do not leave it in the notebook), or make the practice repository public
!python train.py saves results/ on the runtime, and it disappears after the session Give --results a Drive path
I saved to Drive but it does not show up on my computer Desktop Drive sync delay. Wait a moment, or open the folder in streaming mode
Debugging on the local CPU is too slow Reduce the data (add a --limit argument), 1 epoch, a small batch. Debugging is "checking that it works," not "training"

Working with an AI assistant

[Advanced] This chapter is practice in checking AI's answer against the terms.

Tell me how to connect to the GPU of Google Colab over SSH from VS Code. Then tell me, with the source document, whether that is allowed under the terms for a free Colab account as of September 2026.

It will usually answer the first question in detail, and it is likely to answer the second with "this needs to be checked" or with outdated information. Check it against the original FAQ in Section 9.2. That AI knows a method and that the method is allowed are two different things. This distinction holds outside coding too.

Part

Part 2. Implementing deep learning yourself

Part 2

Chapter 10. How deep learning learns: the four ingredients and the loop

What you get from this chapter

  • You understand, with pictures and words and no code, what "training" in deep learning actually repeats.
  • You learn the frame of the four ingredients needed for training (data, model, loss, optimizer) and the loop that runs them. Every chapter of Part 2 is a story about changing one of these four.
  • You get an early look at the difference between two branches, "discriminative" and "generative."
  • You map the flow of mnist_main.py, which you read in Chapter 8, onto this frame.

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I can explain to someone else what a loss function and gradient descent are.
  • [ ] I know what each of the three lines zero_grad → backward → step does.

If both are "yes," you can look only at the mapping table in Section 10.4 and go on to Chapter 11.

10.0 The only chapter where pictures come before code

[Basic] Part 2 is the part where you write code yourself. Yet this chapter has no code. There is one reason. Every line of the code from Chapter 11 on sits on a single frame, and if you do not see that frame first, the code looks like nothing more than a list of unfamiliar commands. Once you know the frame, you can read each line by asking "which of the four is this line preparing?"

[Basic] Just as a lawyer who takes on a type of case never seen before first grasps "what is the structure of judgment for this type?" before looking at the provisions, this chapter grasps the structure of judgment of deep learning code.

10.1 What does training do?

[Basic] Think of a program that looks at an image of a handwritten digit and tells which of 0 to 9 it is. If a person had to write the rules, it would be hopeless. Even if you write "if there is a circle at the top and a tail going down, it is a 9," handwriting differs from person to person and the rules grow without end.

[Basic] Deep learning does not write rules. Instead, it sets up one function made of a very large number of numbers (weights) and changes those numbers little by little so that "image → correct answer" comes out right. At first the numbers are random, so it answers nonsense (the 10% accuracy in the dry run of Chapter 8 is that), and if you repeat showing it examples and correcting the numbers by as much as it was wrong, tens of thousands of times, it gets better and better at answering. "Training" is the name of this repetition.

[Basic] Four questions come up here, and their answers are the ingredients.

  • What do you show it? → data
  • What function do you set up? → model
  • How do you measure "by as much as it was wrong"? → loss
  • Having measured, how do you correct the numbers? → optimizer

10.2 The four ingredients

Figure 10-1. The four ingredients and the flow. The data passes through the model and becomes a prediction, the loss measures the difference, and the optimizer corrects the weights in the direction that makes that difference smaller. This is one step.

Data: pairs of input and correct answer

[Basic] Training data is pairs of (input, label). For MNIST, there are 60,000 pairs of (a 28×28 image, one of 0 to 9). Recall the list of dictionaries (records) from Chapter 3. Just as one case was a dictionary, one example is a pair, and these sit in a list. The model receives them not one at a time but in bundles (batches). The 64 in the [64, 1, 28, 28] you saw in Chapter 8 is the batch size.

[Basic] The data is split into a training set and a test set. You correct the weights with the training set, and with the test set you measure "does it also get right the examples it has never seen?" If you reuse the training set for testing, you cannot tell whether the model memorized the answers or learned. It is like how, in a trial, the party that submitted a piece of evidence cannot itself rule that it proved the facts with that evidence.

Model: a function that has weights

[Basic] A model is a function that takes an input and produces a prediction. Inside it are numbers called weights, and training changes only these numbers. The simplest model is "multiply the input by numbers and add" (linear), and if you stack several such layers and insert a nonlinear transformation between them, you get a neural network. The MLP class you previewed at the end of Chapter 4 is that. With two layers it is shallow, with dozens of layers it is called "deep," and hence deep learning.

[Basic] The kind of model (MLP, CNN, RNN, Transformer) depends on the nature of the input. In an image, neighboring pixels are related to each other (CNN, Chapter 16), and in a sentence earlier words affect later words (RNN and Transformer, Chapters 20 to 22); each kind reflects that nature in the shape of the function. But whatever the model, it is still "a function that has weights," and the frame of the four ingredients is the same. This is why the training code stays almost the same in Part 2 even as the models change.

Loss: how wrong it was, as a single number

[Basic] To train, you have to turn "it was wrong" into a single number. That is the loss. It has to be a number because only then does the word "reduce" make sense. It is defined so that it is close to 0 when the prediction matches the correct answer and grows larger the more they differ.

[Basic] Each type of problem has a standard loss. For regression, which predicts a number, it is the squared difference (MSE), and for classification, it is the −log of the probability of the correct answer (cross-entropy). The F.nll_loss and log_softmax in the Chapter 8 code are one form of the latter, and Chapter 12 checks this in code. For now it is enough to get as far as "the loss is a ruler that measures how wrong the model is, and the kind of ruler is chosen according to the problem."

[Intermediate] The loss is a standard a person sets. The model learns only in the direction that reduces the loss, so if the loss is defined wrongly, it learns the wrong thing. For example, if you give a model that predicts "whether a claim is granted" data in which 95% of the cases are claim-granted cases, the loss is low even if it answers "claim granted" for every case. What you measure decides what it learns. That setting the standard of judgment is half of the judgment is true in law as well.

Optimizer: in which direction, and by how much, to correct

[Basic] Once you have the loss, you have to correct the weights. In which direction? Here calculus appears exactly once. You can compute whether the loss gets larger or smaller when each weight is made a little larger (the gradient), and you move the weights a little in the direction that makes the loss smaller. This is called gradient descent. It is compared to walking down a fog-covered mountain one step at a time toward lower ground, looking only at the slope under your feet.

[Basic] How much "a little" is, is the learning rate. If it is too large, the model jumps across the valley and diverges; if it is too small, it takes forever. The --lr in the Chapter 8 code is this, and it is the number you will touch most often in Part 2. The optimizer is the way of taking these steps, and there are kinds from the basic form (SGD) to ones that refine the steps with momentum and step-size adjustment (Adam, Adadelta, and others). Chapter 12 swaps them and compares.

[Advanced] The algorithm that computes the gradient for all weights at once is backpropagation. It applies the chain rule of differentiation from back to front, and PyTorch does this automatically with the single line loss.backward() (autograd in Chapter 11). If you want to follow the principle by hand, Appendix E and Karpathy's lectures (Appendix D) are the starting point.

10.3 The loop: one step, one lap, many laps

[Basic] Once the ingredients are ready, you run the loop. The loop has three levels.

Figure 10-2. The three levels of the training loop. One step is doing ① to ⑤ with one batch, one lap (epoch) is going through every batch once, and training is many laps of that.

[Basic] One step is doing five things with one batch. ① Clear the gradients from the previous step, ② put the batch into the model to get predictions, ③ measure the loss, ④ compute the gradients, and ⑤ have the optimizer correct the weights. The five lines inside the train function of the Chapter 8 code are in exactly this order.

optimizer.zero_grad()          # ①
output = model(data)           # ②
loss = F.nll_loss(output, target)   # ③
loss.backward()                # ④
optimizer.step()               # ⑤

[Basic] One lap (an epoch) is passing once through the whole training set, batch by batch. For MNIST's 60,000 images at 64 at a time, 938 steps make one lap. Training is going around many laps (the Chapter 8 code does 14 laps by default), and after each lap you measure accuracy on the test set to see whether it is getting better.

[Basic] Why split into batches instead of putting everything in at once? For two reasons. You cannot load 60,000 images into memory all at once, and correcting often with small bundles trains better than correcting rarely with a large bundle. Case law, too, has its standards refined as the judgments of individual cases accumulate; it is not made by gathering a year's cases and deciding them all at once.

[Intermediate] Look again at how the structure is the same as the tallying loop of Chapter 3: "prepare the container before the loop (model, optimizer), fill it inside the loop (weight updates), and look at the result after the loop (evaluation)." Once you see this correspondence, training code is an extension of Chapter 3.

10.4 Mapping onto the Chapter 8 code

[Basic] Dividing the main() of mnist_main.py into the four ingredients and the loop gives the following.

Ingredient Lines in mnist_main.py Chapter that covers it
Data transform = ..., dataset1 = datasets.MNIST(...), train_loader = DataLoader(...) 15
Model class Net(nn.Module), model = Net().to(device) 11, 16
Loss loss = F.nll_loss(output, target) (inside train) 12
Optimizer optimizer = optim.Adadelta(...), scheduler = StepLR(...) 12, 24 (the scheduler StepLR is outside the scope of this book)
The loop for epoch in range(...): train(...), test(...), scheduler.step() 12, 13
Other argparse (settings), device (device), torch.save (saving) 11, 13

[Basic] The order of the chapters in Part 2 follows this table. Chapter 11 covers the materials of the model (tensors, nn.Module), Chapter 12 puts all four in place and runs one lap, Chapter 13 covers saving, evaluation, and settings, Chapter 14 splits the files, Chapter 15 swaps in different data, and from Chapter 16 on the model changes. At the head of each chapter, "which of the four this chapter changes" is written down.

10.5 Discriminative and generative: two branches

[Basic] The examples so far have been "look at an image and tell what it is." Such a model is called a discriminative model. Given an input, it discriminates the correct answer. Classification (which kind is it?) and regression (how much is the value?) belong here, and most of Part 2 is discriminative models.

[Basic] There is another branch. A generative model learns what the data looks like and makes new data. Instead of recognizing handwritten digits, it draws handwritten digits, and instead of classifying sentences, it writes sentences. Language models such as ChatGPT are generative models. The only difference is that the correct answer takes the form "what is the next character?" rather than "this image is a 7"; the frame of the four ingredients and the loop is the same. Chapter 23 looks at this branch by building a small language model yourself.

[Intermediate] Put in terms of probability, the difference between the two branches is that a discriminative model learns the probability of the correct answer y given an input x, p(y|x), while a generative model learns the probability of the data itself, p(x) (or p(x|y)). Generation is the harder problem because it has to capture the whole of "what the data looks like," and that is why discriminative models developed first. However, the achievements of language models in the 2020s reversed this relationship, and the current state of things is that a simple generative objective, "predict the next token," solves even discriminative tasks.

10.6 Looking again with a lawyer's eye

[Basic] If you put this frame into a lawyer's language, you can use it throughout Part 2.

Deep learning Legal judgment
Training set The accumulation of precedents and facts
Model The standard of judgment (weight = the weight given to each factor)
Loss The standard that measures "the judgment was wrong"
Optimizer How to reflect a mistake in the standard
Test set Validity in a new case never seen before
Overfitting A standard that gets every past case right but gets new cases wrong

[Basic] An analogy is only an analogy, but one thing in it is exact. A model learns only what the loss defines. The moment you decide what to measure as "wrong," what the model will become is decided. In Chapter 24 (experiment records) and Chapter 25 (language models), this point comes back as a practical question. "What was this model trained to minimize?" is the first question you can ask when judging the nature of AI-generated output.

Where people get stuck

[Basic] This is a concept chapter, so there are no errors. Instead, here are three common misunderstandings.

Misunderstanding Correction
"The model understands the rules" The model only found weights that reduce the loss. Grounds for saying it knows the rules come from separate verification
"High accuracy means it learned well" Accuracy on the training set may be memorization. Only accuracy on the test set means something
"The larger the learning rate, the faster it learns" Too large and it diverges. Make it diverge yourself in Chapter 12

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] When you are learning concepts, AI is a good conversation partner. But verify the analogy.

Explain gradient descent with the analogy of a fog-covered mountain, and tell me two ways in which the analogy departs from reality.

[Basic] The second request is the key. A person who knows where an analogy breaks down is a person who knows the concept. (Hint: a mountain is 3-dimensional but the weights have millions of dimensions, and the terrain of a mountain is fixed while the terrain differs a little from batch to batch.)

  2. Write down the order of the five stages of "one step," and guess what would happen if you left out ① (checked in Chapter 12).
  3. Explain the reason for splitting the training set and the test set without the trial analogy.
