Part 2

Chapter 25. Working with public language models: load, freeze, and train just a little

This chapter replaces the "model," one of the four ingredients, with one someone else built. From Hugging Face you fetch the same structure as the Transformer you built yourself in Chapters 22 and 23, already trained by someone on 34GB of Korean. Then you repeat the transfer learning of Chapter 18 on text. Freeze it and train only the classification head, or use LoRA.

What you get from this chapter

  • You load a public model and its tokenizer with the transformers library and confirm that its insides carry the same names as the parts of Chapter 22.
  • You see how subword tokenization differs from the whitespace tokenization of Chapter 19, and why the <unk> problem goes away.
  • You see by measurement that the sentence vectors of a pretrained model as they are do not reflect similarity of meaning.
  • You solve the provision classification task of Chapter 19 by training only 1.2% of the whole with LoRA. You read the result of Chapter 25 side by side with the tables of Chapters 19 to 22.
  • You learn how all of this connects to the "AI tools" of Chapter 6, and what is different.

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I have used AutoModel.from_pretrained and AutoTokenizer.
  • [ ] I have fine-tuned a model with LoraConfig from peft.

If both are "yes," you can read only the results table in Section 25.3 and Section 25.4.

25.0 The problem of scale

[Basic] The language model built in Chapter 23 had 530,000 parameters, 150,000 characters of data, and 2 minutes of training, and it imitated the form of provisions but made no sense. The Transformer you built yourself in Chapter 22 did not beat the bag of words on 2,108 provisions. The structure was right, but the scale was not enough.

[Basic] An individual cannot supply the scale. Instead, you take what someone else has supplied. Just as you took a ResNet-18 trained on ImageNet in Chapter 18, here you take a model trained on 34GB of Korean text. The repository is the Hugging Face Hub, and the library is transformers. To prepare, pip install transformers peft.

[Basic] The model in this chapter is KoELECTRA-small (monologg, Apache-2.0). With 14 million parameters, it is small enough to fine-tune on a CPU within a few minutes, and it was pretrained on 34GB of Korean, including news, wiki, and the "모두의 말뭉치" [Everyone's Corpus]. It is small next to today's conversational language models (billions to hundreds of billions of parameters), but it is enough to see the principles, and it is a size that the readers of this book can run on their own computers.

25.1 Loading: the parts of Chapter 22, as they are

[Basic] code/25/p01_load_model.py:

NAME = "monologg/koelectra-small-v3-discriminator"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(NAME)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(NAME)

모델 monologg/koelectra-small-v3-discriminator
파라미터 14,056,192 | 어휘 35,000
원문  : 제4조(성년) 사람은 19세로 성년에 이르게 된다.
토큰  : ['[CLS]', '제', '##4', '##조', '(', '성년', ')', '사람', '##은', '19', '##세', '##로', '성년', '##에', '이르', '##게', '된다', '.', '[SEP]']
번호  : [2, 3288, 4204, 4084, 12, 26556, 13, 6226, 4112, 6238, 4246, 4239, 26556, 4073, 6952, 4325, 6236, 18, 3]
shape : (1, 19) (배치 1, 토큰 수)
출력 shape: (1, 19, 256) = [배치, 토큰 수, 차원]
  embeddings  ElectraEmbeddings
  embeddings_project Linear
  encoder     ElectraEncoder
  encoder 층 수: 12
    layer[0].attention     ElectraAttention
    layer[0].intermediate  ElectraIntermediate
    layer[0].output        ElectraOutput

In English: 모델 = model; 파라미터 = parameters; 어휘 = vocabulary; 원문 = original text; 토큰 = tokens; 번호 = token IDs; (배치 1, 토큰 수) = (batch 1, number of tokens); 출력 shape = output shape; [배치, 토큰 수, 차원] = [batch, number of tokens, dimension]; encoder 층 수 = number of encoder layers. The original text is Article 4 (성년, adulthood): "A person reaches adulthood at the age of 19" (here and in the rest of this chapter, the English given for statutory text is a working translation by the editor, not an official translation).

[Basic] Look at three things.

  1. Tokenization. In Chapter 19, 제4조(성년) was a single <unk>. Here it is split into 제, ##4, ##조, (, 성년, ). ## is a mark meaning "attaches to the previous piece." This is subword tokenization (previewed in Section 19.1), and with a vocabulary of 35,000 it represents almost all Korean without <unk>. [CLS] and [SEP] are special tokens for the start and end of a sentence.
  2. The output shape [1, 19, 256]. A 256-dimensional vector for each of the 19 tokens. It is the same shape as the x that has passed through the blocks of TransformerClassifier in Chapter 22.
  3. Structure. embeddings → encoder (12 layers) → in each layer, attention, intermediate (feedforward), and output. Only the names differ from the embedding, encoder block, attention, and feedforward of Chapter 22. Open layer[0].attention further and there are query, key, and value linear layers, which are the wq, wk, and wv of Chapter 22. The LoRA of Section 25.2 names them.

[Intermediate] AutoModel/AutoTokenizer are conveniences that pick the right class when given only the model name. On the first run they download the weights and keep them in ~/.cache/huggingface. The weights themselves are about 55MB, but in this book's verification environment the same weights were downloaded in two formats (pytorch_model.bin and model.safetensors), about 110MB in all. It is the same principle as the torchvision weights of Chapter 18. The "UNEXPECTED key" notice that appears when loading is there because the head for pretraining (discriminator_predictions) is not in AutoModel, and you can ignore it.

Sentence vectors cannot be used as they are

유사도 0.915 : 사람은 19세로 성년에 이르게 된… ↔ 미성년자가 법률행위를 함에는 법정…
유사도 0.919 : 사람은 19세로 성년에 이르게 된… ↔ 검사는 공소를 제기하고 수행한다.…

In English: 유사도 = similarity; "사람은 19세로 성년에 이르게 된…" = "A person reaches adulthood at the age of 19…"; "미성년자가 법률행위를 함에는 법정…" = "For a minor to perform a juristic act, the legal…"; "검사는 공소를 제기하고 수행한다." = "The public prosecutor institutes and conducts the prosecution."

[Basic] The token vectors were averaged to make sentence vectors, and cosine similarity was measured. The adulthood provision and the minors provision (close in meaning) scored 0.915, and the adulthood provision and the provision on the prosecutor's prosecution (far in meaning) scored 0.919. They are almost the same, and the far pair is actually higher. If you simply average the outputs of a pretrained encoder, every sentence tends to point in a similar direction (anisotropy), so similarity search needs a model trained again for that purpose (a sentence embedding model). One measurement corrects the misunderstanding that "a pretrained model, once loaded, knows the meaning of sentences." As the principle of Chapter 6 says, what you take from others must also be verified.

25.2 Fine-tuning: a repeat of Chapter 18

[Basic] You solve the task of Chapter 19 (the four-way classification of statutory provisions) with this model. p02_finetune_lora.py compares the same two methods as Chapter 18.

A. Freeze and train only the classification head. The whole pretrained part is requires_grad = False, and only the newly attached classification head is trained.

    m = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(NAME, num_labels=len(LAWS))
    for p in m.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = False
    for p in m.classifier.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = True
    run("A. 분류층만", m, list(m.classifier.parameters()), lr=1e-3)

B. LoRA. Attach two small matrices (rank r=8) beside the query and value linear layers of the attention, and train only those.

    m = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(NAME, num_labels=len(LAWS))
    cfg = LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["query", "value"], lora_dropout=0.1,
                     task_type="SEQ_CLS")
    m = get_peft_model(m, cfg)
    trainable = [p for p in m.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
    run("B. LoRA(r=8)", m, trainable, lr=5e-4)

[Basic] The idea of LoRA is this. Instead of changing the weight W (256×256) of a linear layer as a whole, you keep W frozen and put A (8×256) and B (256×8) beside it, using W+BA. Multiplied, (256×8)(8×256) = 256×256, so the size matches W. A and B have 2×256×8=4,096 parameters, 6% of W, and such a pair is attached to 12 layers × 2 (query and value). The assumption is that "the change that is needed can be expressed well enough as the product of two small matrices," and it sits between B (freeze and train only the last layer) and C (fine-tune everything) of Chapter 18. LoRA is a method that greatly reduces the parameters to train and the memory, and it is used when there is not enough memory to fine-tune the whole model.

25.3 Results

[Basic] Provisions: training 2,108 / test 526, CPU. 2 epochs:

  A. 분류층만 에포크 1: 시험 정확도 0.418  (17초)
  A. 분류층만 에포크 2: 시험 정확도 0.508  (49초)
A. 분류층만            학습 파라미터     66,820 / 전체 14,123,012 (0.47%)
  B. LoRA(r=8) 에포크 1: 시험 정확도 0.639  (49초)
  B. LoRA(r=8) 에포크 2: 시험 정확도 0.827  (107초)
B. LoRA(r=8)       학습 파라미터    165,124 / 전체 14,288,136 (1.16%)

In English: A. 분류층만 = A. classification head only; 에포크 = epoch; 시험 정확도 = test accuracy; (…초) = (… seconds); 학습 파라미터 … / 전체 … = trainable parameters … / total ….

The result of running the same code again with EPOCHS=4 (test accuracy per epoch):

Method 1 2 3 4 Trainable parameters
A. Classification head only 0.418 0.508 0.593 0.578 66,820 (0.47%)
B. LoRA(r=8) 0.639 0.827 0.816 0.861 165,124 (1.16%)

In 4 epochs (about 4 minutes), LoRA reached 86.1%, beating the Transformer you built yourself (83.8%) but still short of the bag of words (89.2%). A stops around 59%.

[Basic] There are four things to read.

  • LoRA trained only 1.16% of the whole and still rose to 82.7% in 2 epochs and 86.1% in 4 epochs. Of the 165,124 trained parameters, 66,820 belong to the classification head, so the LoRA matrices themselves are about 98,000.
  • The classification head alone (A) is slow. The pretrained representation does not fit this task (telling statutes apart) as it is, so the last layer alone gets 50% in 2 epochs. It is a different result from the shapes of Chapter 18 (where B reached 100%), and it has the same cause as the similarity measurement of Section 25.1. A pretrained representation is not "something you can use right away for any task."
  • Side by side with the tables of Chapters 19 to 22. Bag of words 89.2% (1 second), the Transformer you built yourself 83.8% (16 seconds), LoRA 4 epochs 86.1% (228 seconds). With small data and short training, even a pretrained model does not beat the bag of words at one stroke. Add this result to the lesson of Chapter 20 (the power of a model is relative to the data and the task) and you get: pretraining is not a cure-all, and fine-tuning also takes data and time. Still, it has already passed the Transformer you built yourself, and the curve is still rising, so in check question 4 you add more epochs and see how far it goes.
  • Time. On a CPU, about 1 minute per LoRA epoch. On data where the bag of words finishes in 1 second, a model with 14 million parameters takes this long, and billions of parameters are impossible without a GPU. That is why this book chose a small model. The same single training step takes about 43ms on a Colab T4 GPU, a little more than ten times faster than the CPU of this book's PC (about 500ms) (the table in Section 9.5).

[Intermediate] This is one seed and one run (Chapter 24). The 30-percentage-point difference between A and B overwhelms the variation, but the difference between B and the bag of words does not. The lr differs between A (1e-3) and B (5e-4), and that also affects the result. The convention for the learning rate in fine-tuning is to set it small so as not to ruin the pretrained weights (Chapter 18 C), and since LoRA has frozen parts, you may set it a little larger.

25.4 Between this model and conversational AI

[Basic] What is the same and what is different between this chapter's model and the conversational AI used in Chapter 6?

KoELECTRA-small (this chapter) Conversational language model (Chapter 6)
Structure Transformer encoder, 12 layers Transformer decoder, tens to a hundred layers
Parameters 14 million Billions to hundreds of billions
Pretraining 34GB of Korean, token discrimination Trillions of tokens in many languages, next-token prediction (Chapter 23)
After that You fine-tune it (this chapter) The maker adjusts it with instruction following and preference training
What you can do View, modify, and retrain all the weights Usually only input and output through an API

[Basic] The principle is the same line. The parts of Chapters 22 and 23 and the "freeze and train just a little" of Chapters 18 and 25 carry on, differing only in scale. What differs is transparency. This chapter's model keeps its weights on your computer where you can open them, what it was trained on (the source of the 34GB) is documented, and you do the fine-tuning. Conversational AI usually is not like that. When judging the nature of AI output, the question becomes "what was it trained on, and who adjusted it and how," and the last observation of this chapter is that with a public model you can see the answer and with a closed model you cannot.

[Intermediate] "Open" also has grades. Weights only (most), training data too (rare), training code too (rarer). KoELECTRA is a case where the weights, the code, and a description of the sources of the data are public. The license (Apache-2.0) allows free use, including commercial use, but it differs from model to model, so checking the license item of the model card is an extension of check question 7 in Chapter 18.

Where people get stuck

[Basic]

Symptom Cause and fix
OSError: … is not a local folder and is not a valid model identifier A typo in the model name, or the network. Copy the name from the Hub
The download is slow About 110MB. Only once. Check the cache folder
On Colab, get_peft_model gives ImportError: Found an incompatible version of torchao peft rejects the old torchao preinstalled on Colab. This chapter does not use torchao, so run !pip uninstall -y torchao and run it again
The UNEXPECTED key notice The pretraining head is not in the current class. Ignore it
ValueError: Target modules … not found (LoRA) The target_modules names differ from the model. Check the actual names with model.named_modules() (for ELECTRA, query and value)
Accuracy stays near 25% and does not rise The learning rate is too small (A), or requires_grad is all False. Check whether the trainable list is empty
Out of memory Reduce the batch size and max_len. This model has room to spare on a CPU with 32GB
Test accuracy differs from the value during training model.eval(). HF models also have Dropout
The tokenizer results do not match the Chapter 19 vocabulary That is expected. This chapter uses only the HF tokenizer. Only the original text and the correct labels are borrowed from the Chapter 19 dataset

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] This chapter is the one closest to AI tools, so the box is also about that relationship.

Tell me the names of the linear layers inside the attention layers of monologg/koelectra-small-v3-discriminator, and answer what should go into target_modules of peft.LoraConfig.

[Basic] Check AI's answer (query, key, value, dense, and so on) with [n for n, _ in model.named_modules() if "attention" in n][:20]. The names differ from model to model (q_proj, c_attn, and so on), and it is common for AI to answer with the names of a different model.

[Intermediate] If you ask conversational AI "which statute is this provision from," it will probably get it right more often than this chapter's model. Then why is this chapter needed? The answer is in the table of Section 25.4. The answers of conversational AI are not reproducible (Chapter 6), you do not know what it was trained on, and you have to send it your data (Section 6.5). This chapter's model runs on your computer, with your data, reproducibly (Chapter 24). It is not a question of which is better but of which to use when.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. Explain the rule for which tokens in the token list of Section 25.1 carry ## and which do not. 성년 appears twice; why is its number the same?
  2. Explain the 66,820 trainable parameters of A by calculation (the ELECTRA classification head: a 256→256 linear layer + a 256→4 linear layer).
  3. Calculate the number of parameters attached to one linear layer (256×256) at LoRA r=8, and confirm that the total over 12 layers × 2 is about 98,304.

[Intermediate]

  1. Run B with EPOCHS=6 and see whether accuracy passes the bag of words (89.2%), and if so, at which epoch.
  2. If you add key and dense to target_modules, how do the trainable parameters and the accuracy change?
  3. Redo the similarity experiment of Section 25.1 with the vectors of the fine-tuned model (B). Does the similarity come to reflect meaning?

[Advanced]

  1. Change r to 2, 8, and 32 and make a table of parameters, accuracy, and time, then run 3 seeds in the manner of Chapter 24 and attach ±.

Code-reading assignment for this chapter (Chapter 8 format)

Open the ELECTRA attention source with inspect.getsource(type(model.encoder.layer[0].attention.self)), apply step 1, and make a table of its correspondence with MultiHeadAttention of Chapter 22 (query/key/value ↔ wq/wk/wv, num_attention_heads ↔ h). Have AI explain "the differences between the two implementations," and check the differences in how dropout and masks are handled.

Part 2

Chapter 26. Showing the model you built: Gradio

This chapter does not change any of the four ingredients. As the last chapter of Part 2, it turns the model saved in Chapter 13 into a browser screen. A page where you draw a digit on a sketchpad and probabilities come out. It is not app development but a finishing step: "seeing with your own eyes that what you built actually works, and showing it to others."

What you get from this chapter

  • You learn how to make a web screen by attaching an input widget and an output widget to one Python function (Gradio Interface). The code is 40 lines.
  • You see the inference code of Chapter 13 used as it is behind the screen. The model definition is imported, not copied.
  • You learn how to test the screen's function and server without a browser (the four steps of Chapter 6).
  • You check again the cautions for making a public link (Section 6.5).

Who can skip this chapter

  • [ ] I have used gr.Interface(fn, inputs, outputs).launch().

If so, you can look only at the test procedure in Section 26.3.

26.0 Why a screen

[Basic] The infer.py of Chapter 13 prints numbers in the terminal. That is enough, but two things are missing. First, you cannot put in a digit you drew yourself. You put in only images from the test set. Second, you cannot show it to someone who does not know code. The screen in this chapter solves both. You draw directly on the sketchpad, and if you send the link, anyone can try it.

[Basic] And a screen is also a verification tool. A test accuracy of 94.7% is an abstract number, but when you see it call the 7 you drew a 1, you know physically what the model is weak at (check question 3).

26.1 The code

[Basic] This is code/26/app.py. To prepare, one line: pip install gradio.

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "13"))
from train import MLP                                     # 13장의 모델 정의를 그대로

RUN_DIR = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "13", "results", "lr01")


def load_model():
    with open(os.path.join(RUN_DIR, "config.json"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
        cfg = json.load(f)
    m = MLP(hidden=cfg["hidden"])
    m.load_state_dict(torch.load(os.path.join(RUN_DIR, "model_best.pt"), map_location="cpu"))
    m.eval()
    return m


model = load_model()


def predict(image):
    """그림판 입력(딕셔너리 또는 배열) → 28x28 흑백 → 확률 10개"""
    if image is None:
        return {}
    if isinstance(image, dict):                            # Sketchpad 는 {"composite": 배열} 형태
        image = image["composite"]
    img = Image.fromarray(np.asarray(image)).convert("L").resize((28, 28))
    x = torch.tensor(np.asarray(img), dtype=torch.float32) / 255.0
    if x.mean() > 0.5:                                     # 흰 바탕에 검은 글씨면 반전 (MNIST 는 검은 바탕)
        x = 1.0 - x
    with torch.no_grad():
        probs = torch.softmax(model(x[None, None]), dim=1)[0]
    return {str(i): float(p) for i, p in enumerate(probs)}


demo = gr.Interface(
    fn=predict,
    inputs=gr.Sketchpad(label="숫자를 그려 보세요", image_mode="L"),
    outputs=gr.Label(num_top_classes=3, label="예측"),
    title="손글씨 숫자 분류기 (12·13장 MLP)",
    description="13장에서 학습한 모델(시험 정확도 94.7%)입니다. 그림판에 0~9를 그리면 확률을 보여 줍니다.",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch()                                          # share=True 를 주면 1주일짜리 공개 링크가 생긴다

In English: 13장의 모델 정의를 그대로 = the model definition of Chapter 13, as it is; 흰 바탕에 검은 글씨면 반전 (MNIST 는 검은 바탕) = invert if it is black writing on a white background (MNIST has a black background); 숫자를 그려 보세요 = "Draw a digit"; 예측 = prediction; 손글씨 숫자 분류기 (12·13장 MLP) = handwritten digit classifier (the MLP of Chapters 12 and 13); the description says the model was trained in Chapter 13 (test accuracy 94.7%) and shows probabilities when you draw 0 to 9 on the sketchpad; share=True 를 주면 1주일짜리 공개 링크가 생긴다 = with share=True, a public link valid for 1 week is created.

[Basic] There are three parts.

  1. Loading the model: this is the load_model of the Chapter 13 infer.py as it is. It restores the model from the config.json and model_best.pt in the results folder.
  2. The predict function: it turns the picture the screen hands over into a [1, 1, 28, 28] tensor that the model can take (the preprocessing of Chapter 15, by hand), and returns 10 probabilities as a dictionary. The sketchpad has black writing on a white background while MNIST has white writing on a black background, so the line that inverts it is the key. Without this one line, accuracy collapses (check question 1).
  3. gr.Interface: one function (fn), one input widget (Sketchpad), one output widget (Label). When you call launch(), a local server starts and you open it in the browser at http://127.0.0.1:7860.

[Basic] When you run it, the address is printed in the terminal, and when you draw a digit on the sketchpad in the browser, probability bars for the top 3 classes appear on the right.

[Intermediate] The form of the value that Sketchpad hands over differed from one Gradio version to another (an array → {"composite": array}). That is why predict accepts both, and it is a typical spot for what Chapter 6 called "AI gives you code for an old version." This book's verification environment is gradio 6.26.0.

26.2 What happens behind the screen

Figure 26-1. The screen is a shell around the predict function. The model is the very file saved in Chapter 13.

[Basic] All Gradio does is wrap a Python function in web requests. If you tell it, as widget types, what the function takes and what it returns, it builds the screen for you. So the model and the screen are separated. If you want to switch to the LeNet of Chapter 16, you only fix load_model, and the screen code stays as it is. The "flow and parts" of Chapter 14 applies here too.

26.3 Testing without a browser

[Basic] A program with a screen is also verified with the four steps of Chapter 6. In particular, "Test it" can be done without opening a browser. test_app.py:

# 26장 검증: 브라우저 없이 app.py 의 predict 함수와 서버 기동을 확인한다 (6장의 '시험한다').
import os
import sys
import numpy as np
import torch
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
import app

# 1) predict 가 시험 이미지에 대해 13장 infer.py 와 같은 답을 내는가
test_set = datasets.MNIST(os.environ.get("JUCOS_DATA", "./data"), train=False, download=True)
for i in (0, 1, 2, 8):
    img, label = test_set[i]                               # PIL, 검은 바탕 흰 글씨
    arr = 255 - np.asarray(img)                            # 그림판처럼 흰 바탕 검은 글씨로 뒤집어 넣는다
    probs = app.predict(arr)
    pred = max(probs, key=probs.get)
    print(f"시험 이미지 {i}: 정답 {label}  예측 {pred}  확신 {probs[pred]:.3f}")

# 2) 서버가 뜨고 HTTP 로 응답하는가
app.demo.launch(prevent_thread_lock=True, quiet=True)
import urllib.request
with urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:7860/", timeout=10) as r:
    html = r.read().decode("utf-8", "ignore")
print("서버 응답:", r.status, "| 제목 포함:", "손글씨" in html or "gradio" in html.lower())
app.demo.close()
print("서버 종료")

시험 이미지 0: 정답 7  예측 7  확신 0.996
시험 이미지 1: 정답 2  예측 2  확신 0.984
시험 이미지 2: 정답 1  예측 1  확신 0.979
시험 이미지 8: 정답 5  예측 6  확신 0.976
서버 응답: 200 | 제목 포함: True
Closing server running on port: 7860
서버 종료

In English: 시험 이미지 … = test image …; 정답 = correct label; 예측 = prediction; 확신 = confidence; 서버 응답 = server response; 제목 포함 = title included; 서버 종료 = server closed.

[Basic] Two things were confirmed. ① predict gives the same answers as the Chapter 13 infer.py. It gets numbers 0, 1, and 2 right, and, as in Chapter 13, gets number 8 wrong, calling a 5 a 6 (confidence 0.976). That is evidence that the preprocessing and inversion were done correctly. The confidence values differ a little from the output in the main text of Chapter 13 (0.994, 0.966, 0.978), but you must not pin this on a single cause. That output in the Chapter 13 text is from the lr005 model and what the app here reads is the lr01 model, so the checkpoints themselves differ, and on top of that the pixels changed slightly through resize. To separate the two, you would have to measure again with the same checkpoint. ② The server starts and responds with HTTP 200.

[Basic] The reason import app alone is enough for the test is that app.py puts demo.launch() inside if __name__ == "__main__": (Chapter 4). On import, the model and the screen object are created but the server does not start, and the test code starts and closes it when it wants. Writing code with a screen so that it can still be tested is the lesson of this section.

[Intermediate] prevent_thread_lock=True is an option that starts the server in the background and lets the code go on to the next line. In real app development you would test at the API level with gradio_client or TestClient, but within the scope of this book the two checks above are enough.

26.4 Public links: Section 6.5 again

[Basic] With demo.launch(share=True), Gradio makes a temporary public address for you (https://….gradio.live, 1 week). It connects the server running on your computer through an internet tunnel, so the input of anyone who receives that link comes into your computer, and your computer's response goes out. For a handwritten digit classifier that is no problem, but if the model takes documents, the principle of Section 6.5 applies as it is. A model that handles case materials is not opened through a public link.

[Intermediate] If you need it public all the time, you can upload app.py and the model file to hosting such as Hugging Face Spaces. This book does not. Chapter 9 of the Hugging Face LLM Course in Appendix D covers that procedure.

26.5 Closing Part 2

[Basic] The lr01 model you saved in Chapter 13 (test accuracy 94.73%) is now behind the screen. It is a descendant of the pipeline that reached 94.6% in 10 seconds in Chapter 12. In between, you changed the data (15), changed the model (16 to 22), changed the objective (23), turned a number into a claim (24), and borrowed someone else's model (25). Here you can see why the start of every chapter said "which of the four ingredients it changes." Every chapter was a variation on Chapter 12.

[Basic] Go back to Chapter 8 and read mnist_main.py again. How many of the lines you did not understand in the table of Section 8.6 remain is your report card for Part 2. And you may now lift the rule of Section 6.7 (do not use AI for Follow along). You now have the eyes to review the code AI gives you.

Working with an AI assistant

[Basic] AI writes Gradio code well, but Gradio is a library whose versions change often, so AI's code often does not run on the current version. Put the version number in your request.

Based on gradio 6.26, write an Interface that takes Sketchpad input, converts it to 28×28 grayscale, feeds it to a PyTorch model, and shows the probabilities with Label. First tell me the form of the value that Sketchpad hands over.

[Basic] Verify it the test_app.py way of Section 26.3. Put a few test images directly into predict and see whether the same answers as Chapter 13 come out. Drawing on the screen comes after that.

Check questions

[Basic]

  1. What happens if you delete the inversion line in predict and run test_app.py?
  2. Connect a model trained with the LeNet of Chapter 16 (the one registered in the Chapter 14 package) to this screen. Which function alone changes?
  3. On the screen, draw each of the ten digits three times and count the share it gets right. How does it compare with the test accuracy of 94.7%? Why would it differ (the difference in distribution between sketchpad writing and MNIST writing)?

[Intermediate]

  1. Change it to show all 10 probabilities with gr.BarPlot or as text instead of gr.Label.
  2. Put the provision classifier of Chapter 19 (bag of words) on a screen with gr.Textbox input. A page that guesses which statute a provision is from when you paste it in.

[Advanced]

  1. Connect the LoRA model of Chapter 25 to the same screen, and make a gr.Blocks screen that shows its results side by side with the Chapter 19 model.

Appendix B

Appendix B. Glossary

In alphabetical order by the English term. The Korean term in parentheses is the one used in the Korean edition, in the practice notebooks, and in the output printed in this book. The number at the end of each entry is the chapter where the term first properly appears. Definitions are cut down to one or two sentences to fit the context of this book.

A

  • activation function (활성화 함수): A nonlinear function between layers. ReLU, GELU, sigmoid, tanh. [11]
  • attention (어텐션): A computation that turns the scores of a query against keys into weights with softmax and mixes the values. "Where to look and how much." [21]
  • autoregressive (자기회귀): A way of generating in sequence by feeding the previous output in as the next input. Generation in a language model. [21, 23]

B

  • backpropagation (역전파): The algorithm that applies the chain rule backward from the loss to get the gradient of every weight. [10, Appendix E]
  • bag of words (단어 주머니): A text representation that throws away token order and uses only the mean (or frequency) of the embeddings. In this book, the strong performer on small data. [19]
  • batch (배치): The bundle of data put in together in one step. The first dimension of a tensor. [10, 11]
  • batch normalization (배치 정규화, BatchNorm): A layer that sets the output of a layer to mean 0 and variance 1 within the batch. It stabilizes the training of deep networks. [17]
  • breakpoint (중단점): The line where the debugger stops. F9. [5]

C

  • causal mask (인과 마스크): In a language model, a mask that keeps each position from seeing what comes after it. [23]
  • channel (채널): The second dimension of an image tensor. 1 for grayscale, 3 for color, and the number of filters after a convolution. [11, 16]
  • class (클래스): A template that defines data and behavior as one bundle. An object is a value made from that template. In classification problems it is also used to mean "a kind of correct answer." [4]
  • commit (커밋): In Git, a snapshot of the files at some point in time. [7]
  • confidence interval (신뢰구간): The range over which a value swings when measured several times with different seeds and the like. This book calculates it as mean ± 1.96·SE and gives the t-distribution correction alongside. [24]
  • convolution (합성곱): A computation that slides a small kernel over an image, multiplying and adding. It finds features regardless of position. [16]
  • cross-entropy (교차 엔트로피): The standard loss for classification. The −log of the probability of the correct class. [12]

D

  • DataLoader (데이터로더): A device that bundles the items of a dataset into batches, shuffles them, and hands them out one at a time. [15]
  • Dataset (데이터셋): A class with __len__ and __getitem__. It answers "how many are there" and "what is the i-th one." [4, 15]
  • debugger (디버거): A tool that stops a program at the line you want and lets you step one line at a time while looking at variables. The VS Code debugger, pdb. [5]
  • Dropout (드롭아웃): A layer that turns off some neurons at random during training to reduce overfitting. Neurons are not turned off during evaluation, so model.eval() is needed. [17]

E

  • embedding (임베딩): A trained lookup table that turns token numbers into real-valued vectors. nn.Embedding. [19]
  • epoch (에포크): One full pass over all the training data. [10]
  • exception (예외): An error that occurs during a run. It is caught with try/except. [4]

F

  • fine-tuning (미세조정): Starting from pretrained weights and training further (some or all of them) on your own data. [18, 25]

G

  • gate (게이트): In LSTM and GRU, a device that decides with a value from 0 to 1 "how much to forget, put in, and let out." It is made with a sigmoid. [20]
  • gradient (기울기): The vector that collects how much the loss changes when each weight is changed a little. loss.backward() computes it and puts it in .grad. [11]
  • gradient descent (경사 하강): A training method that moves the weights a little at a time in the direction in which the loss goes down (the opposite of the gradient). [10]

H

  • hallucination (환각): The phenomenon of AI stating something that does not exist as if it did. By the principle of next-token prediction, there is no source. [6, 23]
  • hyperparameter (하이퍼파라미터): A number that a person chooses. Learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, layer size. [12, 13]

I

  • inference (추론): Predicting on new input with a trained model. No gradients are needed. [13]
  • inheritance (상속): A class taking over the attributes and methods of another class. class MLP(nn.Module). [4]
  • interpreter (인터프리터): The Python executable. In VS Code, the choice of which environment's Python to use. [2]

K

  • kernel (커널; filter, 필터): The small window of weights slid over an image in a convolution. [16]

L

  • layer (층): A unit computation that makes up a model. nn.Linear, nn.Conv2d, nn.LSTM. [11]
  • learning rate (학습률): The size of one step of gradient descent. Too large and it diverges, too small and it is slow. [10, 12]
  • logic outline (논리 흐름도): The frame written first as comments before typing code. The same as request form 1 in Chapter 6. [6, 12]
  • logit (로짓): The score before it goes through softmax. The value the last layer of a model puts out. [12]
  • loss (손실): A single number that measures how wrong the prediction is. Training reduces it. [10]

M

  • mask (마스크): A true/false tensor that marks the positions not to be looked at (padding, future tokens) in attention or in a mean. [19, 22, 23]
  • module (모듈): One Python file. It is brought in with import filename. nn.Module is the parent class of layers and models in PyTorch. [4, 11]
  • multi-head attention (멀티헤드 어텐션): Splitting the dimension into several heads, computing attention separately in each, and joining the results. The effect is having several points of view. [22]

N

  • nonlinearity (비선형): An activation function such as ReLU, GELU, or tanh. Without it, stacked layers are the same as a single linear layer. [11, Appendix E]
  • normalization (정규화): Setting the mean and variance of values. Input normalization (Normalize), batch normalization, layer normalization (LayerNorm). [15, 17, 22]

O

  • optimizer (옵티마이저): An object that takes the gradients and decides how to update the weights. SGD, Adam, AdamW. [10, 12]
  • overfitting (과적합): The state of getting the training data right but new data wrong. When the test loss starts to rise, that is the signal. [10, 13, 15]

P

  • padding (패딩): An empty token (<pad>) filled in to make lengths equal, or the zeros wrapped around the edge in a convolution. [16, 19]
  • parameter (파라미터): A weight that is trained. model.parameters(). [11]
  • perplexity (퍼플렉시티): The exponential of a language model's loss. "The same uncertainty as picking one out of that many." [23]
  • pooling (풀링): A layer that reduces size by keeping only the maximum (or the mean) within a window. [16]
  • positional encoding (위치 인코딩): Adding to the vectors the token order that attention does not know. [22]
  • pretraining (사전학습): Training done beforehand on large data. Bringing those weights over is transfer learning. [18, 25]

R

  • residual connection (잔차 연결): A shortcut that adds the input of a block to its output. It makes deep networks trainable. [17, 22]

S

  • seed (씨앗): The starting value for random number generation. Fixing it reproduces the same result. [4, 11, 24]
  • self-supervised learning (자기지도 학습): Training that uses the data itself (for example, the next character) as the correct answer, without labels attached by people. [18, 23]
  • softmax (소프트맥스): A function that turns several scores into probabilities that sum to 1. [12, 21]
  • stage (스테이지, Git): The waiting area where you pick the changes to go into the next commit. git add. [7]
  • subword (서브워드): A token made by splitting a word into pieces that occur often. The tokenization method of modern language models. [19, 25]

T

  • tensor (텐서): A multidimensional array of numbers. It has a shape, a data type (dtype), and a device. [11]
  • test set (시험 데이터): Data not used in training and used to measure performance. [10]
  • token (토큰): A piece of text that the model treats as one unit. A character, a word, a subword. [19]
  • transfer learning (전이학습): Taking a model trained on other data and using it for your own problem. [18]
  • Transformer (트랜스포머): A model made by stacking self-attention blocks. The basic structure of modern language models. [22]

V

  • virtual environment (가상환경): A folder that keeps one copy of Python and a set of packages separately for each project. Created with conda create and turned on with conda activate. [2]
  • vocabulary (어휘 사전): The table that maps tokens ↔ numbers. itos (a list), stoi (a dictionary). [19]

W

  • weight (가중치): A number inside the model. Training changes only these numbers. Used with the same meaning as parameter. [10]

Abbreviations

  • CNN: Convolutional Neural Network. [16]
  • GPU: A processing unit specialized for parallel computation. Borrowed for free on Colab. [2]
  • GRU / LSTM: Recurrent neural networks with gates. [20]
  • LoRA: A fine-tuning technique that freezes the weights of a large model and trains only small low-rank matrices (Low-Rank Adaptation). [25]
  • MLP: Multilayer perceptron. The simplest neural network, made by stacking linear layers and nonlinearities in alternation. [11]
  • RNN: Recurrent Neural Network. [20]
  • SGD: Stochastic Gradient Descent. Gradient descent by the batch. [12]
  • shape: The shape of a tensor. The size of each dimension, as in [batch, channel, height, width]. The value you look at most often in Part 2. [11]

Appendix C

Appendix C. Troubleshooting installation

This appendix regroups "Where people get stuck" from Chapter 2 by operating system and by symptom. It assumes a personal computer (Windows 11, macOS). Each item runs in the order symptom → what to check → fix. For a problem not listed here, give AI the whole error message as in Chapter 6, but run commands that change the system only after you understand what they mean.

C.1 Common to all: which Python is running

[Basic] Half of all installation problems come from "there are several Pythons." Checking the current state with the following three commands is the first step of every diagnosis.

conda env list          # 환경 목록, * 가 현재
where python            # Windows: 지금 python 이 어느 파일인가 (Mac: which python)
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"   # 파이썬 스스로가 말하는 위치

In English: 환경 목록, * 가 현재 = list of environments, the * is the current one; Windows: 지금 python 이 어느 파일인가 (Mac: which python) = Windows: which file python is right now (Mac: which python); 파이썬 스스로가 말하는 위치 = the location Python itself reports.

All three results must point to anaconda3/envs/jucos. If even one differs, that difference is the cause of the problem.

C.2 Windows

Symptom What to check Fix

C.7 The last resort: recreating the environment

[Basic] If you cannot find the cause and have spent more than 30 minutes, it is faster to delete the environment and create it again. This is the reason virtual environments exist.

conda deactivate
conda remove -n jucos --all
conda create -n jucos python=3.13
conda activate jucos
pip install torch torchvision
python check_env.py       # 2장의 확인 스크립트

In English: 2장의 확인 스크립트 = the check script from Chapter 2.

It takes 5 minutes. Your code and data are outside the environment, so they do not disappear.

D.4 More broadly

[Basic] This book aimed at "lawyers who can read and fix code." After that, the directions split.

  • You want to build models better → fast.ai and d2l in Section D.1.
  • You want to actually use language models → the Hugging Face LLM Course, and the API documentation of each AI service.
  • You want to know the principles in mathematics → the whole of Zero to Hero, the math chapters of d2l, and Appendix E.
  • You want to research the problems of AI and law → that is outside the scope of this book. Still, the three things checked in code in Chapter 23 (plausible ≠ correct, no source, probabilistic output) become the technical starting point for that research.

Appendix E

Appendix E. The minimum of mathematics: just as much as you need

The default marker for this appendix is [Advanced]. You do not need this appendix to follow the main text. When you become curious about the "why" in the main text, look up only that item and read it. Each section first states which chapter of the main text uses it.

E.1 Vectors and matrices: arithmetic on bundles of numbers (Chapter 11)

[Intermediate] A vector is numbers laid out in a row. One token embedding in Chapter 19 is a vector. Vectors are added position by position (a + b), and stretched or shrunk by multiplying by a number (2a). The dot product is a single number obtained by multiplying position by position and adding everything up.

a·b=∑iaibi

The dot product measures "how much two vectors point the same way." It is large if they point the same way, 0 if they are at right angles, and negative if they are opposite. The scores of the attention in Chapter 21 are exactly this dot product, and the sentence similarity (cosine similarity) of Chapter 25 is the dot product divided by the lengths of the two vectors.

[Intermediate] A matrix is a table of vectors stacked in several rows. The product Wx of a matrix and a vector is "the vector that collects the dot products of each row of W with x," and that is all that nn.Linear in Chapter 11 does.

y=Wx+b,W∈ℝm×n,x∈ℝn,y∈ℝm

n inputs turn into m outputs, and the shape of W being [m,n] is the reason fc1.weight was [128, 784] in Chapter 11. If you process B items of a batch at once, x becomes a [B,n] matrix and the result is [B,m]. The rule in Chapter 11 that "the last dimension of the input must equal the input size of the layer" comes from the definition of matrix multiplication ([B,n]×[n,m]).

[Advanced] The convolution of Chapter 16 is also a matrix multiplication. If you write out the sliding of the window with multiplying and adding, it becomes a product with a very large matrix that is mostly 0, and the nonzero values of that matrix are repetitions of the filter values. "The same filter at every position" is the same as "many elements of the matrix share the same value," and that is why there are few parameters.

E.2 Why a nonlinearity is needed (Chapter 11)

[Intermediate] If you stack two linear layers, W2(W1x)=(W2W1)x, so it is the same as one linear layer. Stack a hundred layers and in the end it is one matrix. So a function that is not linear is inserted in between. ReLU, max(0,x), is the simplest, and with this alone it becomes possible to approximate any function by combining "bent straight lines" (the universal approximation theorem). This is why, if you remove torch.relu in Chapter 11, the expressive power of the model collapses to that of a single linear map, even though the number of parameters and the output shape are the same.

[Advanced] The kinds of activation function (ReLU, GELU, tanh, sigmoid) differ in the shape of the bend. sigmoid squeezes values to 0 to 1 and is used for the gates ("how much") of Chapter 20, tanh squeezes to −1 to 1 and is used for the state of an RNN, and GELU is a smooth version of ReLU used in the Transformer of Chapter 22.

E.3 Derivatives and gradients: "how much does it change if you change it a little" (Chapters 10 and 11)

[Intermediate] For a function L(w), the rate at which L changes when you change w by a very small amount is the derivative dLdw. In the example of Chapter 11, if L=(2w−7)2, then

dLdw=2(2w−7)·2=4(2w−7)

At w=1, it is −20. That means "if you increase w, L decreases steeply," and that is why w was moved in the direction of increasing it. When there are several weights, the vector collecting the derivatives with respect to each is the gradient ∇L, and gradient descent is

w←w−η∇L(w)

η is the learning rate. The reason that, in the experiment table of Chapter 12, training diverges when η is too large and is slow when it is too small lies in this one formula.

[Intermediate] The chain rule is the rule for differentiating when functions are nested. If L=f(g(w)), then

dLdw=dfdg·dgdw

In the example above, g=2w−7 and f=g2, so dfdg=2g and dgdw=2, and multiplied, 4g=4(2w−7). A neural network is a function made of nested layers, so the derivative from the loss to the first layer means multiplying the derivatives of each layer from the back to the front, and that is backpropagation. loss.backward() does this multiplication automatically.

[Advanced] When the multiplications in backpropagation pile up dozens of times, the values run off to 0 or infinity (vanishing and exploding gradients). The residual connection y=F(x)+x of Chapter 17 has dydx=F′(x)+1, so a "+1" is inserted into the chain of multiplications and the gradient flows at least as it is, and the ct=f⊙ct−1+i⊙g of the LSTM in Chapter 20 has the same structure. That is why the "one line of addition" in Chapters 17 and 20 is mathematically the same.

E.4 Softmax and cross-entropy (Chapter 12)

[Intermediate] Turning the scores z1,…,zK into probabilities is softmax.

pk=ezk∑jezj

All are positive and sum to 1, and the larger the score, the larger the probability. When the correct label is y, the loss is the negative log of the probability of the correct label.

L=−logpy

If py=1 it is 0, and if py=0.1 it is log10≈2.30. The loss before training was near 2.30 in Chapter 12 because the model was in a state of giving a probability of 0.1 to each of 10 classes, and the perplexity eL of Chapter 23 rewrites this loss as "uncertainty equal to guessing one out of so many" (a loss of 2.9 means a perplexity of 18, that is, guessing one out of 18).

[Advanced] If you differentiate this loss together with softmax, you get the surprisingly simple formula ∂L∂zk=pk−1[k=y]. "The predicted probability minus the correct label (1 or 0)" is the gradient of the score. The reason CrossEntropyLoss computes softmax and the log together is that this formula is numerically more stable than computing them separately.

E.5 Mean, variance, normalization (Chapters 15 and 17)

[Intermediate] If you find the mean μ of the values and the standard deviation σ, the degree of spread, and change each value to (x−μ)/σ, you get mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The Normalize of Chapter 15 does this once over the whole dataset, the BatchNorm of Chapter 17 within a batch at each layer, and the LayerNorm of Chapter 22 within one vector. The purpose is one. To keep the size of the values steady so that, with one learning rate, every layer moves with a similar stride.

E.6 Samples, uncertainty, confidence intervals (Chapter 24)

[Intermediate] The "accuracy 0.925" in the experiment table of Chapter 12 is a value measured once with one seed. Change the seed and measure five times, and the value wobbles, and only by measuring that wobble can you say "A is better than B." If the mean accuracy over n seeds is a¯ and the standard deviation is s, a rough 95% confidence interval is

a¯±1.96sn

The code of Chapter 24 calculates this. At n=5 the normal approximation is rough, so it is correct in practice to use the t-distribution (for n=5, 2.78 instead of 1.96), and the main text of Chapter 24 says so. The standard of this book is not to say "there is a difference" when the intervals of two settings overlap.

[Intermediate] There is also uncertainty in the test accuracy itself. If you measured accuracy a on N test items, its standard error is roughly a(1−a)/N. With the 150 test images of Chapter 15, if a=0.95 it is about 0.018, which as a 95% confidence interval is ±3.5 percentage points. One digit of accuracy on a small test set is noise.

E.7 What this book did not use

[Basic] The following appear often in deep learning textbooks but were left out because the practice in this book does not need them. If you come to need them, look in the materials of Appendix D. Eigenvalue and singular value decomposition, the detailed theory of probability distributions (Bayes, maximum likelihood), optimization theory (convergence proofs), information theory (the general definition of entropy). The "low-rank" of LoRA in Chapter 25 means approximating a matrix by the product of two small matrices; it is explained with the matrix formulas in the main text of Chapter 25 and not covered here.

About this book

These are personal study materials and do not represent the views or work of any institution the editor belongs to. Not legal advice.

It was written so that lawyers with no coding experience can read and follow it alone, starting from the development environment and going as far as implementing deep learning models themselves. Every case in the examples is invented. So that they do not overlap with real cases, the year in every case number is 2099 and the court is called the "Fictional District Court" (가상지방법원 in the code). The data for the text practice is statutory provisions, which are not protected under Article 7 of the Copyright Act (저작권법) of Korea.

How it was made

The editor made this book together with generative AI (Claude Code). The editor decided the direction and the content, and the AI wrote the first draft. Because the text was produced with generative AI, errors may remain even after verification.

  • The code printed in the book was actually run and its output copied over (a few cells that run only on Colab could not be run and are marked "not run" at the end of their chapters). The environment is Windows 11, a CPU with no GPU, Python 3.13, and PyTorch 2.14, and the date of the run is September 6, 2026 (training times were measured again on September 13). The output of the stage 1 notebooks is from a rerun on November 17, 2026.
  • An AI model from another company (OpenAI Codex) reviewed the manuscript. In September 2026 it looked once at whether the manuscript was internally consistent. In November 2026, before edition 1.0 was released, it verified the manuscript and the practice repository without knowing how the work had been done (the whole once, then a short round on the places that had been changed). It compared external facts such as tool prices and installation commands against official documentation, compared the 59 notebooks against the practice code by machine, and reran some of the notebooks from the beginning to compare the figures. Each point it raised was checked again against the original source before being adopted.
  • Some things could not be confirmed. The on-screen operations in VS Code, Colab, and the sketchpad were not run directly, and this is marked in the "Sources and verification record" at the end of each chapter. The Colab paid price list (Section 2.7.2) is as of the pricing page on September 6, 2026, and could not be checked again after that.
  • This English edition was translated from Korean edition 1.0.1 with the same generative AI. The code listings, commands, and program output were carried over unchanged, so comments and output labels in them are in Korean. The same model from another company compared the English text with the Korean edition, again without knowing how the translation had been done.
